question: Why prefer semantic HTML elements like nav, main, article and section over generic divs?
concise: Semantic elements communicate document structure and meaning to browsers, assistive technology and search engines, which divs cannot do on their own.
strong: Semantic HTML gives free accessibility and SEO benefits because screen readers use landmark elements like nav, main and header to let users jump straight to a section instead of reading the whole page linearly. Search engines also weight content inside article or heading tags more meaningfully when ranking pages. On a dashboard app, using main for the primary content area and nav for the sidebar means keyboard and screen reader users can skip navigation instantly with landmark shortcuts. It also makes the codebase more readable for other engineers because the markup itself documents intent. The trade-off is small: semantic tags still need the same CSS as divs, so there is no styling cost to using them. I try to reserve div and span purely for styling hooks that have no semantic meaning.
code:
<header>
  <nav aria-label="Primary">...</nav>
</header>
<main>
  <article>...</article>
</main>
weak: A weak answer just says 'it looks cleaner' or 'it is best practice' without explaining the concrete accessibility or SEO mechanism, which signals the candidate memorized the term without understanding why it matters.
followUp: How would you decide between using a section and an article for a given block of content?

question: How does native HTML form validation work, and when would you still need custom JavaScript validation?
concise: The Constraint Validation API (required, pattern, min/max, type=email) gives free browser-level validation and messages, but you still need JS validation for cross-field rules, async checks like uniqueness, and consistent styling across browsers.
strong: Native validation attributes like required, minlength, pattern and type give you validation for free with zero JavaScript, and the browser exposes a checkValidity method and a ValidityState object so you can inspect exactly which constraint failed. In a signup form I would still layer JavaScript validation on top because native messages are not styleable consistently across browsers, and because rules like 'password must match confirm password' or 'email is already registered' need custom logic and an API call. A good pattern is to use noValidate on the form, then run your own validation on submit and on blur, while still keeping the semantic input types and required attributes for accessibility and so mobile keyboards show the right layout. I also make sure error messages are tied to the input with aria-describedby so screen reader users hear the specific error, not just a red border.
weak: A weak answer says 'just use JavaScript to validate everything' and ignores that native attributes still provide real accessibility and mobile UX value even when you add custom logic on top.
followUp: How would you announce a validation error to a screen reader user without moving keyboard focus unexpectedly?

question: When is it appropriate to add ARIA attributes, and what is the 'first rule of ARIA'?
concise: The first rule of ARIA is: if a native HTML element or attribute already has the semantics and behavior you need, use it instead of adding ARIA to a div or span.
strong: ARIA exists to patch gaps where native HTML cannot express a role, state or relationship, such as a custom combobox, a tab panel, or a live region that announces async updates. The first rule of ARIA is to prefer native elements first, because a button element already has keyboard support, focus handling and the correct role built in, while a div with role='button' requires you to manually add tabindex, keydown handlers for Enter and Space, and manage focus styles yourself, and it is easy to get one of those wrong. In a dashboard I would use aria-live='polite' on a region that shows 'data refreshed' toasts so screen reader users are notified without focus jumping there. Overusing ARIA, like adding role='button' to elements that already behave like buttons, or adding redundant roles, can actually make the experience worse because it can override or conflict with the browser's native accessibility tree. The rule of thumb is: ARIA is a last resort, not a first choice.
weak: A weak answer treats ARIA as something you sprinkle everywhere to 'be accessible' without understanding that misused ARIA (wrong roles, redundant labels) can actively harm screen reader users.
followUp: How would you make a custom dropdown component fully keyboard accessible without using a native select?

question: What matters for SEO on a modern JavaScript-heavy web app, and how does rendering strategy affect it?
concise: Crawlers need meaningful HTML in the initial response (title, meta description, headings, structured data) plus fast load times; a pure client-side rendered SPA can hurt SEO because crawlers may not wait for JS to render content, which is why SSR or static generation is often preferred for public pages.
strong: Good SEO starts with the HTML that is returned before JavaScript runs: a correct title tag, meta description, canonical URL, Open Graph tags, and semantic heading hierarchy. Search engines like Google can execute JavaScript but do it on a delayed second wave of crawling, so a fully client-side rendered marketing or blog page risks being indexed late or incompletely, especially for other crawlers like social media link previewers that do not execute JS at all. This is why frameworks like Next.js offer server-side rendering or static generation for public-facing pages, so the crawler gets fully-formed HTML immediately. Structured data using JSON-LD schema markup also helps search engines understand the content type, like a product page or an article, and can produce rich snippets in search results. Core Web Vitals also factor into ranking, so a slow LCP or high CLS can hurt SEO even if the content itself is well marked up. For an internal dashboard behind auth, none of this matters since it is not meant to be indexed, and I would add a noindex meta tag instead.
weak: A weak answer says 'just add meta tags' without mentioning that rendering strategy and crawlability of JS-rendered content is often the bigger lever, or without distinguishing public marketing pages from authenticated app pages.
followUp: How would you generate a sitemap and robots.txt for a Next.js app with both public and authenticated routes?

question: How do srcset and sizes help with responsive images, and how is that different from using the picture element?
concise: srcset with sizes lets the browser pick the best resolution of the same image for the viewport and device pixel ratio, while picture lets you serve entirely different image sources or formats (like art-directed crops or WebP with a fallback) based on media conditions.
strong: srcset gives the browser a list of the same image at different resolutions plus a sizes hint describing how wide the image will render at different breakpoints, and the browser then picks the smallest sufficient file, which saves bandwidth on mobile. picture is for a different problem: when you need a different image entirely, not just a different resolution, for example showing a cropped square image on mobile versus a wide banner on desktop (art direction), or serving a modern format like WebP or AVIF with a JPEG fallback for older browsers. In practice on a product listing page I would use srcset/sizes for the product thumbnails since they are the same image at different sizes, and picture with source elements when the design team wants a different crop on mobile. Both approaches let the browser, not JavaScript, decide which asset to fetch, which is faster and avoids layout shift if width and height attributes are also set.
weak: A weak answer treats srcset and picture as interchangeable ways to 'make images responsive' without explaining that one is resolution switching and the other is art direction or format switching.
followUp: How would you prevent layout shift (CLS) caused by images loading after the page renders?

question: What is the difference between async and defer on a script tag, and when would you use neither?
concise: async downloads the script in parallel with HTML parsing and executes it as soon as it's ready, potentially out of order with other scripts, while defer also downloads in parallel but executes only after HTML parsing finishes and in document order; you'd use neither (a plain blocking script) only for tiny inline critical scripts that must run before anything else, like a theme flash-prevention snippet.
strong: Without async or defer, the browser stops parsing HTML entirely to fetch and execute the script, which blocks rendering and is why blocking scripts in the head hurt page load. defer is generally the safest default for app scripts because it preserves execution order and guarantees the DOM is fully parsed before the script runs, similar to putting a script at the end of body but without blocking the parser during download. async is better for independent scripts with no dependencies on the DOM or on each other, like analytics tags, since it runs as soon as it downloads which could be before or after parsing finishes. Module scripts (type='module') are deferred by default. I would only use a plain blocking script for something tiny and critical that must execute before first paint, like an inline snippet that reads a stored theme preference and sets a class on html before any CSS renders, to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.
weak: A weak answer says 'defer is just async but better' or cannot explain the concrete difference in execution timing and ordering guarantees between the two.
followUp: How does type='module' affect script loading and execution order by default?

question: Compare localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies and IndexedDB for storing frontend data.
concise: localStorage persists across tabs and browser restarts with no expiry and ~5-10MB limit; sessionStorage is scoped to a single tab and cleared on tab close; cookies are small (~4KB), sent automatically with every HTTP request, and needed for server-readable auth tokens; IndexedDB is for larger structured or binary data with async access and indexing.
strong: I choose based on who needs to read the data and how much of it there is. Cookies are the only option that the server can read automatically on every request, so they are the right place for session or auth tokens, especially with HttpOnly and Secure and SameSite flags so JavaScript cannot read them and they resist CSRF and XSS theft. localStorage is convenient for small client-only preferences like a saved theme or a collapsed sidebar state, but I never store sensitive tokens there because any injected script (XSS) can read it directly. sessionStorage is useful for per-tab state like a multi-step form draft that should not leak into a second tab. IndexedDB is what I reach for when storing larger datasets, like offline-cached dashboard data or file blobs, because it is asynchronous, does not block the main thread, and can hold far more than the roughly 5 to 10 megabyte limit of the Web Storage APIs. All client storage is visible to the user and to any script running on the page, so nothing genuinely secret should live in any of them.
weak: A weak answer says 'store the JWT in localStorage, it's simple' without acknowledging the well-known XSS token-theft risk, which is a common real interview red flag.
followUp: If you can't use HttpOnly cookies because the API is on a different domain, how would you mitigate XSS risk to a token stored in memory or localStorage?

question: What is event delegation in the DOM and why is it useful for large lists?
concise: Event delegation attaches a single listener to a common ancestor and uses event bubbling plus event.target to handle events for many child elements, instead of attaching a listener to each child individually, which saves memory and automatically works for dynamically added elements.
strong: Instead of adding a click listener to every row in a table with a thousand rows, I attach one listener to the table body and inspect event.target (or use closest) to figure out which row or button was actually clicked. This is far cheaper in memory since there's one listener instead of a thousand, and it automatically handles rows added later, like after a paginated fetch, without needing to re-bind listeners. The trade-off is that the delegation logic needs to correctly identify the actual target, especially when the click lands on a nested icon inside a button, which is why closest('button') is safer than checking event.target directly. In React this pattern is largely handled for you since React attaches a single root-level listener and does its own synthetic event dispatch, but understanding the underlying DOM mechanism still matters when working with non-React widgets or performance-critical vanilla JS code.
weak: A weak answer describes delegation correctly but misses the practical reason to use closest() instead of a strict equality check on event.target, which breaks when the click lands on a child element like an icon.
followUp: How does React's synthetic event system relate to native event delegation under the hood?

question: How would you build an accessible modal dialog, including focus management?
concise: An accessible modal needs role='dialog' with aria-modal='true', a label, focus moved into the modal when it opens, focus trapped inside it while open (Tab cycles only through its content), and focus returned to the triggering element when it closes, plus Escape to close.
strong: When a modal opens I move focus to the first focusable element inside it, or to the modal container itself if there is no obvious first field, and I trap Tab and Shift+Tab so focus cycles only among elements inside the modal instead of escaping to the page behind it. I mark the container with role='dialog', aria-modal='true', and an aria-labelledby pointing at the modal's heading so screen readers announce its purpose. Escape should close it, and clicking the backdrop is a nice-to-have but should not be the only way to close it since some users navigate by keyboard only. When the modal closes, focus must return to whatever element triggered it, like the button that opened it, otherwise keyboard and screen reader users lose their place in the page entirely. In React I usually reach for a maintained library like Radix or Headless UI for this because focus trapping has many edge cases (like inert background content, nested modals, or elements added dynamically inside the dialog) that are easy to get subtly wrong if built from scratch.
weak: A weak answer only mentions 'add a close button and an overlay' and misses focus trapping and focus restoration entirely, which are the parts screen reader and keyboard-only users actually depend on.
followUp: What does the inert attribute do, and how could it simplify hiding background content from assistive tech while a modal is open?

question: What's the difference between canvas and SVG, and when would you pick one over the other?
concise: SVG is a DOM-based, resolution-independent vector format where each shape is an element you can style with CSS and attach event listeners to individually, while canvas is a single bitmap surface you draw onto imperatively with JavaScript and has no per-shape DOM nodes.
strong: I reach for SVG when I need a moderate number of discrete, interactive shapes, like an icon set, a simple chart with tooltips per data point, or a diagram where each node needs its own click handler and accessible label, because every shape is a real DOM node I can style and attach listeners to declaratively. I reach for canvas when I'm rendering a very large number of elements or doing pixel-level work, like a data visualization with tens of thousands of points, a game, or an image editor, because canvas avoids the overhead of maintaining thousands of DOM nodes and just paints pixels directly, which is much faster at that scale. The trade-off is that canvas content isn't individually accessible or stylable with CSS by default, so you lose built-in accessibility and have to reimplement things like focus and screen reader descriptions manually if needed. For a typical dashboard chart with a few hundred points, SVG (via a library like Recharts or D3) is usually the right choice; for a real-time chart streaming thousands of points per second, canvas-based libraries perform noticeably better.
weak: A weak answer says 'SVG for simple stuff, canvas for complex stuff' without identifying the real distinguishing factors: DOM node count/scale and per-element interactivity/accessibility.
followUp: How would you make a canvas-rendered chart accessible to screen reader users?

question: What are Web Components (custom elements, shadow DOM, templates) and where do they fit alongside a framework like React?
concise: Web Components are a browser-native way to define reusable, encapsulated custom HTML tags with their own styling and markup via shadow DOM, useful for framework-agnostic widgets (like a design system shared across teams using different frameworks) but with rougher edges for state management and SSR than React.
strong: Custom elements let you define a new HTML tag with its own lifecycle callbacks, and shadow DOM gives that element style and markup encapsulation so its internal CSS doesn't leak out and external CSS doesn't leak in. This is genuinely useful when a design system needs to be consumed by teams on different stacks, like an Angular team and a React team both embedding the same button or date-picker component without shipping framework-specific code. In practice React does not use Web Components internally, and integrating them with React has friction points, like passing complex props (React passes primitives easily but objects and events across the shadow boundary need extra wiring) and no built-in SSR story comparable to React server components. For a single-framework app I would not reach for Web Components since React's own component model is more ergonomic and has better tooling and state management; I'd consider them specifically for a cross-framework component library or for embeddable third-party widgets, like a support chat widget that needs to be dropped into any customer's site regardless of their stack.
weak: A weak answer conflates Web Components with React components as if they solve the same problem, missing that their real value is framework interoperability, not being a general replacement for React.
followUp: How would you pass a complex object prop, like an array of table rows, into a custom element built with shadow DOM?

question: Why does the meta viewport tag matter for mobile, and what's a common mistake with it?
concise: Without <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>, mobile browsers render the page at a desktop width (like 980px) and then scale it down, making text tiny; a common mistake is adding user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1, which disables pinch-zoom and hurts accessibility for low-vision users.
strong: Mobile browsers historically assumed pages were built for desktop, so without the viewport meta tag they render at a fixed desktop-like width and then shrink the whole page to fit the screen, which makes text unreadably small until the user manually zooms. Setting width=device-width, initial-scale=1 tells the browser to use the actual device width as the CSS pixel width and start at 100% zoom, which is what makes responsive CSS media queries actually work as intended on phones. A mistake I see often is teams adding user-scalable=no or a maximum-scale close to 1 to 'prevent accidental zoom', which actually violates accessibility guidelines because low-vision users rely on pinch-to-zoom to read content, and some browsers now ignore that restriction anyway. The fix is to just allow zooming and instead solve the 'accidental zoom' complaint by fixing actual layout or input-focus issues (like iOS auto-zooming into a text input with font-size below 16px) rather than disabling zoom entirely.
code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
weak: A weak answer just recites the tag from memory without knowing why disabling zoom is a real accessibility anti-pattern, or without knowing why iOS zooms into small-font inputs.
followUp: Why does iOS Safari zoom in when a user taps a text input, and how do you prevent that without disabling zoom?

question: How would you make a data table accessible, especially one with sortable columns and pagination?
concise: Use a real table element with th scope attributes for headers, caption or aria-label describing the table's purpose, aria-sort on sortable column headers reflecting current sort state, and announce pagination or sort changes via an aria-live region since those changes are not naturally announced by assistive tech.
strong: A real table with proper th elements and scope='col' or scope='row' lets screen readers announce which column and row a cell belongs to as the user navigates, which a div-based grid built purely with CSS does not give you for free. For sortable columns, clicking a header button should update aria-sort to ascending, descending, or none on that header, so screen reader users know the current sort state without having to infer it visually. Since re-sorting or changing pages updates the table's content without a full page navigation, I add a visually-hidden aria-live='polite' region that announces something like 'Sorted by amount, descending' or 'Showing page 3 of 12' so users relying on a screen reader are not left wondering whether anything happened. I also make sure the sort control is a real button, not a clickable span or div, so it's keyboard operable by default. For very large or virtualized tables this gets harder since only visible rows exist in the DOM, so I make sure the virtualization library still exposes correct row/column indices via aria attributes rather than silently breaking the table semantics.
weak: A weak answer focuses only on visual styling of the table (borders, zebra striping) and never mentions aria-sort, live region announcements, or scope attributes, missing the actual accessibility requirements being tested.
followUp: How does aria-live='polite' differ from aria-live='assertive', and which would you use for a toast notification versus a form validation error?

question: What's the difference between the alt attribute being empty (alt='') versus omitted entirely on an img tag?
concise: alt='' explicitly marks the image as decorative, so screen readers skip it silently; omitting alt entirely is invalid/ambiguous and many screen readers will instead announce the image's filename or 'image', which is a worse experience.
strong: Every img element should have an alt attribute; the question is what value. If the image conveys information, like a chart or a product photo, alt should describe that content concisely. If the image is purely decorative, like a background flourish or a duplicate of text already on the page, alt should be an explicit empty string so assistive technology skips over it entirely rather than announcing something meaningless. Leaving the attribute off completely is different from an empty string: some screen readers fall back to reading the file path or just saying 'image' or 'graphic', which is noisy and unhelpful. In a dashboard, an icon-only button (like a trash icon with no visible text) needs either an aria-label on the button itself or descriptive alt text on the icon image, since a screen reader user needs to know what the button does, not just that there's an icon there.
weak: A weak answer says 'always add alt text to every image' without distinguishing decorative images (which need empty alt) from meaningful images (which need descriptive alt), which leads to noisy, unhelpful screen reader output in real apps.
followUp: How would you handle alt text for an image that is also a link, like a logo that links to the homepage?

question: Explain the CSS box model and the difference between content-box and border-box.
concise: The box model is content, padding, border and margin stacked outward from an element; content-box (the default) sizes width/height to content only, while border-box includes padding and border inside the specified width/height, which is why most teams set box-sizing: border-box globally.
strong: With the default content-box, if you set width: 200px and then add 20px of padding and a 2px border, the element actually renders at 244px wide, which makes building predictable grid layouts painful because padding changes the rendered size. border-box changes the meaning of width and height to include padding and border, so a 200px wide box stays 200px wide regardless of padding, and only the content area shrinks to accommodate it. This is why almost every modern reset applies box-sizing: border-box to the universal selector, since it makes sizing math intuitive when building forms, cards, and grid layouts where you want a fixed column width. Margin is never included in either box-sizing mode since margin is space outside the box, not part of its size, which matters when calculating things like margin collapsing between adjacent block elements.
weak: A weak answer recites 'content, padding, border, margin' without explaining what box-sizing: border-box actually changes about width/height calculations, which is the part that actually matters for building layouts.
followUp: What is margin collapsing, and what are two ways to prevent it between a parent and its first child?

question: When would you use Flexbox versus CSS Grid?
concise: Flexbox is for one-dimensional layout (a row or a column) where content naturally sizes itself, like a navbar or a button group; Grid is for two-dimensional layout where you need explicit control over both rows and columns simultaneously, like a full page layout or a dashboard with cards in a grid.
strong: I reach for Flexbox when I'm laying out items along a single axis and want the browser to distribute space intelligently, like a toolbar where buttons should be spaced apart, or a card where I want an icon, text and a chevron aligned in a row with the text taking up remaining space. I reach for Grid when I need to control both dimensions at once, for example a dashboard layout with a fixed sidebar, a header, and a main content area that needs specific row and column tracks, or a photo gallery where I want items to wrap into a consistent grid with defined gutters. They are not mutually exclusive: a common pattern is Grid for the page-level layout and Flexbox inside individual grid cells for aligning their contents. A concrete tell for interviews is that Grid has grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows to define an explicit two-dimensional structure, while Flexbox only has flex-direction, meaning it fundamentally reasons about one line (or wrapped lines) at a time.
weak: A weak answer says 'Grid is newer/better, always use Grid' or 'they're interchangeable', missing that the real distinction is one-dimensional versus two-dimensional layout control.
followUp: How would you build a responsive card grid that fits as many equal-width cards per row as space allows, without media queries?

question: How does CSS specificity work, and how would you debug a style that isn't being applied?
concise: Specificity is calculated per selector as a tuple of (inline styles, ID selectors, class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors, element/pseudo-element selectors); higher specificity wins regardless of source order, and !important overrides specificity entirely (highest precedence, aside from user !important styles); to debug, I inspect the element in DevTools and look at the computed styles panel to see which rule is winning and which are struck through.
strong: Specificity is often visualized as four numbers: inline style beats an ID selector, an ID selector beats any number of classes, and classes beat element selectors like div or p. Two selectors with equal specificity are resolved by source order, with the later one winning, which is why utility-class libraries like Tailwind rely heavily on keeping specificity flat and consistent, since mixing hand-written CSS with utility classes can cause confusing specificity fights. When a style isn't applying, my first move in DevTools is the Elements panel's Styles pane, which shows every matching rule with strikethrough on ones that lost, plus the actual computed value; that immediately tells me which selector is winning and why. !important should be treated as an escape hatch of last resort, since once one team starts using it to win specificity wars, others respond by adding more !important elsewhere, and the cascade becomes unmanageable; a better fix is usually to reduce the specificity of the conflicting rule or reorganize class order.
weak: A weak answer says 'just add !important' as the actual fix, rather than as a debugging technique to confirm the diagnosis, which creates long-term maintainability problems.
followUp: How do CSS Modules or Tailwind reduce specificity conflicts compared to hand-written global CSS with BEM?

question: Explain the difference between position: relative, absolute, fixed and sticky.
concise: relative positions an element relative to its own normal position without removing it from flow; absolute removes it from flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor (or the viewport if none); fixed positions relative to the viewport and stays fixed during scroll; sticky toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll position within its containing block.
strong: relative keeps the element in normal document flow but lets you nudge it with top/left/right/bottom offsets relative to where it would have been, and it also creates a positioning context for any absolutely positioned children. absolute takes the element completely out of flow, so surrounding elements act as if it isn't there, and it positions relative to the closest ancestor that has a position other than static, which is why a common pattern is position: relative on a card and position: absolute on a badge inside it. fixed is similar to absolute but always positions relative to the viewport, ignoring scrolling, which is how a persistent header or a floating action button stays on screen while the page scrolls. sticky is the trickiest: the element behaves like relative until the scroll position crosses a threshold defined by its top/bottom value, at which point it 'sticks' like fixed, but only within the bounds of its containing block, so it un-sticks again once its parent scrolls out of view. A common gotcha with sticky is that overflow: hidden or overflow: auto on any ancestor can silently break it.
weak: A weak answer can define each keyword individually but cannot explain the sticky-breaking-with-overflow gotcha, which is the detail that actually trips people up in real layouts.
followUp: Why would a position: sticky element stop sticking if a parent container has overflow: hidden set?

question: What's the difference between media queries and container queries, and when would you use container queries?
concise: Media queries respond to the viewport's size, so a component styled with a media query looks the same regardless of where it's placed on the page; container queries respond to the size of a containing element, so the same component can adapt its layout differently depending on whether it's rendered in a narrow sidebar or a wide main content area.
strong: Media queries answer 'how big is the browser window', which works fine for page-level layout decisions but breaks down for reusable components, because a card component might need to look different depending on whether it's placed in a 300px sidebar or a 900px main content column, regardless of the overall viewport width. Container queries solve exactly that: you mark an ancestor with container-type: inline-size, and then a descendant can use @container to change its own layout based on that ancestor's width, independent of the viewport. This is a big deal for component libraries and design systems, since a Card component can now genuinely be self-contained and context-aware instead of needing prop flags like 'compact' passed down manually to fake this behavior. Browser support has matured enough in the last couple of years that I'd default to container queries for any component meant to be reused across different layout contexts, and reserve media queries for true page-level breakpoint decisions like collapsing a sidebar to a bottom nav on mobile.
weak: A weak answer isn't aware container queries exist as a shipped CSS feature and assumes JavaScript (like a ResizeObserver) is the only way to make a component respond to its own container's width.
followUp: Before container queries were available, how would you have used a ResizeObserver to achieve similar container-aware styling?

question: What are CSS custom properties (variables), and how are they different from Sass/Less variables?
concise: CSS custom properties (--name: value, read with var(--name)) are live in the browser, inherit through the cascade, can be changed at runtime with JavaScript or media queries, and can be scoped per-element; Sass/Less variables are compile-time only, get replaced with static values during the build, and have no runtime presence in the browser at all.
strong: Because custom properties are resolved by the browser at render time, not at build time, they can be changed dynamically, for example toggling a data-theme attribute on the html element and having every component that reads var(--bg-color) instantly update, which is the standard way to implement dark mode without needing to re-render or re-fetch any CSS. They also cascade and can be overridden at any level of the DOM tree, so a component can define a local override of --spacing just for itself and its children, which Sass variables cannot do since they are just find-and-replaced at compile time into whatever value was in scope when the Sass compiled. The trade-off is that Sass variables can be used inside more places, like in selector names or media query definitions, where raw custom properties can't be used directly since the browser doesn't understand CSS-in-selector interpolation the way a preprocessor does at build time. In practice many teams use both together: Sass for build-time logic like mixins and loops, and custom properties for anything that needs to be theme-able or JS-controllable at runtime.
weak: A weak answer says 'they're basically the same as Sass variables but with a different syntax', missing the crucial runtime-versus-compile-time distinction that is the entire reason custom properties are useful for theming.
followUp: How would you use a custom property together with a JavaScript ResizeObserver to drive a CSS animation based on element size?

question: What are the common ways to center an element horizontally and vertically with CSS?
concise: For a flex or grid container, display: flex with justify-content: center and align-items: center (or place-items: center on a grid) is the simplest modern approach; for absolute positioning, top/left: 50% combined with transform: translate(-50%, -50%) centers an element of unknown size relative to its positioned ancestor.
strong: The flex approach is what I default to for centering content inside a container, like centering a spinner or a modal's content, since justify-content and align-items handle both axes cleanly and adapt automatically if the content's size changes. Grid's place-items: center is even shorter for the same result on a grid container. The absolute-positioning-plus-transform trick is useful specifically when you need to center something relative to a positioned ancestor without it participating in normal flow at all, like centering a tooltip arrow or a badge precisely regardless of the parent's own content, because transform: translate(-50%, -50%) shifts the element back by half of its own rendered width and height, which works even if you don't know its exact pixel dimensions ahead of time. Older tricks like using margin: auto with a fixed width, or using line-height equal to container height for single-line vertical centering, still work but are more limited and mostly a historical artifact from before Flexbox and Grid had wide browser support.
weak: A weak answer only knows the margin: 0 auto trick, which only centers horizontally and only works for block elements with a fixed width, and cannot solve vertical centering at all.
followUp: How would you center an element vertically inside a container whose height is unknown, without using Flexbox or Grid?

question: What is a stacking context, and why might z-index not work as expected?
concise: A stacking context is a self-contained layer for z-index ordering created by certain CSS properties (like position with a z-index value, opacity less than 1, transform, or will-change); z-index values only compete against siblings within the same stacking context, so a high z-index inside one stacking context can never appear above an element in a different, later stacking context regardless of the number used.
strong: z-index looks simple until you realize it's not a single global ordering axis; it only determines order among elements that share the same stacking context. If a parent element has a transform or opacity less than one, it creates a new stacking context for all of its children, meaning a child inside it with z-index: 9999 still can't visually appear above a sibling of that parent, even if that sibling has z-index: 1, because they're being compared at the parent level, not the child level. This trips people up constantly with dropdowns and modals: if a dropdown is rendered inside a card that has a subtle transform for a hover effect, the dropdown can get visually clipped or layered incorrectly behind other page content, even with an enormous z-index, because it's trapped inside its parent's stacking context. The fix is usually to render the dropdown or modal content via a portal, appending it to the document body outside of any transformed ancestor, so it participates in the top-level stacking context instead.
weak: A weak answer says 'just increase the z-index number higher' as a fix, without understanding that stacking contexts, not raw z-index values, are usually the actual root cause of the layering bug.
followUp: Why do React portals help solve stacking-context problems for modals and tooltips?

question: Compare CSS Modules, styled-components/CSS-in-JS, and Tailwind's utility-first approach.
concise: CSS Modules give locally-scoped class names with plain CSS syntax and zero runtime cost; CSS-in-JS (styled-components/emotion) colocates styles with components and supports dynamic prop-based styling but adds runtime or build-step overhead; Tailwind trades separate stylesheet authoring for utility classes composed directly in markup, which speeds up iteration and keeps bundle size predictable since unused classes are purged.
strong: CSS Modules solve the classic global-namespace collision problem by generating unique class names per file at build time, while still letting you write ordinary CSS, so there's no new syntax to learn and no runtime cost since it's resolved entirely at build time. CSS-in-JS libraries like styled-components let you write styles as JavaScript colocated with the component and interpolate props directly into the CSS, which is powerful for truly dynamic styling, like a progress bar whose width depends on a numeric prop, but historically came with a runtime cost of injecting style tags on every render, though newer zero-runtime variants have mitigated this. Tailwind flips the model entirely: instead of writing CSS at all, you compose small utility classes directly in JSX, which speeds up iteration since you never leave the markup to tweak spacing or color, and its build step purges unused classes so the shipped CSS stays small regardless of how large the utility set is. In practice, for a team building a design system with a consistent component API, I'd lean toward Tailwind plus a component layer (like shadcn/ui) for velocity and consistency, but CSS Modules remain a solid, dependency-light choice, especially for teams that prefer separating markup from styling.
weak: A weak answer just states a personal preference ('I like Tailwind because it's popular') without being able to articulate the actual runtime, bundle-size, and maintainability trade-offs between the three approaches.
followUp: What's a common criticism of Tailwind's utility-first approach, and how do teams address it for reusable components?

question: Why should you animate transform and opacity instead of properties like width, top, or margin?
concise: transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor thread using the GPU without triggering layout (reflow) or paint, so animations stay smooth at 60fps even under load; animating layout-affecting properties like width or top forces the browser to recompute layout and repaint every frame, which is expensive and can cause jank.
strong: The rendering pipeline goes layout, then paint, then composite; properties like width, height, top and margin affect an element's geometry, so changing them every animation frame forces the browser to redo layout for potentially the whole page, then repaint the affected pixels, then recomposite, all 60 times a second if you want smooth animation. transform (translate, scale, rotate) and opacity can skip layout and paint entirely in most cases and be handled purely by the compositor thread, often GPU-accelerated, which is dramatically cheaper and stays smooth even while the main thread is busy with other JavaScript work. In practice this means a sliding panel should animate with transform: translateX() rather than animating left or margin-left, and a fade should use opacity rather than toggling visibility with a color/background transition. For a dashboard with frequent data updates and animated transitions, this difference is the reason one implementation feels buttery smooth and another visibly stutters under load. The will-change CSS property can hint to the browser to promote an element to its own compositor layer ahead of time, but it should be used sparingly since promoting too many layers has its own memory cost.
weak: A weak answer knows 'transform is faster' as a fact to recite but cannot explain why, in terms of layout/paint/composite, which suggests memorized trivia rather than real understanding.
followUp: What does the will-change property do, and what's the risk of overusing it on many elements?

question: What naming convention like BEM solves, and how does it compare to scoped styling approaches like CSS Modules?
concise: BEM (Block__Element--Modifier) is a manual naming discipline that prevents specificity conflicts and makes relationships between classes explicit purely through convention, whereas CSS Modules or scoped CSS-in-JS solve the same collision problem automatically at the tooling level by generating unique class names, removing the need for developers to enforce a naming convention by hand.
strong: BEM was designed for a world of global stylesheets, where every class name lives in one shared namespace and could collide with any other class anywhere in the codebase; the block__element--modifier convention makes ownership and hierarchy explicit in the name itself, so seeing .card__title--highlighted immediately tells you it's the title element inside a card block with a highlighted modifier, without needing nested selectors that raise specificity. The trade-off is that BEM is purely a human discipline, enforced by code review and habit, not by tooling, so a large team can still drift or violate it inconsistently over time. CSS Modules solve the identical underlying problem, accidental global collisions, but automatically: the build tool hashes class names to be unique per file, so you can write .title without ever worrying about another file's .title colliding with it, and there's no convention to remember or enforce. In a codebase already using CSS Modules or Tailwind, BEM is largely redundant since the scoping problem it was designed to solve doesn't exist anymore; I'd only reach for BEM today on a project stuck with plain global CSS and no build-time scoping tool available.
weak: A weak answer treats BEM as an arbitrary style preference rather than understanding it exists specifically to solve global CSS specificity and naming collisions, a problem modern scoped tooling solves differently.
followUp: If a legacy codebase mixes BEM-named global CSS with newly-added CSS Modules, what issues could arise and how would you migrate safely?

question: How would you implement a dark mode toggle that respects both user choice and system preference?
concise: Use the prefers-color-scheme media query as the default, store the user's explicit override (light/dark/system) in localStorage, apply it by setting a data-theme attribute on the html element as early as possible (ideally via an inline script before CSS renders, to avoid a flash of the wrong theme), and define color values as CSS custom properties that change based on that attribute.
strong: I define all theme-dependent colors as CSS custom properties on :root for light mode, and override them either inside a prefers-color-scheme: dark media query (for users who haven't made an explicit choice) or under a [data-theme='dark'] attribute selector (for an explicit user override), with the attribute selector taking precedence since it reflects a conscious choice. The tricky part is avoiding a flash of the wrong theme on page load: if you only apply the theme class via a React useEffect, there's a visible flash before JavaScript runs, so I put a small inline, blocking script in the document head that reads localStorage synchronously and sets the data-theme attribute before any CSS is parsed. I persist the user's explicit choice (light, dark, or 'system' meaning follow the OS) in localStorage, and if they've chosen 'system', I still listen for changes to the prefers-color-scheme media query at runtime via matchMedia so the app updates live if they change their OS theme while the tab is open. This pattern generalizes to Next.js too, though there you have to be careful that the inline script and the eventual client-rendered markup agree, or you'll get a hydration mismatch warning.
code:
<script>
  const saved = localStorage.getItem('theme');
  const theme = saved || 'system';
  if (theme !== 'system') document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme;
</script>
weak: A weak answer only implements a toggle button that flips a class with useState, ignoring both the system preference and the flash-of-wrong-theme problem, which is exactly the part interviewers probe on for senior candidates.
followUp: How would you avoid a hydration mismatch in Next.js when the theme is read from localStorage on the client but the server has no way to know it?

question: Explain auto-fit versus auto-fill with minmax() in CSS Grid for a responsive card layout.
concise: Both create as many tracks as fit the container using minmax(min, max) sizing per track, but auto-fill keeps empty tracks in place (collapsing to zero width, potentially leaving unused space if there aren't enough items to fill a row), while auto-fit collapses those empty tracks entirely, letting the existing items stretch to fill the leftover space.
strong: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) tells the grid to create as many 200px-minimum columns as will fit the container width, and if you only have three items but room for five columns, auto-fill still reserves those two extra empty column tracks, so your three cards stay at their minmax minimum width and don't stretch to fill the row. auto-fit instead collapses those unused empty tracks to zero, so the existing three cards expand to share the remaining space, which is almost always the visually correct behavior for a typical responsive card grid where you want cards to grow and fill the row when there aren't enough of them. I use auto-fit for the vast majority of card grids, product listings, or dashboard tile layouts. auto-fill is more appropriate in the rarer case where you specifically want consistent, fixed-width tracks regardless of item count, like a calendar grid where empty cells should stay visually reserved rather than have adjacent cells expand into them. This whole pattern also removes the need for manual breakpoint-based media queries just to control column count.
weak: A weak answer cannot articulate the actual difference between auto-fit and auto-fill and just picks one from memory without understanding what 'collapsing empty tracks' means in practice.
followUp: How would you cap the maximum number of columns in this pattern so cards don't become excessively wide on an ultra-wide monitor?

question: What does the prefers-reduced-motion media query do, and why should you support it?
concise: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce detects a user's OS-level accessibility setting indicating they want minimal animation, typically because motion triggers vestibular disorders, migraines, or motion sickness; respecting it by disabling or shortening non-essential animations and transitions is an accessibility requirement, not just a nice-to-have.
strong: Some users enable 'reduce motion' at the operating system level because large-scale animations, parallax effects, or auto-playing motion can trigger real physical symptoms like nausea or dizziness for people with vestibular disorders, not just personal preference. In CSS I wrap non-essential transitions and animations in an @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) block and either remove them or replace them with an instant state change or a very subtle opacity fade instead. I keep functionally important motion, like a progress spinner indicating an operation is in progress, since removing all feedback entirely would hurt usability, but I do remove large sliding, scaling, or parallax effects that serve a decorative purpose. It's a small addition, usually just a handful of extra CSS rules, but it's frequently skipped, and interviewers who ask about it are checking whether accessibility is a genuine habit rather than an afterthought.
weak: A weak answer has never heard of this media query, or dismisses it as an edge case not worth handling, which signals a gap in accessibility awareness expected at a senior level.
followUp: How would you apply this preference not just in CSS but also to a JavaScript-driven animation library like Framer Motion?

question: Walk through the critical rendering pipeline: what happens between receiving HTML and pixels on screen?
concise: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, computes layout (geometry and position of each node), paints pixels into layers, and finally composites those layers onto the screen; JavaScript and CSS in the head can block this pipeline if not loaded carefully.
strong: The browser streams the HTML and builds the DOM incrementally, and in parallel it parses any CSS into the CSSOM; render-blocking CSS in the head means the browser won't paint anything until the CSSOM is fully built, since it doesn't want to paint content that will immediately need to be repainted with real styles. Once both trees exist, the browser combines them into a render tree containing only visible nodes (display: none nodes are excluded, but visibility: hidden nodes remain, just invisible), then runs layout to calculate exact size and position of every box, then paint fills in pixels for text, colors, images, and borders into layers, and finally the compositor thread combines those layers in the correct order, applying transforms and opacity cheaply without redoing layout or paint. Understanding this pipeline is what tells you why animating transform/opacity is fast (compositor-only) while animating width or top is slow (triggers layout then paint then composite), and why placing large synchronous scripts in the head blocks first paint since the parser must stop and execute them before continuing to build the DOM.
weak: A weak answer lists the stage names from memory (parse, layout, paint) but can't connect them to practical consequences like why certain CSS animations are smoother or why script placement in the head affects load performance.
followUp: Why does adding a font via @font-face sometimes cause a 'flash of invisible text' (FOIT), and how would you mitigate it?

question: Explain the JavaScript event loop, including the call stack, microtask queue, and macrotask queue.
concise: JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack for synchronous code; async work is queued as either a microtask (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) or a macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks); after each synchronous execution completes and the call stack empties, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue before running even one macrotask, which is why Promise callbacks always run before a setTimeout(fn, 0).
strong: The call stack executes synchronous code first, top to bottom, and nothing else runs until it's empty. Once it's empty, the event loop checks the microtask queue and drains it completely, running every queued Promise .then/.catch/.finally callback and queueMicrotask callback, including any new microtasks that get added while draining, before moving on. Only after the microtask queue is fully empty does the event loop pick a single task from the macrotask queue, like a setTimeout callback, execute it, and then repeat the cycle by checking microtasks again. This ordering is why a common trick question, logging inside a setTimeout(fn, 0) versus a Promise.resolve().then(fn) logged in the same synchronous block, always prints the Promise callback first, regardless of the zero delay, because the setTimeout callback is a macrotask and has to wait for microtasks to fully drain first. This matters practically in a dashboard app when you're chaining multiple async state updates: if you fire off several Promise .then() calls versus a setTimeout-based poll, their relative execution order is different, and getting this wrong is a common source of subtle race conditions and flaky tests around timing.
weak: A weak answer says 'JavaScript is single-threaded and async things happen later' without being able to correctly predict output ordering between setTimeout and Promise callbacks, which is the concrete test of real understanding here.
followUp: Where do requestAnimationFrame callbacks and MutationObserver callbacks fit into this ordering relative to microtasks and macrotasks?

question: What are the practical differences between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 that matter for frontend performance?
concise: HTTP/1.1 opens a limited number of TCP connections per origin and processes requests somewhat serially per connection (motivating old tricks like domain sharding and spriting); HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over a single connection with header compression, removing the need for those workarounds; HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC over UDP, eliminating head-of-line blocking at the transport level and improving performance on unreliable or high-latency mobile networks.
strong: Under HTTP/1.1, browsers typically limit around six concurrent connections per origin, so pages historically used tricks like splitting assets across subdomains (domain sharding) or bundling many small images into a single sprite sheet just to reduce the number of round trips needed. HTTP/2 solved this at the protocol level by multiplexing many logical streams over one physical connection, so dozens of requests can be in flight simultaneously without opening new connections, plus HPACK header compression reduces overhead for repetitive headers like cookies sent on every request; this is part of why bundling everything into one giant JS file became less universally beneficial, since many smaller cacheable chunks over HTTP/2 can now load in parallel efficiently. HTTP/2 still has one weakness: it runs over TCP, so a single lost packet blocks all multiplexed streams on that connection until it's retransmitted (head-of-line blocking at the TCP layer). HTTP/3 fixes this by using QUIC over UDP, where each stream's packet loss is handled independently, which is a meaningful win on flaky mobile networks. For frontend work day to day, the actionable takeaway is that with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, aggressive code-splitting into smaller chunks is usually better for caching and parallel loading than one large bundle.
weak: A weak answer knows the version numbers exist but can't explain multiplexing or head-of-line blocking, and can't connect any of it to an actual frontend bundling decision.
followUp: How does HTTP/2 server push work, and why has it largely fallen out of favor compared to techniques like resource hints (preload/prefetch)?

question: Explain CORS: what triggers a preflight request, and what headers actually control it?
concise: CORS is a browser-enforced restriction on cross-origin requests; simple requests (GET/POST/HEAD with only a small allow-list of headers and content types) go through directly and the browser just checks the response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin header before exposing it to JS, while non-simple requests (custom headers, methods like PUT/DELETE/PATCH, or content-type: application/json in some setups) trigger an OPTIONS preflight first, which the server must explicitly respond to with the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers before the browser sends the real request.
strong: CORS exists purely as a browser-side protection: the actual request often still reaches the server either way, but the browser withholds the response from JavaScript unless the server's response includes the right Access-Control-Allow-Origin header (or a wildcard, though wildcards can't be used together with credentials). For anything beyond a 'simple' request, meaning it uses a method like PUT, PATCH or DELETE, or sends a custom header like Authorization or a JSON content-type that isn't in the safelisted set, the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking permission, and the server must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, and Access-Control-Allow-Origin for the browser to proceed with the actual request. If the request includes credentials (cookies) via credentials: 'include', the server must also explicitly set Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, and Access-Control-Allow-Origin cannot be a wildcard in that case, it must echo back the exact origin. A common real-world mistake is a frontend team assuming a CORS error means the backend is broken, when actually it's often a misconfigured allow-list, a missing preflight handler, or the backend simply not expecting to serve that origin, which is a config problem to fix on the server, not something the frontend can bypass.
weak: A weak answer says 'CORS errors mean the backend is down' or tries to 'fix' CORS purely from the frontend, not understanding that CORS is enforced by the browser and must be resolved with correct server-side headers.
followUp: If a CORS preflight succeeds but the actual request still fails with a CORS error, what's a likely mismatch between the preflight response and the real response?

question: What is Content Security Policy (CSP), and how does it help prevent XSS?
concise: CSP is a response header (or meta tag) that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images, and other resources are allowed to load and execute on a page; by restricting script-src to trusted origins and disallowing inline scripts and eval, CSP acts as a strong second layer of defense against XSS even if an attacker manages to inject markup into the page.
strong: Even with careful output encoding, XSS vulnerabilities can slip through, especially in large codebases with many contributors, so CSP is a defense-in-depth layer: it tells the browser explicitly which origins are allowed to serve scripts, styles, fonts, images, and connect (fetch/XHR/WebSocket) destinations, and the browser refuses to execute or load anything outside that allow-list, regardless of what markup ends up in the DOM. A strict policy disallows unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval for scripts, which means even if an attacker injects a script tag through a stored XSS vulnerability, the browser simply won't execute it because it didn't come from an allowed origin or match a nonce. The common friction point is that many apps use inline scripts or styles for legitimate reasons (like a critical CSS snippet, or a theme-detection script in the head), which a strict CSP blocks by default, so the fix is either moving that logic to an external allowed file or using a per-request cryptographic nonce that's regenerated on every server response and can never be predicted or reused by an attacker. CSP also supports a report-only mode and a report-uri or report-to directive, so teams can roll out a new policy gradually, monitoring what would have been blocked before actually enforcing it in production. For a payment or auth-heavy dashboard app, I'd treat a properly tuned CSP as a required security control, not optional hardening.
code: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-r4nd0m123'; object-src 'none';
weak: A weak answer says 'CSP blocks XSS' without explaining the mechanism (allow-listing sources, blocking inline scripts) or knowing that CSP is a layered defense, not a replacement for proper output escaping and input validation.
followUp: How would you roll out a CSP on an existing large app without immediately breaking third-party scripts like analytics tags?

question: What are the main types of XSS (stored, reflected, DOM-based), and how do you prevent them in a React app?
concise: Stored XSS persists malicious script in the database (e.g. a comment field) and executes for every user who views it; reflected XSS executes immediately by echoing unsanitized input from the request (like a URL query param) back into the page; DOM-based XSS happens entirely client-side when JavaScript writes untrusted data into the DOM via unsafe sinks like innerHTML; React helps by auto-escaping text content by default, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, direct DOM manipulation, or unsanitized href/src attributes can still reintroduce all three.
strong: Stored XSS is the most dangerous because a single malicious submission, like a crafted comment or profile bio, gets served to every subsequent visitor until it's cleaned up; reflected XSS requires tricking a specific user into clicking a malicious link that embeds a script in a query parameter the page echoes back unsanitized; DOM-based XSS doesn't even need the server to be involved, it happens when client-side JavaScript itself takes some untrusted value, like window.location.hash, and writes it into the DOM through an unsafe sink like innerHTML or document.write. React's default behavior of rendering values inside JSX as text nodes (not raw HTML) closes off most of this by auto-escaping, but that protection disappears the moment you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML to render rich text or markdown, or when you build a URL like a href={userSuppliedUrl} without validating the scheme, since a javascript: URL can execute code when clicked. For any feature that renders user-generated rich content (like a comments section with formatting, or a WYSIWYG description field), I sanitize the HTML server-side or client-side with a trusted library like DOMPurify before it ever reaches dangerouslySetInnerHTML, and I validate that any user-supplied URL uses an expected protocol like https before rendering it as a link.
weak: A weak answer claims 'React is immune to XSS' as an absolute statement, missing that dangerouslySetInnerHTML, unsanitized links, and third-party libraries that manipulate the DOM directly can all reintroduce the exact same vulnerability.
followUp: Why is validating a URL's protocol important before rendering user-supplied links, and what's a real-world attack that exploits a javascript: URL?

question: What is CSRF, and how do SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens each help prevent it?
concise: CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into submitting an unwanted authenticated request to another site (like a bank transfer form auto-submitted from a malicious page), exploiting the fact that cookies are sent automatically with requests to their origin regardless of which site initiated them; SameSite=Lax or Strict on the auth cookie stops the browser from sending it on most cross-site requests, while a CSRF token (a random value tied to the user's session, required on state-changing requests) ensures even if a cookie were sent, the attacker's page has no way to know or supply the correct token.
strong: CSRF works because browsers attach cookies to requests based on the destination domain, not the origin the request came from, so if a user is logged into a banking site in one tab and visits a malicious site in another tab that auto-submits a hidden form to the bank's transfer endpoint, the browser happily attaches the user's real session cookie to that request, and the bank's server can't tell it wasn't an intentional action by the logged-in user. SameSite=Lax, which is now the default in modern browsers if unspecified, prevents the cookie from being sent on cross-site POST requests (though it still allows it on top-level GET navigation, which is why Lax isn't a complete fix on its own for state-changing GET endpoints, which shouldn't exist anyway per REST conventions). SameSite=Strict is even tighter but can break legitimate cross-site flows like arriving at a site via an external link while already logged in. CSRF tokens add a second, independent layer: the server embeds a random token in the page or in a cookie separate from the session, and every state-changing request must include that token in the request body or a custom header; since a malicious cross-site page has no way to read that token (same-origin policy prevents it from reading the victim site's DOM or cookies), it can't forge a valid request even if it can trigger one. In practice I use both together: SameSite=Lax/Strict as the baseline plus explicit CSRF tokens for any sensitive state-changing endpoint like a password change or a payment action, since defense in depth matters here.
weak: A weak answer says 'CSRF is basically the same as XSS' or believes SameSite cookies alone are a complete fix without understanding the Lax-still-allows-top-level-GET nuance.
followUp: Why doesn't CSRF apply to APIs that use a Bearer token in an Authorization header instead of cookies for authentication?

question: Explain HTTP caching: what do Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified actually do?
concise: Cache-Control controls how long a response can be reused without revalidation (max-age) and whether it can be cached at all (no-store, private, public); ETag and Last-Modified enable conditional revalidation, letting the browser send an If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since header so the server can respond with a cheap 304 Not Modified instead of resending the full body if the content hasn't changed.
strong: Cache-Control: max-age=3600 tells the browser it can reuse a cached response for up to an hour without even asking the server again, which is the fastest possible case since there's zero network round trip. Once max-age expires, or if the response was marked no-cache (which, confusingly, still allows caching but forces revalidation every time), the browser sends a conditional request, including the ETag value it previously received as an If-None-Match header, or the Last-Modified date as an If-Modified-Since header; if the server determines the content hasn't changed, it returns a 304 with no body at all, saving bandwidth even though the browser still needs a round trip. ETag is generally preferred over Last-Modified since it's a content hash and works even if a file is regenerated with the same content but a different timestamp, which would falsely bust a Last-Modified-based cache. For static assets in a build pipeline, the standard pattern is to fingerprint filenames with a content hash (like main.a1b2c3.js) and set a very long max-age with immutable, since the filename itself changes whenever content changes, eliminating any need for revalidation at all; for the HTML entry point or API responses, shorter max-age or no-store combined with ETag-based revalidation is more appropriate since that content changes independently of the filename.
code: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
weak: A weak answer conflates Cache-Control and ETag as doing the same thing, missing that one avoids the network round trip entirely while the other still requires a round trip but avoids re-sending the full payload.
followUp: Why is Cache-Control: no-cache a misleading name, and how is it different from no-store?

question: What benefits does a CDN provide beyond just 'serving files faster'?
concise: A CDN reduces latency by serving cached content from a location physically closer to the user (edge servers), offloads traffic and load from the origin server, provides DDoS mitigation and absorbs traffic spikes, and often adds features like automatic compression, TLS termination, and image optimization at the edge.
strong: The most obvious benefit is latency: instead of every user's request traveling to a single origin server (which might be in one region), a CDN caches static assets across many geographically distributed edge nodes, so a user in another part of the world gets the response from a nearby node instead of crossing the globe. Beyond latency, a CDN meaningfully reduces load on the origin server since cached assets like JS bundles, images, and fonts are served entirely from the edge without ever reaching your backend, which matters a lot during traffic spikes, like a marketing campaign driving a sudden surge of visitors. Most CDNs also provide built-in DDoS protection by absorbing and filtering malicious traffic at the edge before it ever reaches origin infrastructure, and many offer additional edge capabilities like automatic image format conversion and resizing, Brotli or gzip compression, and TLS termination so the origin doesn't have to manage certificates directly. For a Next.js app deployed on a platform like Vercel, static assets and even server-rendered pages using ISR are automatically distributed this way, which is part of why edge/CDN-aware deployment platforms have become the default choice for production frontend apps.
weak: A weak answer only mentions 'it makes things load faster' without mentioning origin offloading, traffic spike resilience, or DDoS mitigation, which are equally important production benefits.
followUp: What's the difference between a CDN caching a static asset versus caching a dynamically server-rendered HTML page, and what risks come with caching the latter?

question: Explain the three Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, and CLS. What causes a poor score in each?
concise: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measures when the largest visible element renders, hurt by slow server response, render-blocking resources, or large unoptimized images/fonts; INP (Interaction to Next Paint, which replaced FID) measures responsiveness to user interactions throughout the page's life, hurt by long JavaScript tasks blocking the main thread; CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures visual stability, hurt by images/ads/fonts loading without reserved space and pushing content around after initial render.
strong: LCP is usually dominated by one of a few causes: a slow Time to First Byte from the server, render-blocking CSS or synchronous scripts delaying paint, or the largest element itself, often a hero image or a large heading, being slow to load or discover, which is why preloading the LCP image and prioritizing critical CSS matters a lot. INP replaced First Input Delay as the responsiveness metric because FID only measured the delay before the first interaction started processing, while INP measures the full cost of processing any interaction throughout the page's lifetime, including ones far into the session, and it's usually hurt by long JavaScript tasks on the main thread, like a heavy synchronous computation or an oversized component re-render blocking the browser from responding to a click for hundreds of milliseconds; breaking up long tasks or moving heavy work off the main thread (like to a Web Worker) is the usual fix. CLS is caused by content shifting after initial paint, most commonly images or ads without explicit width/height (or aspect-ratio) reserving their space, web fonts swapping in and reflowing text (FOUT), or content being injected above existing content, like a banner loading in after the page already rendered; the fix is almost always to reserve layout space up front for anything that loads asynchronously. On a dashboard with dynamically loaded widgets, I'd specifically watch CLS and INP, since LCP matters more for a first-visit marketing page than for an authenticated app a user already has open.
weak: A weak answer can name the three metrics but can't explain a concrete cause for a poor score in each one, which is what actually demonstrates the ability to diagnose and fix real performance problems.
followUp: How would you measure these metrics in production (real user data) versus in a lab environment like Lighthouse, and why might the two disagree?

question: What's the difference between reflow (layout), repaint, and compositing, and what causes 'layout thrashing'?
concise: Reflow recalculates the geometry (size/position) of elements and is the most expensive; repaint redraws pixels for elements whose appearance changed but geometry didn't; compositing just combines already-painted layers, which is cheapest and can be GPU-accelerated; layout thrashing happens when JavaScript repeatedly writes a style then reads a layout-dependent property (like offsetHeight) in a loop, forcing the browser to synchronously recalculate layout on every iteration instead of batching it once.
strong: Any DOM change that affects geometry, like changing width, adding/removing an element, or changing text content, triggers a reflow, which the browser has to propagate potentially through the entire tree since one element's size can affect its siblings' and ancestors' layout too. Changes that only affect appearance without changing geometry, like changing background-color or visibility, only trigger a repaint, skipping the expensive layout recalculation step. Layout thrashing is a specific JavaScript anti-pattern: if you write to a style (which invalidates layout) and then immediately read a layout-dependent property like offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect (which forces the browser to synchronously recompute layout right then, rather than batching it with the next natural render), and you do this in a loop over many elements, you force dozens or hundreds of synchronous forced reflows in a single frame, which can visibly stall the page. The fix is to batch all your reads first, store them in variables, and then perform all your writes afterward, so the browser only needs to do one recalculation total instead of one per iteration. This is a classic issue in code that measures and repositions many DOM elements, like a custom virtualized list or a drag-and-drop reordering feature, and it's exactly the kind of bug that Chrome DevTools' Performance panel will show as many small purple 'Layout' blocks stacked back to back in a single frame.
weak: A weak answer knows the words 'reflow' and 'repaint' but has never heard of layout thrashing and cannot explain why interleaving DOM reads and writes in a loop is specifically the trigger.
followUp: How would the Chrome DevTools Performance panel visually show you that layout thrashing is happening in your app?

question: What do service workers enable, and what's a realistic use case beyond 'offline support'?
concise: A service worker is a script that runs separately from the page as a network proxy, letting you intercept fetch requests to implement custom caching strategies (cache-first, network-first, stale-while-revalidate), enable offline functionality, handle background sync, and receive push notifications, even when the site's tab isn't open.
strong: A service worker sits between your app and the network, so you can implement caching strategies far more nuanced than what the browser's default HTTP cache gives you, for example serving the app shell instantly from cache while revalidating in the background (stale-while-revalidate), which makes an app feel instant on repeat visits even on a flaky connection. Beyond classic offline support, a realistic use case is push notifications for a dashboard app, where the service worker can receive a push event and show a system notification even if the user doesn't have the tab open, which is how many web apps replicate native-app-style re-engagement. Another is background sync: if a user submits a form while offline, the service worker can queue that request and automatically retry it once connectivity returns, without the user needing to manually resubmit. The trade-off is real complexity: service worker lifecycle (install, activate, fetch events) and cache invalidation are notoriously tricky to get right, and a poorly-updated service worker can serve stale content indefinitely since it controls the update cycle itself; tools like Workbox exist specifically to provide battle-tested caching strategy recipes instead of hand-rolling this logic.
weak: A weak answer only mentions 'lets the site work offline' and stops there, without knowing about background sync, push notifications, or the actual caching-strategy trade-offs service workers introduce.
followUp: How does a service worker's update lifecycle work, and why can users sometimes get stuck seeing an old cached version of your app after you deploy a new one?

question: What do the HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie flags each protect against?
concise: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie via document.cookie, protecting against token theft via XSS; Secure ensures the cookie is only sent over HTTPS, protecting against network interception; SameSite controls whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests, protecting against CSRF.
strong: HttpOnly is specifically about making a cookie invisible to JavaScript entirely, so even if an attacker manages to inject a script through an XSS vulnerability, document.cookie simply won't include that cookie, meaning they can't exfiltrate a session token even with full script execution on the page. Secure ensures the browser only ever transmits the cookie over an HTTPS connection, which prevents it from being sniffed in plaintext if a user is on an insecure network like public WiFi performing a man-in-the-middle attack. SameSite governs cross-site behavior specifically: Strict never sends the cookie on cross-site requests at all (even top-level navigation from an external link), Lax (the modern default) sends it on top-level GET navigations but not on cross-site POSTs or embedded resource requests, and None allows it everywhere but requires Secure to also be set. For an auth session cookie in a real app, I'd set all three: HttpOnly and Secure always, and SameSite=Lax or Strict depending on whether the app needs to support being embedded or linked to from external sites while already authenticated.
