weak: A weak answer claims interface and type are 'basically the same thing, pick either' without knowing that unions, tuples, and conditional types require type specifically, or without knowing about declaration merging.
followUp: What is declaration merging, and can you give an example of when it's genuinely useful rather than confusing?

question: Explain mapped types with a practical example, like building your own version of Readonly or Partial.
concise: A mapped type iterates over the keys of an existing type ([K in keyof T]) and produces a new type by transforming each property, which is exactly how built-in utility types like Partial, Readonly, and Record are implemented; you can combine modifiers (making properties optional with ?, readonly, or removing those modifiers with - prefixes) and even remap keys entirely using 'as' clauses (key remapping) for more advanced transformations.
strong: The syntax [K in keyof T]: T[K] loops over every key K in T's key set and, for each one, defines a property with that same key, typed as whatever T[K] was, which by itself just reproduces T identically; the actual utility types library adds modifiers on top of that basic loop, like appending a question mark to make each property optional (which is exactly how Partial<T> is defined internally) or prefixing with readonly to make every property immutable (how Readonly<T> is defined). You can also strip existing modifiers using a minus prefix, like -readonly or -?, which is how Required<T> removes optionality that a source type had. A more advanced feature, key remapping with an 'as' clause inside the mapped type, lets you transform the actual property names themselves, not just their value types, for example automatically generating a set of getter method names like getName, getAge from an object type's original property names, which is genuinely useful for building typed API client generators or ORMs that derive method signatures directly from a schema type. Understanding mapped types well enough to write a custom one is a strong signal in interviews, since it shows the utility types aren't magic, they're just regular TypeScript syntax that ships as a small standard library.
weak: A weak answer has used Partial and Readonly as black-box utility types but has never written a custom mapped type and can't explain the [K in keyof T] mechanism that powers all of them.
followUp: How would you write a mapped type that makes only a specific subset of a type's properties optional, while keeping the rest required?

question: Explain conditional types and the infer keyword, with a realistic example.
concise: A conditional type (T extends U ? X : Y) selects between two types based on whether T is assignable to U, evaluated per-member when T is a union (distributive conditional types); infer lets you introduce a new type variable inside the extends clause to extract and capture part of a matched type's structure, which is how built-in utility types like ReturnType<T> and Parameters<T> are implemented.
strong: Conditional types let you branch at the type level the way an if statement branches at the value level: type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false evaluates to the literal type true or false depending on what T actually is at each usage site. When T is a union type, the conditional distributes automatically over each member of the union unless you specifically wrap it to prevent that, which is a subtlety worth knowing since it can produce surprising results if you're not expecting the distribution. infer is what makes conditional types genuinely powerful rather than just a type-level if-statement: inside the extends clause, you can write something like T extends (...args: infer A) => infer R, which pattern-matches T against 'a function type' and, if it matches, captures its argument tuple as A and its return type as R, letting you extract and reuse those captured types elsewhere, exactly how the built-in ReturnType<T> and Parameters<T> utility types are implemented under the hood. A practical, realistic use is deriving the resolved data type of an async function automatically, so you never have to manually keep a separate type in sync with what an API function actually returns, reducing duplication and the risk of the two drifting apart as the function's implementation changes over time.
weak: A weak answer has memorized that ReturnType<T> and Parameters<T> exist as built-ins but has never understood or used infer directly, and can't explain what pattern-matching a type structure with infer actually does.
followUp: Why does a naive conditional type distribute automatically over a union type, and how would you write one that treats the union as a single whole instead?

question: Why is unknown generally preferred over any, especially for typing external or untrusted data like an API response?
concise: any completely disables type checking for anything it touches, so you can call any method or access any property on it with no compiler errors, even ones that don't exist, silently reintroducing runtime errors that TypeScript exists to prevent; unknown is type-safe by design, it can hold any value just like any, but the compiler forces you to narrow it (via a type guard, typeof, instanceof, or a runtime validation library) before you're allowed to use it as anything specific.
strong: When you type a variable as any, TypeScript effectively stops checking it entirely, which means a typo like calling response.usre.name instead of response.user.name compiles without any error and only fails at runtime when a real user encounters it; this defeats much of the actual value of using TypeScript in the first place, since any spreads through your code, any value derived from an any value also silently becomes any. unknown is the type-safe alternative for exactly the same 'I don't yet know what this is' situation, most commonly the raw result of fetch(...).json() on an API call: the compiler still lets you assign anything to an unknown-typed variable, but it refuses to let you access any property or call any method on it until you've actually proven, through a type guard or a runtime check, what it actually is. In practice, for API responses specifically, I pair unknown with a runtime validation library like Zod, parsing the unknown response through a schema that both validates its actual shape at runtime and gives you a fully-typed, narrowed result if validation succeeds, which closes the real gap that plain TypeScript types alone can't cover: TypeScript's type system only exists at compile time and has no way to actually verify that an external API response matches what you declared it to be.
weak: A weak answer treats any and unknown as basically interchangeable, or defaults to typing every external API response as any 'just to make the compiler stop complaining', missing the entire safety benefit unknown plus a runtime validator provides.
followUp: Why can't TypeScript's compile-time types alone guarantee that data coming back from an API actually matches the type you declared for it?

question: How would you write a custom type guard (type predicate) function, and why is it better than a plain boolean-returning function for narrowing?
concise: A type guard function has a return type annotated as 'value is SomeType' instead of a plain boolean; TypeScript specifically recognizes this syntax and actually narrows the checked value's type in any branch where the guard returns true, whereas a plain function that just happens to return true/false based on the same logic gives TypeScript no such narrowing information, since the compiler can't 'see into' an arbitrary function's implementation to infer that it implies a specific type.
strong: Writing function isUser(value: unknown): value is User { ... } tells the compiler explicitly: whenever this function returns true for some value, treat that value as type User from that point forward in this code path, which is exactly the kind of narrowing you'd get automatically from a typeof or instanceof check, just generalized to arbitrary custom validation logic. If you instead wrote a function returning a plain boolean with identical runtime logic, calling if (checkIsUser(value)) would still correctly evaluate at runtime, but TypeScript would have no idea that a true return value implies anything at all about value's type, so inside that if block value would remain typed as unknown (or whatever it was before), forcing you to redundantly cast it anyway, which defeats the whole purpose of having done the runtime check in the first place. This pattern is especially useful for narrowing discriminated unions with more complex logic than a simple property check allows, or for validating unknown data from an API response, an untyped third-party library, or a value read from localStorage, letting you cleanly bridge 'I've verified this at runtime' with 'now let the type system trust that going forward'.
weak: A weak answer writes a function that returns a plain boolean and then still casts the value with 'as User' right afterward anyway, not realizing a proper type predicate return type would have made that manual cast completely unnecessary.
followUp: How is a type predicate function different from using the 'as' type assertion, in terms of actual runtime safety?

question: How do generic constraints work (T extends ...), and why would you use keyof in a constraint?
concise: A generic constraint (T extends SomeShape) restricts what types can be passed as T, letting the compiler know T is guaranteed to have at least the properties/behavior of SomeShape, so you can safely access those properties inside the generic function; keyof T specifically constrains a second type parameter to be one of T's actual property names, which is exactly how you'd type a safe, generic property-getter function.
strong: Without a constraint, a plain generic T could be anything at all, including a number or a string, so the compiler won't let you access T.id inside the function body since it has no guarantee that whatever T ends up being actually has an id property; adding T extends { id: string } tells the compiler that whatever concrete type is used for T, it's guaranteed to at least have that shape, which then lets you safely reference .id inside the function while still preserving the caller's specific, more precise type for everything else. keyof T is a related but distinct tool: given an object type T, keyof T produces a union of all of its literal property-name keys as a type, and combining that with a second generic parameter constrained as K extends keyof T is exactly how you'd type a generic getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] function, guaranteeing at compile time that you can only ever pass a key that actually exists on the object, and that the return type is correctly inferred as whatever that specific property's type is, catching typos in property names as compile errors instead of returning undefined silently at runtime.
weak: A weak answer knows T extends SomeType exists but has never used keyof in a constraint, and would instead type a generic key parameter as a plain string, losing all compile-time protection against typos in property names.
followUp: How would you write a generic function that updates a single property on an object immutably, fully type-safe for both the key and the value's type?

question: How would you type a React component's props, including children, and event handler props?
concise: Define an interface (or type) listing each prop with its precise type, using React.ReactNode for children (since it correctly covers strings, numbers, elements, fragments, and arrays of nodes, unlike the narrower JSX.Element), and typing event handler props either as a plain function signature like (value: string) => void for custom callbacks, or using React's built-in event types like React.MouseEventHandler<HTMLButtonElement> or React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for native DOM event handlers.
strong: For children, React.ReactNode is almost always the right type since it's a broad union covering everything actually renderable, including strings, numbers, booleans (which render as nothing), JSX elements, fragments, and arrays of any of those; a common mistake is typing children as JSX.Element, which is much narrower and incorrectly rejects perfectly valid children like a plain string or an array of elements. For a custom callback prop, like onSubmit or onValueChange, I define its exact function signature directly, for example onValueChange: (value: string) => void, rather than something looser like Function, which would allow calling it with any number or type of arguments without any compile-time check. For props that wrap a native DOM event handler, like a custom Input component's onChange, I type it using React's built-in generic event types, like React.ChangeEventHandler<HTMLInputElement>, which correctly types the event object passed to the handler, including e.target.value as a string, rather than manually reconstructing that type or falling back to any. For components accepting arbitrary native HTML attributes alongside custom props, extending React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> (or similar) is the pattern I'd use so the component can transparently forward props like disabled, aria-label, or onClick without redeclaring each one manually.
weak: A weak answer types children as JSX.Element (too narrow, breaks on strings or arrays), or types every callback prop as a generic Function type, losing all argument and return-type checking for that callback.
followUp: Why is JSX.Element narrower than React.ReactNode, and what real prop value would fail to satisfy a children: JSX.Element type but work fine as React.ReactNode?

question: How would you type API responses end-to-end, combining TypeScript's static types with runtime validation using a library like Zod?
concise: Define a Zod schema describing the expected shape of the API response, derive the corresponding static TypeScript type from that schema with z.infer (rather than hand-writing a separate interface that could drift out of sync), and parse every raw API response through the schema at the network boundary, so any mismatch between what the backend actually returns and what you expected throws a clear validation error immediately, instead of silently propagating malformed or unexpected data deeper into the app.
strong: TypeScript's type system is completely erased at runtime, it has zero ability to actually verify that data coming back from fetch matches the interface you declared for it, so declaring interface User { id: string; name: string } and casting a fetch response 'as User' is really just telling the compiler to trust you, with no actual verification happening; if the backend changes a field name or the network returns malformed data, your app has no way to know until something downstream breaks in a confusing way. Zod (or a similar library like Yup or Valibot) solves this by defining the shape once as a schema, both a runtime validator you can call at the actual API boundary, and, via z.infer<typeof UserSchema>, a fully accurate static TypeScript type derived directly from that same schema, so the two can never drift apart the way a hand-written interface and the actual runtime data could. Parsing the raw response through the schema at the boundary (right after the fetch call, before the data goes anywhere else in the app) means any unexpected shape, a missing field, a wrong type, an extra field if you use strict mode, throws immediately with a clear, specific error message pointing at exactly which field failed, which is far easier to debug than a mysterious 'undefined is not a function' three components deeper in the render tree. This pattern is especially valuable at a company where frontend and backend evolve somewhat independently, since it turns silent contract drift between the two into a loud, immediate, actionable error right where the data enters your app.
weak: A weak answer relies entirely on a hand-written TypeScript interface plus an 'as User' cast on the raw fetch response, with no runtime validation at all, meaning any actual mismatch between backend and frontend expectations is invisible until it causes a downstream bug.
followUp: What's the difference between Zod's .parse() and .safeParse(), and when would you use each in an API client function?

question: When would you use function overloads in TypeScript, and how are they different from a single function with union-typed parameters?
concise: Overloads let you declare multiple distinct call signatures for the same function name, each specifying a precise relationship between specific input and output types; they're most useful when a function's return type genuinely depends on which specific argument type was passed in a way a single union signature can't express precisely, whereas a plain union parameter type is sufficient (and simpler) when the return type doesn't need to vary based on which union member was passed.
strong: A single signature like function parse(input: string | number): string | number technically type-checks calls correctly, but it forces every caller to deal with a return type that's a union of both possibilities, even though in reality passing a string always returns a string and passing a number always returns a number; the caller ends up needing an unnecessary type guard or cast after every call just to narrow the result back down, even though the actual runtime behavior was never ambiguous. Overloads solve this precisely: you declare several specific signatures above the implementation, like parse(input: string): string and parse(input: number): number, and TypeScript picks whichever overload signature matches the actual argument type at each call site, giving you back a precisely typed result with no extra narrowing needed by the caller. The actual function implementation itself still needs a single, more permissive signature that's compatible with every declared overload, and its body has to handle all the cases at runtime, but that implementation signature stays invisible to callers, they only ever see the specific overload signatures. I'd reach for overloads specifically when the return type meaningfully depends on which specific input type was passed; if the return type stays the same union regardless of which specific input variant was given, a plain union parameter is simpler and just as correct.
weak: A weak answer has never used function overloads and instead always returns a union type from every function, forcing every single caller to redundantly narrow the result themselves after every call, even when the actual relationship between input and output was never really ambiguous.
followUp: How does the function implementation's own signature (below the overload declarations) need to relate to the individual overload signatures above it?

question: What are template literal types, and how would you use them for something practical like typing CSS-in-JS spacing tokens or API route paths?
concise: Template literal types let you build new string literal types by combining existing literal types and unions inside a template-string-like syntax at the type level, letting TypeScript enforce precise string patterns and shapes (like a valid route path with typed dynamic segments, or a valid CSS custom property name) at compile time instead of accepting any arbitrary string.
strong: A template literal type like type EventName = 'on' + Capitalize<'click' | 'hover' | 'focus'> combines a fixed prefix with a union of capitalized suffixes to produce the literal union type 'onClick' | 'onHover' | 'onFocus', which is a much more precise way to describe a set of valid string values than just typing the field as a plain string. A genuinely practical use is typing route paths with dynamic segments: given a route pattern like '/users/:id', a template literal type combined with conditional types and infer can extract 'id' as the literal parameter name, which some fully-typed routing libraries use to guarantee, at compile time, that every place a route is used passes exactly the right named parameters with the right types, catching a typo'd or missing route parameter as a compile error rather than a runtime bug. Another practical case is enforcing a naming convention for CSS custom properties or design tokens, like type SpacingToken = '--space-' + ('xs' | 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' | 'xl'), which restricts a given string prop to only the design system's actual defined spacing tokens rather than accepting any arbitrary string, catching a typo'd token name at compile time instead of it silently failing to apply any style at runtime.
weak: A weak answer has never encountered template literal types and doesn't realize TypeScript can enforce compile-time constraints on the actual structure of a string value, not just that it's 'a string'.
followUp: How would a fully-typed routing library use template literal types combined with infer to guarantee a route's dynamic parameters are passed correctly at every call site?

question: What is declaration merging, and how does module augmentation let you safely extend a third-party library's types?
concise: Declaration merging is TypeScript's behavior of automatically combining multiple declarations of the same name (interfaces, namespaces, or a namespace with a function/class of the same name) into a single merged definition; module augmentation uses this mechanism deliberately to add new properties or methods to an existing module's exported types, for example adding a custom property to Express's Request type, or extending a state-management library's root state type, without modifying that library's own source code.
strong: If two separate interface declarations share the same name, even across different files, TypeScript merges their members into one combined interface rather than treating the second as an error or an override, which at first sounds like a footgun but is actually the deliberate mechanism that makes several important patterns possible. A concrete real example: many teams using Express with TypeScript need to attach custom data to the request object, like req.user after an auth middleware runs; since you can't (and shouldn't) directly edit Express's own shipped type definitions, you instead write a small ambient declaration file that reopens and augments the existing Express namespace's Request interface, adding your custom user: AuthUser property, and TypeScript merges your addition with Express's original definition everywhere in your codebase. The same technique is used to extend libraries' module-level types generally, for example augmenting a CSS-in-JS library's base theme interface with your app's actual design tokens so that every usage of the theme object throughout the codebase is fully typed with your specific colors and spacing values, without needing to fork or modify the library itself. The main risk to be aware of is that this is a global, ambient effect: an augmentation applies everywhere that type is used across the entire codebase, so it should be used deliberately and documented clearly, not scattered casually across many files.
weak: A weak answer has never heard of module augmentation and would instead resort to casting req as any every time they need to access a custom property, silently losing type safety at every one of those call sites instead of fixing it once, globally, at the source.
followUp: What's the difference between augmenting an existing module's types (module augmentation) versus declaring a brand-new ambient module for a library that ships with no types at all?

question: What do the strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny compiler flags actually do, and why is enabling 'strict' mode as a whole worth the friction?
concise: strictNullChecks makes null and undefined distinct types that must be explicitly included in a type's definition wherever they're actually possible, rather than silently assignable to any type by default, which catches a huge class of 'cannot read property of undefined' runtime errors at compile time instead; noImplicitAny requires every value's type to be explicit or correctly inferred rather than silently falling back to any when the compiler can't infer one, which prevents type safety from silently leaking away in exactly the places it matters most, like an untyped function parameter.
strong: Without strictNullChecks, every type implicitly includes null and undefined as valid values, meaning code like user.name.toUpperCase() type-checks fine even if user could genuinely be undefined at that point, and the resulting runtime crash, 'cannot read properties of undefined', is one of the single most common production JavaScript errors; enabling strictNullChecks forces you to explicitly narrow (with an if check, optional chaining, or a default value) before accessing a property on anything typed as possibly null or undefined, converting what would have been a runtime crash into a compile-time reminder to handle that case. noImplicitAny targets a different but related gap: without it, if TypeScript can't infer a specific type for a function parameter (commonly because you forgot to annotate it), it silently falls back to any rather than erroring, meaning that parameter, and everything derived from it, quietly loses type safety without any visible warning in your code; enabling the flag turns that silent fallback into a compile error instead, forcing an explicit type annotation. Together with the other strict-family flags, this front-loads real friction, since a codebase not built with strict mode from the start typically surfaces a large number of previously-hidden real bugs the moment you turn it on, but that friction is exactly the point: it's finding bugs during development instead of in production, and virtually every team I've seen that adopted strict mode considers the migration cost worth it once past the initial cleanup.
weak: A weak answer treats strict mode as just 'more annoying red squiggly lines' without being able to name specifically what class of real, common runtime bugs (null/undefined access, silently untyped parameters) each flag actually prevents.
followUp: If your team inherits a large existing codebase with strict mode disabled, how would you approach turning it on incrementally rather than all at once?

question: How would you type a form using react-hook-form with TypeScript, including nested fields and a resolver for validation?
concise: Define a TypeScript type (or infer one from a Zod schema) describing the form's full data shape, pass it as the generic parameter to useForm<FormValues>(), and use a resolver (like zodResolver from a Zod schema) so validation rules and the static type stay defined in exactly one place instead of two separately-maintained sources of truth; nested fields are typed automatically through dot-path autocomplete (like address.city) as long as the generic type itself correctly models the nested structure.
strong: Defining the schema once with Zod and deriving both the runtime validator and the static FormValues type from it (via z.infer) means the validation rules and the TypeScript type can never silently drift apart, which is a common real bug when a team maintains a hand-written interface separately from a hand-written validation function and one of them gets updated without the other. Passing that FormValues type into useForm<FormValues>() makes register, watch, setValue, and formState.errors all fully typed, so register('addres.city') (a typo) is a compile error rather than a silently-ignored, never-registered field, and nested object fields are correctly represented as dot-path strings like 'address.city' as long as the FormValues type itself models that nested shape correctly. Wiring up zodResolver(FormSchema) as the resolver means react-hook-form runs the actual Zod validation on submit (and optionally on blur/change) and populates formState.errors with field-specific messages automatically, without needing to hand-write parallel validation logic separately from the schema. For a multi-step or deeply nested form, like a checkout form with a nested shipping address and a nested payment method, this pattern keeps the whole form's shape, validation, and error messages defined in one schema, which scales much better than maintaining validation logic by hand alongside a separately hand-written type.
weak: A weak answer hand-writes a separate TypeScript interface for the form values and separately hand-writes validation logic (or skips a resolver entirely and validates manually on submit), risking the schema and the type silently drifting out of sync over time.
followUp: How would you type a dynamically-added array field in react-hook-form, like a list of line items in an invoice form, using useFieldArray?

question: What's the difference between readonly on a property and Readonly<T> as a utility type, and does either provide deep immutability?
concise: readonly on an individual property prevents reassigning just that one property after the object is created; Readonly<T> applies that same readonly modifier to every top-level property of T via a mapped type; neither is deep, meaning if a readonly property's value is itself an object or array, that nested value can still be freely mutated, exactly like the shallow-only limitation of Object.freeze at runtime.
strong: Marking a single property readonly in an interface, like readonly id: string, means TypeScript will produce a compile error if any code tries to reassign obj.id after the object is constructed, though this is purely a compile-time check, since actual runtime code compiled to plain JavaScript has no such protection built in unless you also apply something like Object.freeze at runtime. Readonly<T> is really just a mapped type that applies that same readonly modifier across every property of T at once, saving you from manually writing readonly in front of every single field individually. The shallow limitation matters in exactly the same way it does for Object.freeze: if a readonly property holds a nested object or array, TypeScript happily prevents you from reassigning that top-level property to a different object entirely, but it does nothing to stop you from mutating that nested object's own properties or pushing into a nested array, since the readonly modifier only ever applies to the one property slot it's directly attached to, not recursively to everything reachable through it. For genuine deep immutability, at both the type level and the runtime level, you'd typically reach for a dedicated pattern, either a recursive DeepReadonly mapped type combined with an actual runtime deep-freeze, or simply adopting an immutability-focused state library like Immer, which handles the runtime side of this correctly by default.
weak: A weak answer assumes Readonly<T> (or readonly individually) makes an object's entire nested structure immutable, missing that both are shallow, exactly analogous to the same well-known limitation of Object.freeze at runtime.
followUp: How would you write a recursive DeepReadonly<T> mapped type that applies readonly to every nested level of an object type?

question: How would you design types for an RBAC (role-based access control) system so that invalid role/permission combinations are caught at compile time rather than only at runtime?
concise: Model roles and permissions as literal union types (not plain strings), define a typed mapping (often a Record<Role, Permission[]> or a more granular per-action mapping) describing exactly which permissions each role grants, and expose a typed hasPermission(role: Role, permission: Permission) helper so any place in the codebase checking access goes through a single, exhaustively-typed source of truth rather than scattered string comparisons that could silently typo a role or permission name.
strong: Typing role and permission as plain strings anywhere in the codebase means a typo like checking for 'Admin' instead of the actual 'admin' literal silently fails at runtime with no warning at all, quietly granting or denying access incorrectly; defining them instead as literal union types, like type Role = 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer', makes any such typo a compile error immediately, everywhere that value is used throughout the codebase. Building a single, centralized Record<Role, Permission[]> (or a similarly-typed structure) mapping each role to its granted permissions, and using TypeScript's Record type specifically, means the compiler will actually force you to provide an entry for every role in the union, catching the case where a new role is added to the Role union but someone forgets to define what permissions it actually grants, which is exactly the kind of silent gap that's dangerous in an authorization system. Any place in the app that needs to check access, like conditionally rendering an admin-only button, should go through one shared, typed helper function rather than duplicating the permission-check logic (and the string literals it compares against) at every individual call site, since duplicated logic is what eventually drifts out of sync as the permission model evolves. It's critical to remember, though, that this entire typed system only guards the frontend's UI decisions, like which buttons to show; the backend must independently and redundantly enforce every one of these same authorization rules on every actual request, since a user can always bypass frontend code entirely and call the API directly, so frontend RBAC typing is strictly a UX layer, never a security boundary on its own.
weak: A weak answer types roles and permissions as plain strings scattered across many files with ad hoc string comparisons, and, separately, treats this frontend typing as if it were itself a real security boundary rather than purely a UX convenience that the backend must independently re-enforce.
followUp: Why must the backend independently re-check every one of these same permission rules on every request, even though the frontend already hides unauthorized UI elements?

question: Explain the virtual DOM and reconciliation, and why keys matter when rendering a list.
concise: React keeps a lightweight in-memory representation of the UI (the virtual DOM), and on every update it diffs the new tree against the previous one (reconciliation) to compute the minimal set of real DOM changes needed; keys give React a stable identity for each list item across renders, so it can correctly match, reorder, update, or remove specific DOM nodes and component state instead of naively diffing by position, which breaks badly when items are inserted, removed, or reordered.
strong: Reconciliation compares the previous and new element trees level by level, and for lists specifically, React needs some way to know 'this new item corresponds to that old item' so it can preserve DOM nodes, focus state, and component-local state correctly across a re-render, rather than assuming the item at index 2 last time is still the same logical item at index 2 this time. Using the array index as a key works fine only if the list never reorders, inserts, or removes items from anywhere except the very end; the moment an item is removed from the middle or the list is reordered (like a sortable table), index-based keys cause React to misattribute state, for example a text input's typed value or a checkbox's checked state can end up attached to the wrong row after a reorder, since React thinks 'index 2' is still the same logical item even though the underlying data at that position changed. Using a stable, unique identifier from the actual data, like a database id, instead of the array index, fixes this because React can correctly track each item's true identity across renders regardless of how the list is reordered or filtered. This matters concretely in a dashboard with a sortable, filterable table: without stable keys, sorting the table can cause row-level UI state (like an expanded detail row, or a locally-edited but unsaved cell) to visually 'jump' to the wrong row.
weak: A weak answer says 'always add a key to satisfy the React warning' without understanding that using the array index as that key is often functionally wrong, not just a style nitpick, and can cause real state-mismatch bugs in reorderable or filterable lists.
followUp: What specific bug would you actually observe in the UI if a sortable table used array index as the key and a user sorted a column while one row had an open inline edit field?

question: When would you use useReducer instead of useState?
concise: useReducer is preferable when a component's state involves multiple related sub-values that update together, when the next state depends on complex logic involving the previous state and an action, or when you want to centralize and test state transition logic separately from the component, similar to a mini Redux reducer scoped to a single component.
strong: useState is perfectly fine, and usually simpler, for independent pieces of state that update on their own, like a single boolean toggle or a text input's value. useReducer becomes the better choice once a component's state has several fields that change together in response to the same event, since with useState you often end up calling several setters back-to-back inside one handler, which works but scatters the actual state-transition logic across many separate handler functions instead of having one clear, centralized place describing every possible way the state can change. A concrete example is a multi-step form wizard, where a single 'go to next step' action might need to simultaneously advance the current step, validate the outgoing step's data, and update a combined form-values object; modeling this as a reducer with explicit action types like NEXT_STEP, SET_FIELD, and RESET makes the state machine's behavior explicit, testable in isolation from any component, and much easier to reason about as the number of possible transitions grows. useReducer also composes naturally with useContext for passing a dispatch function down to deeply nested components without prop drilling every individual setter function, which is a pattern I use often for complex forms or multi-panel dashboards with shared, related state.
weak: A weak answer treats useReducer as strictly more complex and therefore worse in every case, without recognizing the concrete scenario, several related state fields updating together through well-defined transitions, where it actually produces clearer, more testable code than several separate useState calls.
followUp: How would you test a reducer function in isolation, without rendering the component that uses it at all?

question: Explain the useEffect dependency array, and what actually happens if you omit a value that the effect uses.
concise: The dependency array tells React when to re-run the effect: React compares each value in the array to its previous render's value using Object.is (roughly ===), and re-runs the effect if any of them changed; omitting a value the effect actually reads from creates a stale closure bug, where the effect keeps using the value from whatever render it was originally created in, rather than the latest one, since the function isn't being recreated and re-run to pick up the new value.
strong: Every render creates a brand-new version of the effect function (since it's just a regular function defined inside the component body), closing over that specific render's props and state values; the dependency array is what tells React whether it's actually necessary to discard the previous effect's cleanup and run this new version, by comparing each listed dependency's current value to its value from the previous render. If you omit a value the effect body actually reads, like a prop or state variable referenced inside it, React has no way to know it needs to re-run the effect when that value changes, so the effect keeps executing using the stale value captured in the closure from whichever render it last actually ran in, this is the classic 'stale closure' bug, extremely common with effects that set up an interval or a WebSocket handler referencing some piece of state without including it in the dependency array. ESLint's exhaustive-deps rule exists specifically to catch this class of bug by flagging any value used inside an effect that isn't listed in its dependency array, and while it's tempting to silence that warning to 'fix' an infinite-loop symptom, the actual underlying fix is almost always different: either genuinely include the dependency and make sure it doesn't change unnecessarily every render (by memoizing it, or moving it inside the effect if it doesn't need to be a prop/state at all), or restructure the effect using a functional state updater or a ref for values that shouldn't trigger a re-run but still need their latest value read inside the effect.
weak: A weak answer silences the exhaustive-deps ESLint warning by disabling the rule inline whenever it's inconvenient, without understanding that the warning is usually pointing at a real, reproducible stale-closure bug rather than a false positive.
followUp: How would you fix the stale-closure interval bug above without adding count to the dependency array and causing the interval to be recreated on every count change?

question: What's the difference between useMemo and useCallback, and when do either actually matter for performance?
concise: useMemo memoizes a computed value, recomputing it only when its dependencies change, useful for expensive calculations; useCallback memoizes a function reference itself (it's actually just useMemo returning the function unchanged instead of its result), useful for keeping a stable function identity across renders; both only actually matter for performance when the memoized value/function is either genuinely expensive to (re)compute, or when its referential stability is required to avoid breaking a downstream optimization like React.memo or a dependency array.
strong: useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a, b), [a, b]) re-runs the computation only when a or b changes between renders, which is worth doing specifically when that computation is genuinely expensive, like filtering and sorting a large dataset for a table, since otherwise it would redo that work on every single render regardless of whether the relevant inputs actually changed. useCallback(fn, deps) is really just useMemo applied to a function value instead of a computed result, giving you back the exact same function reference across renders as long as its dependencies haven't changed, rather than a brand-new function identity every render; this matters specifically when that function is passed as a prop to a child wrapped in React.memo, since React.memo's shallow prop comparison would otherwise see a 'new' function prop on every parent render (even if its actual behavior is identical) and re-render the child anyway, defeating the memoization entirely. The important nuance interviewers look for is knowing that both hooks have a real cost too, since they still run on every render to check whether dependencies changed, and they use additional memory to store the cached value, so wrapping every single value and function in useMemo/useCallback by default, 'just in case', is itself a mild performance anti-pattern that adds needless complexity without any actual measured benefit for cheap computations or components that don't rely on referential stability anywhere downstream.
weak: A weak answer wraps every function and computed value in useCallback/useMemo indiscriminately across an entire codebase as a blanket 'best practice', without being able to articulate when it actually provides a measurable benefit versus just adding overhead and complexity for no real gain.
followUp: If a child component isn't wrapped in React.memo at all, does passing it a useCallback-memoized function prop provide any actual performance benefit?

question: What are common performance pitfalls with React Context, and how would you avoid unnecessary re-renders when using it?
concise: Every component that consumes a context via useContext re-renders whenever that context's value changes, regardless of which specific part of the value it actually uses, so passing a large object (or one that's recreated fresh on every provider render) causes broad, often unnecessary re-renders across the whole consuming subtree; mitigations include splitting a large context into several smaller, more narrowly-scoped contexts, memoizing the context value object itself so it only changes reference when its actual contents change, and, for very high-frequency updates, avoiding context entirely in favor of a dedicated state management library with selector-based subscriptions.
strong: Context intentionally has no built-in mechanism for a consumer to subscribe to only part of the provided value, so the moment a Provider's value prop changes reference, every single component anywhere below it that calls useContext for that context re-renders, even if that particular component only ever reads one small, unrelated field from a large combined value object. A very common, easy-to-miss version of this bug is defining the context value inline in the Provider's JSX, like value={{ user, theme, setTheme }}, since that creates a brand-new object reference on every single render of the provider component, causing every consumer to re-render every single time, regardless of whether user or theme actually changed at all; wrapping that value in useMemo with the correct dependencies fixes the unnecessary-object-identity-churn part of the problem, but does nothing about the more fundamental issue that consumers still can't subscribe to just a subset of the value. The more structural fix is splitting one large context into several smaller, independently-scoped contexts, for example a separate UserContext and ThemeContext instead of one combined AppContext, so a component that only cares about theme never re-renders due to unrelated user data changing. For state that updates very frequently, like real-time collaborative cursor positions or live-streaming numeric values on a trading dashboard, I'd avoid Context entirely and reach for a state library like Zustand or Redux with selector-based subscriptions instead, since those let a component subscribe to and re-render based on only the specific narrow slice of state it actually reads, which Context structurally cannot do on its own.
weak: A weak answer assumes Context is a general-purpose, fully optimized global state solution equivalent to Redux, without knowing its fundamental lack of selective subscription is the actual root cause of a whole category of real-world React performance bugs.
followUp: How does a library like Zustand or Redux achieve selective re-rendering (subscribing to only a slice of state) in a way that plain React Context structurally cannot?

question: What is a custom hook, and what are the rules of hooks it must still follow?
concise: A custom hook is just a regular JavaScript function, conventionally named starting with 'use', that calls one or more of React's built-in hooks internally to encapsulate and reuse stateful logic across components; it must still follow the same rules of hooks as any component: only call hooks at the top level (never inside conditionals, loops, or nested functions) and only call hooks from a React function component or from another custom hook, never from a plain function.
strong: The entire point of a custom hook is code reuse for stateful logic, without needing a higher-order component or a render-props wrapper: for example, a useDebounce(value, delay) custom hook internally uses useState and useEffect to return a debounced version of a value, and any component that needs that exact behavior can just call it directly, hiding the setTimeout/clearTimeout bookkeeping entirely behind a simple, reusable interface. Because a custom hook still ultimately calls React's actual hooks underneath, it's bound by the same rules: hooks can't be called conditionally, since React relies on hooks being called in the exact same order on every render to correctly match each hook call to its associated internal state slot, so wrapping a hook call in an if statement can silently misalign state between renders in a way that's very hard to debug; this is exactly why the built-in eslint-plugin-react-hooks rule flags conditional hook calls as an error, not just a style suggestion. A well-designed custom hook should also have a clear, minimal return interface, typically returning just the specific value(s) and function(s) a consuming component actually needs, and should be named descriptively enough that its purpose is clear without needing to read its implementation, like useAuthUser() or usePagination() rather than a vague, overly generic name.
weak: A weak answer describes a custom hook vaguely as 'a reusable function' without mentioning that it must still obey the rules of hooks (no conditional calls), which is the actual constraint interviewers are checking for real understanding of.
followUp: Why does calling a hook conditionally (inside an if statement) risk misaligning a component's internal state between renders?

question: When would you use React.memo, and what's a common reason it doesn't prevent a re-render even when props look unchanged?
concise: React.memo skips re-rendering a component if its props are shallowly equal to the previous render's props, which is worth applying to components that render often, are relatively expensive to render, and whose props don't change on most parent re-renders; it commonly fails to prevent a re-render anyway because a shallow comparison considers a newly-created object, array, or function prop (even one with identical contents) to be a different value, since it's a different reference, so passing an inline object literal or an unmemoized callback as a prop defeats React.memo every time regardless of the actual data inside it.
strong: React.memo wraps a component and, before re-rendering it, does a shallow comparison of every prop against its value in the previous render, bailing out of re-rendering entirely if all of them are reference-equal (or, for primitives, value-equal); this is genuinely valuable for something like a single row in a large virtualized table, where re-rendering hundreds of rows every time any unrelated piece of parent state changes is wasteful if most rows' actual data hasn't changed. The classic reason it silently fails to help is passing a prop that's recreated fresh on every parent render, most commonly an inline object literal like style={{ color: 'red' }} or an inline arrow function like onClick={() => handleClick(item.id)} directly in JSX; both create a brand-new reference every single render, so React.memo's shallow comparison correctly (from its own narrow perspective) determines the prop 'changed' and re-renders the child anyway, even though the actual meaningful content of that prop is identical to last time. The fix is to memoize whatever's being passed, wrapping the object in useMemo and the function in useCallback with correct dependencies, so their references genuinely stay stable across renders when their underlying values haven't changed, letting React.memo's shallow comparison actually succeed and skip the unnecessary re-render.
weak: A weak answer applies React.memo to a component and, when it doesn't seem to help, concludes 'memo doesn't really work' rather than investigating whether an inline object or function prop is defeating the shallow comparison, which is by far the most common real cause.
followUp: How would you write a custom comparison function for React.memo's second argument if you specifically need a deep comparison for one particular object prop?

question: What's the difference between controlled and uncontrolled form inputs in React?
concise: A controlled input's value is driven entirely by React state (value={state} plus an onChange handler that updates that state), making React the single source of truth for the input's current value at all times; an uncontrolled input manages its own value internally in the DOM, and React only reads its current value on demand, typically via a ref, rather than tracking every keystroke in state.
strong: Controlled inputs give you full, real-time visibility into and control over the value on every keystroke, which is what you need for live validation feedback, formatting input as the user types (like automatically inserting dashes in a phone number), or conditionally enabling a submit button based on the current value; the trade-off is that every keystroke triggers a state update and a re-render of at least that component. Uncontrolled inputs let the DOM manage the value natively and you only pull the current value out when you actually need it, typically on form submit via a ref, which avoids a re-render on every keystroke and can be simpler for very large forms where per-keystroke reactivity genuinely isn't needed anywhere. In practice, most real-world forms end up controlled, especially once you're using a library like react-hook-form, which actually uses uncontrolled inputs with refs internally by default for performance, while still giving you the ergonomics of a controlled-feeling API, subscribing to specific fields' values only where a component actually needs to react to them, which is a good middle ground for large forms with many fields where per-keystroke re-rendering the entire form would be wasteful.
weak: A weak answer claims uncontrolled inputs are simply 'the old, wrong way to do it' and controlled is always strictly better, without recognizing the real performance trade-off (a re-render per keystroke) that libraries like react-hook-form specifically address by leaning on uncontrolled inputs under the hood.
followUp: How does react-hook-form avoid a re-render on every keystroke while still letting a component conditionally react to a specific field's current value when needed?

question: How do error boundaries work in React, and what kinds of errors do they NOT catch?
concise: An error boundary is a class component implementing static getDerivedStateFromError and/or componentDidCatch, which catches JavaScript errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of its child component tree, letting you render a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app; it does not catch errors inside event handlers, errors in asynchronous code (like a setTimeout callback or a rejected promise inside a useEffect), errors during server-side rendering, or errors thrown inside the error boundary itself.
strong: Error boundaries exist because, by default, an uncaught error thrown anywhere during rendering unmounts the entire component tree below the root, which for a full single-page app can mean the entire app going blank on a single unhandled error in one small feature; wrapping a risky subtree, like a single dashboard widget that renders complex third-party chart data, in an error boundary means a rendering bug in just that one widget shows a small 'something went wrong' fallback for that widget specifically, while the rest of the dashboard keeps working normally. The important limitation to know well is exactly what an error boundary does not catch: it only catches errors that occur synchronously during the render phase (including lifecycle methods and constructors) of its children, so an error thrown inside an onClick handler, or a rejected promise inside a useEffect's async logic, or an error inside a setTimeout callback, propagates as a completely separate, uncaught error that the boundary has no visibility into at all, and needs its own try/catch or .catch() handling at the point where that async or event-handler code actually runs. There's currently no hook-based equivalent to error boundaries (they must still be class components, since the relevant lifecycle methods have no hook equivalent), so most teams either use a small maintained library like react-error-boundary, or keep one hand-written class component as the boundary and treat it as boilerplate infrastructure rather than something rewritten per feature.
weak: A weak answer assumes an error boundary catches all errors anywhere in the app, including inside event handlers and async code, and would be surprised in practice when a try/catch-free async error inside a useEffect completely bypasses the boundary they set up.
followUp: How would you handle and report an error that occurs inside an async operation started from a useEffect, given that an error boundary won't catch it?

question: What problem does Suspense solve, and how is Suspense for data fetching different from just showing a loading spinner with useState?
concise: Suspense lets a component 'pause' rendering and show a fallback UI declaratively while it (or a descendant) is waiting on something asynchronous, like a lazily-loaded component chunk or, with a properly integrated data-fetching library, data that hasn't arrived yet; unlike manually managing an isLoading boolean in state, Suspense centralizes loading-state UI at whatever boundary you choose in the tree, coordinates multiple simultaneously-loading children under a single shared fallback without extra bookkeeping, and avoids the need to thread loading and error state through every individual component that fetches something.
strong: With the manual useState-based approach, every single component that fetches its own data typically needs its own isLoading, error, and data state, plus its own conditional rendering logic to show a spinner or an error message, which duplicates the same pattern across dozens of components and makes coordinating multiple simultaneous loading states (like 'show one spinner until both the user profile and their recent orders have loaded, rather than two separate spinners popping in at different times') genuinely awkward to hand-code correctly. Suspense flips this: a component that isn't ready yet 'throws' a promise (this is handled internally by a properly Suspense-integrated data source, not something you write by hand), React catches that thrown promise, and renders the nearest ancestor Suspense boundary's fallback instead, automatically retrying the render once the promise resolves; wrapping several data-dependent children in one shared Suspense boundary means they can all block on the same single fallback together, coordinated for free, without any component needing to know about or coordinate with any of its siblings' loading states. React.lazy for code-split components already works exactly this way today, which is the most common thing people first encounter it for; Suspense for actual data fetching requires a properly integrated library or framework, like React Query in Suspense mode or Next.js's App Router data fetching, since a raw useEffect-based fetch call, by itself, doesn't know how to correctly 'throw' the loading promise in the way Suspense expects.
code:
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
  <UserProfile /> {/* suspends while its data loads */}
  <RecentOrders /> {/* suspends independently, but shares the same fallback */}
</Suspense>
weak: A weak answer treats Suspense as just 'a built-in loading spinner component' without understanding that its real value is coordinating multiple independent async dependencies under one shared boundary, and that a plain useEffect fetch doesn't automatically integrate with it without a properly Suspense-compatible data layer.
followUp: Why doesn't a plain useEffect-based fetch call automatically work with Suspense the way React.lazy does, and what does a data-fetching library need to do differently to support it?

question: How does React Server Components in React 18/19 change the relationship between 'server' and 'client' components, and what can and can't a Server Component do?
concise: Server Components render entirely on the server (or at build time) and never ship their own JavaScript to the browser at all, meaning they can directly access server-only resources, like a database or filesystem, and reduce client bundle size, but they cannot use hooks like useState or useEffect, cannot attach event handlers, and cannot use browser-only APIs, since none of their code ever actually runs in the browser; a Client Component (marked explicitly, in frameworks like Next.js, with a 'use client' directive) works exactly like classic React always has, running in the browser with full access to state, effects, and event handlers, and can be rendered as a child of a Server Component, but a Server Component cannot itself be imported and rendered inside a Client Component's module boundary the same way in reverse.
strong: The core shift is that, for the first time, React components can render exclusively on the server with zero client-side JavaScript footprint at all, not just an initial HTML render that's then re-hydrated with a full copy of the same component's JS, the way traditional SSR has always worked; a Server Component that renders a static product description fetched directly from a database ships literally none of its own component code to the browser, only the resulting HTML/RSC payload, which is a real, measurable reduction in client bundle size for content-heavy pages. Because Server Components never run in the browser, they structurally cannot use any hook that depends on client-side interactivity or lifecycle, like useState or useEffect, and they can't attach event handlers like onClick directly, since there's no client-side JavaScript instance of that component around to respond to the event; anything that needs interactivity, state, or a browser API has to be a Client Component instead, and Server Components render Client Components as children by importing and using them like normal, passing serializable props (an important, easy-to-miss constraint: you can't pass a function or a class instance as a prop from a Server Component into a Client Component, since it has to be serialized across the server/client boundary). A practical mental model I use: default to Server Components for anything that's static or purely data-driven with no need for interactivity, like a page's overall layout, static text, or a data table's initial render, and mark only the genuinely interactive leaf pieces, like a button with an onClick handler or a form with local state, as Client Components, which keeps the client bundle as small as possible.
weak: A weak answer treats Server Components as 'just SSR with extra steps' without understanding the key distinction, that a Server Component ships zero of its own JavaScript to the client at all, and that this is precisely why it can't use hooks or event handlers directly.
followUp: Why can't a Server Component pass a function (like an onClick handler) directly as a prop into a Client Component, and what pattern do you use instead when a Client Component needs to trigger server-side logic?

question: How would you use React Query (TanStack Query) or SWR instead of a manual useEffect-based fetch, and what specific problems does it solve?
concise: A manual useEffect fetch requires hand-rolling loading/error state, request cancellation on unmount, caching (so navigating back to a previously-visited view doesn't refetch unnecessarily), deduplication of identical simultaneous requests, and background refetching/invalidation on demand; a library like React Query or SWR provides all of this out of the box through a single useQuery hook keyed by a query key, dramatically reducing boilerplate and eliminating a whole category of subtle bugs like race conditions and stale-closure fetch effects.
strong: A hand-rolled useEffect fetch has to solve several genuinely tricky problems correctly every single time it's written: canceling or ignoring a request if the component unmounts (or the query's inputs change) before it resolves, to avoid calling setState on an unmounted component or, worse, applying a stale response that resolves after a newer request already started; caching results so that navigating away from a view and back to it doesn't trigger a redundant refetch of data you already have; deduplicating identical requests fired from multiple components at nearly the same time; and providing some mechanism to manually invalidate and refetch data after a mutation, like refreshing a list after successfully creating a new item. React Query solves all of this behind one consistent, small API: useQuery(['users', id], fetchUser) automatically caches by that query key, dedupes simultaneous identical requests, tracks loading/error/success state for you, refetches in the background on window refocus or reconnect (configurably), and exposes an invalidateQueries function so a mutation (via useMutation) can precisely invalidate just the affected cached queries, triggering a background refetch without needing to manually track and update state across unrelated components. In practice, adopting React Query on a dashboard-heavy app usually deletes a large amount of hand-written, bug-prone data-fetching boilerplate, and the built-in devtools make cache state genuinely inspectable, which is difficult to replicate well with ad hoc useEffect-based fetching.
weak: A weak answer dismisses React Query as 'unnecessary overhead for a simple fetch' without recognizing the real, easy-to-get-wrong problems (race conditions, redundant refetches, cache invalidation after a mutation) it solves that a hand-rolled useEffect fetch has to solve correctly every single time from scratch.
followUp: How would React Query handle a race condition where a user rapidly changes a filter, firing off several requests, and an older request's response arrives after a newer one's?

question: What's the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect, and when would you actually need useLayoutEffect?
concise: Both run a side effect after render, but useEffect runs asynchronously after the browser has painted the updated DOM to the screen, while useLayoutEffect runs synchronously immediately after DOM mutations but before the browser paints, blocking the paint until it finishes; useLayoutEffect is needed specifically when you must read a layout value (like an element's measured size or position) and synchronously make a DOM change based on it before the user has a chance to see a visual flicker of the incorrect intermediate state.
strong: For the vast majority of side effects, like fetching data, subscribing to an event, or setting a timer, useEffect is the right choice, since running after paint means it never blocks the browser from showing the user the updated screen as quickly as possible. useLayoutEffect exists for a narrower but real case: when an effect needs to measure something about the just-rendered DOM (like an element's actual rendered height via getBoundingClientRect) and then synchronously apply another DOM change based on that measurement, for example repositioning a tooltip so it doesn't overflow off the edge of the viewport; if you did that measurement-and-adjustment inside useEffect instead, the browser would have already painted the tooltip in its initial, potentially-wrong position, and the user would see a brief, visible flicker or jump as it snaps to the corrected position a frame later, whereas useLayoutEffect's synchronous, pre-paint timing means the correction happens invisibly before anything is shown. The trade-off is that because useLayoutEffect blocks painting until it finishes, an expensive computation inside it can visibly delay the browser from updating the screen at all, so it should be reserved specifically for fast, layout-measurement-driven DOM adjustments, not used as a general-purpose default replacement for useEffect.
weak: A weak answer treats useLayoutEffect as simply 'a version of useEffect that runs a bit earlier' without knowing the actual, concrete symptom (a visible flicker of incorrect layout) that motivates reaching for it specifically, or without knowing it blocks painting.
followUp: What would visually happen if you used useEffect instead of useLayoutEffect for a tooltip repositioning calculation like the one above?

question: What is the compound components pattern, and what problem does it solve compared to a single component with many boolean/config props?
concise: Compound components (like a Tabs component exposing Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab, and Tabs.Panel as related sub-components sharing implicit state via context) let consumers compose a component's internal structure flexibly and declaratively in JSX, instead of the parent component needing an ever-growing list of configuration props (like renderHeader, showIcon, iconPosition) trying to anticipate every possible layout variation up front.
strong: A single monolithic component that tries to support every possible variation through props tends to accumulate a long, awkward list of configuration options over time, like a Tabs component with props for tabLabels, activeTabIndex, renderTabIcon, tabPosition, and so on, and eventually some genuinely reasonable customization (like putting a badge next to one specific tab, or making just one tab disabled) doesn't fit cleanly into any existing prop and forces yet another prop to be bolted on. The compound components pattern instead exposes several related sub-components that share implicit state through context internally, so instead of configuring everything through props on one root component, the consumer composes the actual JSX structure directly, like <Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab>Profile</Tabs.Tab><Tabs.Tab disabled>Billing</Tabs.Tab></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel>...</Tabs.Panel></Tabs>, which reads declaratively and lets the consumer freely intersperse other elements, like a badge or an icon, directly in the markup without the root component needing to know about or expose a prop for that specific case at all. This is exactly the pattern used by well-designed component libraries like Radix UI and shadcn/ui's Tabs, Select, and Dialog components, and it scales much better as a design system grows, since new layout variations are handled by consumers composing existing pieces differently, rather than requiring the library author to anticipate and add a new prop for every future use case.
weak: A weak answer keeps adding more and more boolean and render-prop configuration options to a single monolithic component to handle every new requirement, without recognizing that this is exactly the accumulating complexity problem the compound components pattern is designed to solve.
followUp: How does the compound components pattern typically share state between the parent and its sub-components internally, and what happens if a consumer renders Tabs.Tab outside of a Tabs parent?

question: What is prop drilling, and what are the trade-offs between fixing it with Context, a state management library, or component composition?
concise: Prop drilling is passing a value through several layers of intermediate components that don't use it themselves, just to get it to a deeply nested component that does; Context removes the need to pass it through every intermediate layer but re-renders every consumer on any value change and can encourage overly-global state; a state management library (Zustand, Redux) adds selector-based subscriptions and works well for complex, app-wide state; often the simplest fix, component composition (passing the deeply-nested component itself as a children or slot prop from a level that already has the data), avoids the problem entirely without adding any new abstraction.
strong: Prop drilling itself isn't inherently wrong, it's just explicit and sometimes verbose, but it becomes a genuine maintenance problem once a value has to pass through four or five intermediate components that have no use for it themselves, since every one of those components' prop signatures becomes coupled to a piece of data they don't actually care about, and adding a new intermediate layer later means remembering to thread the prop through it too. Context is the most commonly reached-for fix, and it's appropriate for state that's genuinely broad and relatively infrequent to change, like the current authenticated user or a theme setting, but it's easy to overuse for state that changes often or is really only needed by a couple of components, since every consumer re-renders on any change to the context value, as covered in the Context performance question. A frequently overlooked, simpler fix is component composition: instead of passing a data value down through several layers just so a deeply nested component can use it, you restructure so that the component with the data renders the components that need it directly, passing them as children or a named slot prop at the level where the data actually lives, which avoids threading the data through intermediate components entirely, since composition, not prop-passing, is doing the work of getting the JSX where it needs to be. For genuinely complex, frequently-updated, cross-cutting application state, like a large e-commerce cart or a complex multi-panel dashboard's shared state, a dedicated state management library with selector-based subscriptions is usually the most scalable choice, since it avoids both prop drilling and Context's broad-re-render problem at once.
weak: A weak answer treats Context as the automatic, universal fix for any instance of prop drilling, without considering that component composition often solves the same problem more simply, with no new abstraction and no re-render trade-off at all.
followUp: Give a concrete example of restructuring a component tree with composition (passing a component as a prop) to eliminate prop drilling without introducing Context at all.

question: How would you decide between React Context, Zustand/Redux, and server-state libraries like React Query for managing state in a mid-sized app?
concise: The key question is where the state actually lives conceptually: data fetched from an API is 'server state' and belongs in a library like React Query, which handles caching, background refetching, and invalidation concerns that client-state tools don't address at all; genuinely global client-only UI state that changes at a moderate frequency (like a shopping cart, feature flags, or the currently selected workspace) fits well in a lightweight store like Zustand or Redux with selector-based subscriptions; state that's local to one component or a small, closely related subtree (like a form's current values, or whether a specific dropdown is open) should just be plain useState/useReducer, kept as local as possible, since lifting it higher than necessary only adds complexity without any benefit.
strong: A mistake I see often is treating all state as one undifferentiated category and reaching for one big global store for everything, including data that actually came from an API; server state has fundamentally different characteristics from client state, it can go stale, it can be shared and deduplicated across multiple components requesting the same resource, and it needs revalidation logic, none of which a generic client-state store like Redux was designed to handle well, which is exactly why dedicated server-state libraries like React Query or SWR exist as a separate concern from client-state management entirely. For genuinely global client-only state, meaning UI state that many unrelated parts of the app need to read or write, like a shopping cart's contents, the currently active workspace in a multi-tenant dashboard, or feature flag values, a lightweight store like Zustand gives selector-based subscriptions (so a component only re-renders when the specific slice of state it reads actually changes) with far less boilerplate than Redux, while Redux still makes sense for larger teams that specifically want its more rigid structure, time-travel debugging, and mature middleware ecosystem. The most common actual mistake I try to correct in code review is over-lifting state that's genuinely local to one component or one small subtree, like a single form's draft values or a single dropdown's open/closed state, into a global store 'just in case', which adds real complexity and coupling with no corresponding benefit, since that state was never actually needed anywhere else in the app.
weak: A weak answer reaches for one single tool (usually whatever they know best, often Redux or Context) for every kind of state indiscriminately, without distinguishing server state, global client state, and local component state as genuinely different problems with different appropriate tools.
followUp: What's a concrete symptom you'd see in a codebase where server state was incorrectly being managed in a client-state store like Redux instead of a dedicated server-state library?

question: What are the main use cases for useRef beyond accessing a DOM node?
concise: Beyond holding a reference to a DOM element (for focusing an input, measuring size, or integrating a non-React library like a chart), useRef is also the standard way to hold any mutable value that needs to persist across renders without triggering a re-render when it changes, such as a previous value for comparison, an interval/timeout id for cleanup, a flag tracking whether a component has already mounted, or the latest value of a prop/state for use inside a callback without needing to add it as a dependency and re-create that callback.
strong: The DOM-reference use case, like inputRef.current.focus() or measuring an element's size with getBoundingClientRect, is the most commonly taught one, but useRef's more general underlying purpose is providing a mutable container whose .current property can be read or written directly at any time without causing a re-render, unlike useState, which always triggers a re-render on every update; this makes it the right tool whenever you need to remember something across renders purely for your own internal bookkeeping, not for anything that should visually affect what's rendered. A common pattern is storing an interval or timeout id in a ref specifically so it can be cleared later inside a cleanup function, since that id itself never needs to trigger a re-render, it just needs to persist and be readable when cleanup runs. Another very common pattern is a 'latest value' ref: if a callback (like a WebSocket message handler set up once and never recreated) needs access to the most current value of some prop or state without needing to be recreated every time that value changes (which would otherwise require re-subscribing on every change), you can keep a ref updated with the latest value on every render, and read ref.current inside the stable callback instead, sidestepping the need to include that value as a dependency at all. Refs are also useful for tracking whether an effect is running on the component's very first mount versus a subsequent update, which is a common need when you specifically want to skip an effect's logic on the initial mount.
weak: A weak answer only knows useRef as 'a way to grab a DOM node' and hasn't used it as a general mutable-value container, missing the whole class of 'store something across renders without causing a re-render' use cases that come up constantly in real code.
followUp: Why would storing a WebSocket connection's onmessage callback in a ref, rather than including it directly as a useEffect dependency, prevent the socket from being needlessly closed and reopened on every unrelated re-render?

question: What are React portals, and what's a realistic scenario where you'd need one?
