concise: A portal (created with ReactDOM.createPortal) lets you render a component's children into a DOM node that exists outside of its parent's actual DOM hierarchy, while the component still behaves as if it were nested normally in the React tree for purposes like context, event bubbling, and lifecycle; a realistic use case is a modal, tooltip, or dropdown menu that needs to render at the very end of document.body to avoid being visually clipped or incorrectly layered by an ancestor's overflow: hidden or a lower stacking context, even though logically it's still 'inside' the component that triggered it.
strong: Without a portal, a modal rendered as a normal nested child deep inside a component tree is subject to every ancestor's CSS, including overflow: hidden clipping it, or a transformed/opacity-less-than-one ancestor creating a new stacking context that traps the modal visually behind other page content regardless of its z-index, both of which are exactly the stacking-context problems covered earlier. createPortal(children, domNode) solves this by rendering that JSX into a completely different DOM node, typically one appended directly to document.body specifically to escape any ancestor's clipping or stacking context, while React still treats it as a normal part of the component tree for everything else that matters: context values from any ancestor Providers are still available inside the portaled content, events that occur inside the portaled DOM still bubble up through the React component tree (not the actual DOM tree) to any parent event handlers, and the portal's lifecycle is still tied to its logical parent component, so it unmounts correctly when that parent unmounts. This is exactly the underlying technique that headless component libraries like Radix UI use internally for their Dialog, Popover, and DropdownMenu components, so as an app developer you often get portal behavior for free without needing to call createPortal yourself, but understanding what's actually happening underneath is important for debugging things like an event handler seeming to fire in an unexpected place, or figuring out why a modal's content has access to a parent's context even though it's not actually nested inside that provider in the real DOM.
weak: A weak answer has heard of portals but can't explain the actual stacking-context/overflow-clipping problem they solve, or doesn't know that React events still bubble through the logical component tree, not the physical DOM tree, even across a portal boundary.
followUp: If a portaled modal's content dispatches a click event, does that event bubble up to a click handler on the modal's logical React parent, or only to handlers on its actual DOM parent (document.body)?

question: What is React's concurrent rendering, and what problems do startTransition and useDeferredValue actually solve?
concise: Concurrent rendering lets React interrupt, pause, or abandon an in-progress render if something more urgent (like a new keystroke) comes in, rather than always finishing a render to completion before handling the next update, which used to make React's rendering effectively 'block' the main thread for the whole duration of a large update; startTransition explicitly marks a state update as non-urgent (like updating a large filtered/sorted list), letting React keep the UI responsive to more urgent updates (like the input field itself updating as the user types) while that lower-priority update renders in the background; useDeferredValue achieves a similar effect by giving you a version of a value that 'lags behind' the true latest value until React has spare rendering capacity to catch it up.
strong: Before concurrent rendering, a single state update triggering a large re-render, like re-filtering and re-rendering a list of ten thousand rows in response to a search input, would block the main thread for the entire duration of that render, meaning the actual input field itself would visibly lag behind the user's typing, since React couldn't interrupt the big render to prioritize the smaller, more urgent update of the input's own displayed value. startTransition(() => setFilteredList(newList)) tells React explicitly that this particular state update is lower priority and can be interrupted or delayed if something more urgent needs to render first, so the text input itself stays perfectly responsive to every keystroke (rendered at normal, urgent priority), while the expensive filtered list update happens as a background, interruptible transition that can even be abandoned partway through and restarted if the user types again before it finishes. useDeferredValue solves a very similar underlying problem with a slightly different API shape: rather than wrapping the state update itself, you wrap the value being used for the expensive render, like const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query), and React will render the expensive list using a 'lagging' version of that value that catches up once it has rendering capacity to spare, again keeping the urgent parts of the UI responsive in the meantime. Neither of these speeds up the actual expensive computation itself; they only change its scheduling priority relative to other, more urgent updates, so they're specifically useful when you have some expensive UI update that's genuinely allowed to lag slightly behind more urgent, latency-sensitive updates like direct text input feedback, not a general performance optimization for making renders themselves faster.
weak: A weak answer thinks startTransition or useDeferredValue somehow makes an expensive computation itself run faster, rather than understanding they only change scheduling priority, letting more urgent updates (like the input field's own value) interrupt and go first.
followUp: If startTransition doesn't make an expensive render actually faster, what real, measurable improvement does it produce for the user typing in a search box in front of a large filtered list?

question: How would you use the React DevTools Profiler to actually diagnose why a component is re-rendering too often?
concise: Record an interaction with the Profiler tab, then inspect the flame graph or ranked chart for the commit(s) around that interaction: each rendered component shows its render duration and, critically, the 'why did this render' information (in newer DevTools versions, or by cross-referencing which props/state/context changed) that tells you whether it re-rendered due to its own state changing, a parent re-rendering and passing new props, or a context value change; from there you look specifically for large subtrees re-rendering when only a small, unrelated piece of state actually changed, which usually points to either a missing React.memo, an unmemoized object/function prop defeating an existing React.memo, or an overly broad Context value.
strong: I start by wrapping the interaction I care about, like typing in a filter input or toggling a sidebar, in the Profiler's record button, then look at the resulting commits: each one shows every component that rendered during that specific update, along with its individual render duration, which quickly highlights which components are both re-rendering unnecessarily and expensive enough to actually matter, since not every unnecessary re-render is worth chasing if the component itself renders in under a millisecond anyway. The DevTools Profiler can show, per component, what actually caused it to re-render, whether its own state changed, its props changed, its parent re-rendered, or a context it subscribes to changed, which is the key diagnostic signal: if I see a whole subtree of otherwise-unrelated components re-rendering every time I type a single character into an unrelated filter input, that's a strong signal that either those components aren't wrapped in React.memo at all, or they are wrapped but are receiving a prop, like an inline object or callback, that's being recreated fresh on every parent render, defeating the memoization. Once I've identified the specific expensive, unnecessarily-re-rendering subtree, the actual fix is almost always one of: wrapping the component in React.memo if it wasn't already, memoizing whatever prop is defeating an existing React.memo with useMemo/useCallback, or, if the root cause is a Context value re-created on every render, restructuring the context as covered in the Context performance question. I'd avoid reaching for these fixes preemptively without profiling first, since guessing at performance problems without measuring them often leads to adding memoization in the wrong place, or in places where it provides no real, measurable benefit at all.
weak: A weak answer says 'I'd just add React.memo everywhere and see if it helps' without ever actually opening the Profiler to identify which specific components are re-rendering unnecessarily and why, which risks adding complexity in the wrong place with no measured benefit.
followUp: After identifying an unnecessarily re-rendering component in the Profiler, how would you confirm whether the actual cause is a missing React.memo versus an unmemoized prop defeating an existing one?

question: How would you test a custom hook in isolation, and what's the difference between testing it with renderHook versus testing it only indirectly through a component that uses it?
concise: Testing Library's renderHook utility mounts a custom hook inside a minimal, invisible test harness component, letting you call the hook directly, assert on its returned values, and trigger updates (via the act utility, or renderHook's own rerender function) without needing to render an actual full UI component around it; this is preferable to only testing the hook indirectly through some component that happens to use it, since indirect testing couples the hook's test to that specific component's rendering and markup, making the test more brittle and less clearly focused on the hook's own actual logic.
strong: renderHook(() => useCounter()) runs the hook inside a lightweight, purpose-built test wrapper and returns a result object whose .current property holds whatever the hook itself currently returns, letting you assert directly on the hook's actual behavior, like expect(result.current.count).toBe(0), and then call result.current.increment() (wrapped in act, since it triggers a state update) to simulate the hook being used, all without needing any real UI markup at all. Testing a hook only indirectly, by rendering some component that happens to use it and asserting on the rendered DOM output, technically exercises the hook's logic too, but it couples that test to the specific component's rendering details, meaning a change to the component's markup or structure (that has nothing to do with the hook's actual logic) can break the test, and it also makes it harder to test edge cases of the hook in isolation, since you're forced to reason about a whole component's rendering behavior just to test one small piece of stateful logic. For a hook with dependencies, like a custom useAuth hook that reads from a Context provider, renderHook accepts a wrapper option specifically so you can provide the necessary context providers around the hook during the test, without needing an entire real component tree. I generally test simple, purely-presentational hooks indirectly if they're tightly coupled to one specific component anyway, but for any hook meant to be reused across multiple components, like a useDebounce or a usePagination hook, I test it directly and in isolation with renderHook, since its correctness genuinely doesn't depend on any particular component using it.
weak: A weak answer only knows how to test hooks indirectly by rendering a full component around them, and has never used renderHook directly, which leads to more brittle tests that are coupled to unrelated rendering details instead of the hook's actual logic.
followUp: How would you use renderHook's wrapper option to test a custom hook that depends on a Context provider, like a useAuth hook reading from an AuthContext?

question: Why is using the array index as a React list key considered an anti-pattern, and when is it actually acceptable?
concise: Using the index as a key ties each rendered element's identity to its position in the array rather than to the actual underlying data item, so React can misattribute DOM state (like an input's focus or typed value, or a checkbox's checked state) to the wrong item whenever the list is reordered, filtered, or has items inserted/removed anywhere except the very end; it's acceptable specifically when the list is static and will never be reordered, filtered, or have items added/removed from the middle, and the items themselves have no internal state or identity that matters across re-renders.
strong: React uses the key to match elements between the previous render and the new render, and when the key is just the array index, React has no way to distinguish 'the data at this position changed' from 'a different item now happens to occupy this position', so if an item is removed from the middle of the list, every subsequent item's index key shifts down by one, and React ends up incorrectly reusing DOM nodes and any associated component state (like an input's current typed value, an open/closed accordion state, or a checkbox's checked state) for what is now, logically, a different underlying item. This is a real, reproducible bug, not just a style nitpick: in a to-do list where each item has an inline 'edit' text field, deleting an item in the middle of the list using index-based keys can cause the wrong remaining item to visually retain the deleted item's in-progress edited text. It's genuinely fine to use the index as a key specifically when the list is guaranteed to be static for its entire lifetime, never reordered, filtered, or having items inserted/removed from anywhere but the end, and the items themselves are simple and stateless, like a fixed, unchanging list of category labels rendered once and never modified; in that narrow case there's no actual identity-mismatch risk since the mapping from index to item genuinely never changes.
weak: A weak answer treats 'don't use index as key' as an absolute rule to follow without understanding why, and can't explain the specific narrow case where it's actually safe, or can't describe the concrete state-mismatch bug that motivates the rule in the first place.
followUp: Walk through, step by step, exactly how a checkbox's checked state ends up attached to the wrong to-do item after deleting a middle item from an index-keyed list.

question: How would you virtualize a very large list (tens of thousands of rows) in React, and why is naive rendering of the full list a problem?
concise: Rendering every row of a huge list creates that many real DOM nodes, which is slow to create initially, slow for the browser to lay out and paint, and keeps consuming memory for rows the user can't even see; virtualization (using a library like TanStack Virtual or react-window) renders only the small subset of rows currently visible within the scrollable viewport (plus a small overscan buffer), calculating scroll position and total scrollable height mathematically so the scrollbar still behaves correctly, and swaps which actual data is rendered into that small set of DOM nodes as the user scrolls.
strong: Rendering ten thousand real table rows means the browser has to create, lay out, and paint ten thousand DOM nodes, the vast majority of which are entirely offscreen and invisible to the user at any given moment, which is wasteful both for the initial render time and for ongoing memory usage, and can make scrolling itself feel janky since the browser still has to account for all those offscreen nodes during layout recalculations. A virtualized list instead renders only the handful of rows that are actually visible in the current scroll viewport, plus a small buffer of extra rows just outside the visible area (overscan) so scrolling doesn't show a visible pop-in of unrendered content at the edges; it calculates the total scrollable area's height mathematically, based on the total item count and each item's (measured or estimated) height, and positions the small set of actually-rendered rows absolutely within that total scrollable space so the scrollbar's size and position behave exactly as if every row were really rendered, even though only a tiny fraction of them actually exist as real DOM nodes at any given time. Libraries like TanStack Virtual (or react-window) handle all of this measurement, positioning, and recycling logic for you, including trickier cases like variable-height rows, which require measuring each rendered row and updating the estimated total height as more rows are actually measured while scrolling. For a dashboard with a genuinely large dataset, like an audit log or a transaction history with tens of thousands of entries, virtualization is usually the single highest-impact performance fix available, since it turns an O(total rows) rendering cost into an O(visible rows) cost regardless of how large the underlying dataset grows.
weak: A weak answer suggests pagination as the only solution to a large list's performance problem, without knowing about virtualization as a distinct technique that lets a user scroll through the entire dataset smoothly, without needing discrete pages at all, while still only rendering a small number of actual DOM nodes.
followUp: How does a virtualization library handle rows with variable, not-known-in-advance heights, and why is that meaningfully harder than virtualizing a list of fixed-height rows?

question: How would you make a custom dropdown or combobox component in React fully accessible, matching the keyboard behavior users expect from a native select?
concise: It needs the correct ARIA role structure (typically role='combobox' on the input/trigger, aria-expanded reflecting open state, aria-controls pointing at the listbox, role='listbox' on the options container, and role='option' with aria-selected on each option), full keyboard support (Arrow keys to move the highlighted option, Enter/Space to select it, Escape to close, Home/End to jump to the first/last option, and typeahead so typing a letter jumps to a matching option), and correct focus management so keyboard focus stays logically on the input/trigger while a separate 'active descendant' or visual highlight indicates the currently highlighted option, rather than actually moving DOM focus to each option as the user arrows through them.
strong: Getting this fully right from scratch is genuinely one of the more involved accessibility challenges in frontend work: the correct pattern keeps actual DOM focus on the combobox input itself the entire time (not on individual options as you arrow through them), and instead uses aria-activedescendant on the input, pointing at the id of whichever option is currently highlighted, so screen readers announce the correct option as 'active' without focus ever visibly leaving the input; getting this subtlety wrong, like actually moving focus to each li as the user presses arrow keys, breaks screen reader announcement timing and can cause the on-screen input to lose its blinking cursor unexpectedly. Keyboard support needs to cover arrow keys moving the highlighted option up or down (wrapping or not, depending on the design), Enter or Space selecting the currently highlighted option and closing the dropdown, Escape closing it without selecting anything and returning focus cleanly to the trigger, and often typeahead, where typing a letter jumps the highlight to the next option starting with that letter, matching what users expect from a native select. Given how many subtle edge cases there are here, including correct behavior when the list is filtered as the user types, or handling a currently-highlighted option being removed from a filtered result set, I would strongly prefer building on a well-tested, accessible headless primitive like Radix UI's Combobox or downshift rather than reimplementing all of this from scratch, reserving custom-built accessible widgets for cases with no suitable existing library, since these interaction patterns have many correctness edge cases that are easy to get subtly wrong even with real effort.
weak: A weak answer builds a dropdown using a plain div with an onClick handler and no keyboard support or ARIA attributes at all, which is completely unusable for keyboard-only and screen reader users, and does not meet basic accessibility requirements for an interactive form control.
followUp: Why does the correct combobox pattern keep DOM focus on the input itself and use aria-activedescendant, rather than actually moving focus to each highlighted option as the user presses arrow keys?

question: How does React batch multiple state updates, and how did this behavior change between React 17 and React 18?
concise: React batches multiple setState calls that occur within the same event handler into a single re-render, avoiding a separate re-render for each individual state update; in React 17 and earlier, this batching only happened for updates triggered inside React's own synthetic event handlers, while updates triggered inside a promise callback, a setTimeout, or a native (non-React) event handler each caused their own separate, immediate re-render; React 18's automatic batching extends this same batching behavior to all of those previously-unbatched contexts as well, by default, with no extra code needed.
strong: If a click handler calls setCount and setFlag one after another, React batches both of those state updates together and performs just one single re-render reflecting both changes at once, rather than rendering once after setCount and again after setFlag, which is both more efficient and avoids a component briefly rendering with only one of the two updates applied. The important historical wrinkle, and a common interview follow-up, is that in React 17 this batching behavior only applied inside handlers React itself was directly managing, like an onClick prop; if you instead called setState calls inside a native addEventListener handler, inside a setTimeout callback, or inside a .then() on a promise, each call triggered its own separate, immediate re-render, since React had no visibility into or control over those execution contexts to know it should batch anything. React 18 introduced automatic batching, which batches state updates in all of these contexts by default, without requiring anything special from the developer, meaning code that used to cause multiple re-renders in a promise callback or setTimeout under React 17 now correctly produces just one, consistent with how it always worked inside standard React event handlers. If, in some rare case, you genuinely need to force a state update to apply and re-render immediately, outside of the normal batching behavior, React 18 provides flushSync specifically for that narrow purpose, though it should be used sparingly since it opts back into the less efficient, per-update rendering behavior deliberately.
weak: A weak answer isn't aware that batching behavior changed at all between React versions, and would be surprised (or wrong) if asked to predict how many times a component re-renders for two state updates inside a setTimeout callback under React 17 versus React 18.
followUp: What does flushSync do, and give a realistic (rare) scenario where you'd actually need to opt out of React 18's automatic batching to force an immediate synchronous render.

question: What's the difference between a controlled modal's focus trap using a maintained library versus hand-rolling it, and what accessibility edge cases are easy to miss when building it yourself?
concise: A maintained library (like focus-trap-react, or the focus management built into Radix/Headless UI's Dialog) correctly handles a long list of edge cases: trapping Tab and Shift+Tab so focus cycles only within the modal, restoring focus to the exact triggering element on close, handling focus correctly if the modal's content changes dynamically while open (so newly-added focusable elements are included in the trap), preventing background content from being reachable via screen reader virtual cursor navigation (using inert or aria-hidden on siblings), and correctly handling nested modals or a modal opened from within another modal; hand-rolling this from scratch commonly gets the basic Tab-cycling working but misses several of these less obvious edge cases, which only show up in real usage with assistive technology, not in casual manual testing with a mouse.
strong: The Tab-cycling part of a focus trap looks deceptively simple to implement, just capture Tab and Shift+Tab keydown events and, if focus would move past the first or last focusable element inside the modal, wrap it back around, but a genuinely correct implementation needs to solve several additional problems most hand-rolled attempts miss: hiding the rest of the page from a screen reader's virtual cursor (which can still 'read into' background content even while keyboard Tab focus is correctly trapped, unless you explicitly apply inert or aria-hidden to everything outside the modal while it's open), recomputing the list of focusable elements inside the modal if its content changes dynamically after it opens (like a multi-step modal where step two reveals new form fields that need to be included in the trap), correctly restoring focus to the precise element that triggered the modal on close, not just some generic fallback, and handling nested-modal scenarios, like a confirmation dialog opened from within a larger modal, where focus needs to trap within just the innermost active modal without breaking the outer one's own trap. These edge cases are exactly why I default to a maintained library for anything beyond a trivial one-off case, since they're the kind of bug that's invisible during regular mouse-driven manual testing but immediately obvious and frustrating to an actual screen reader or keyboard-only user, and they're genuinely time-consuming to get fully correct and well-tested from scratch.
weak: A weak answer implements basic Tab-wrapping and calls the focus trap 'done', without being aware of the inert/aria-hidden background-content issue, dynamic content re-scanning, or nested-modal handling, all of which are real, commonly-missed accessibility gaps.
followUp: How does the inert attribute (or manually applying aria-hidden to background siblings) prevent a screen reader's virtual cursor from reading background content while a modal is open, even though keyboard Tab focus is already correctly trapped?

question: How would you structure component composition to avoid unnecessary re-renders, specifically using the 'children as a prop' pattern to isolate frequently-changing state?
concise: If a component holds frequently-changing local state (like mouse position, or an animation value) and directly renders both that changing UI and a large, otherwise-static subtree as its own JSX children, every re-render caused by the changing state also unnecessarily re-renders that entire static subtree; restructuring so the static subtree is passed in as a children (or other) prop from a parent one level up means React can bail out of re-rendering that already-created element tree, since the prop reference itself doesn't change between renders, even though the component holding the frequently-changing state re-renders on every update.
strong: When a component like MouseTracker renders both its own frequently-updating position display and a large children subtree directly inline in its own JSX, every single state update inside MouseTracker (like on every mousemove event) also re-renders that entire children subtree, even if none of that subtree's own props or data have changed at all, simply because it's textually nested inside MouseTracker's own render output and MouseTracker itself just re-rendered. If instead the parent renders <MouseTracker>{expensiveStaticContent}</MouseTracker>, and MouseTracker internally just renders {props.children} rather than the actual JSX for that content directly, then expensiveStaticContent is created once, in the parent's render, and passed down as an already-existing React element reference; when MouseTracker itself re-renders due to its own internal state changing, React sees that the children prop it received is the exact same, unchanged element reference as last time, and can skip re-rendering that subtree entirely without needing React.memo at all, since nothing about that reference actually changed. This is a genuinely underused optimization technique, since it requires no additional memoization APIs at all, just restructuring which component owns the JSX for the static content versus which component owns the frequently-changing local state, and it's a good instinct to reach for before defaulting straight to React.memo plus useMemo/useCallback everywhere, since it solves the same class of problem with less code and less ongoing maintenance overhead.
weak: A weak answer only knows React.memo and useMemo/useCallback as the tools for avoiding unnecessary re-renders, and hasn't considered that restructuring component ownership with the children prop can solve the same problem more simply, with no extra memoization APIs at all.
followUp: Why specifically does passing children as a prop avoid a re-render, in terms of what React actually compares between renders, versus rendering that same JSX directly inline inside the component's own render function?

question: Give a concrete example of a form validation error message that isn't properly accessible, and how you'd fix it.
concise: A red border on an invalid input, with no visible text and no programmatic association to the input, communicates nothing to a screen reader user and relies purely on color, which also fails for colorblind users; the fix is a visible error message with actual text, connected to its input via aria-describedby, with aria-invalid='true' set on the input itself, and ideally the error announced via an aria-live region or moved into focus so it isn't silently missed when it appears after a failed submit.
strong: A form that only shows a red outline around an invalid field, with no text explaining what's wrong, fails in multiple independent ways: a screen reader user gets no indication anything is wrong at all, since a screen reader doesn't announce border color changes; a colorblind user may not even perceive the red styling as meaningfully different from a normal state; and even a sighted user without a screen reader has to guess what specifically is wrong, like whether the field is required, has an invalid format, or is too short. The fix has a few concrete parts: render an actual visible text error message near the field ('Enter a valid email address'), connect that message to the input using aria-describedby pointing at the error message's id, so a screen reader announces the specific error text when the user focuses or interacts with that field, and set aria-invalid='true' on the input itself while it's in an invalid state, which some screen readers announce explicitly as 'invalid'. For errors that appear after a failed form submission rather than live as the user types, I'd also either move focus to the first invalid field or wrap the error summary in an aria-live region, since otherwise a screen reader user who submitted the form has no way to know anything went wrong at all unless they happen to navigate back through the form and re-discover the now-visible error text themselves.
code: {hasError && Enter a valid email address}
weak: A weak answer relies purely on a red border or red text color to indicate a validation error, with no actual programmatic connection to the input (no aria-describedby, no aria-invalid) and no visible error text at all, which communicates nothing to assistive technology users.
followUp: What's the difference between using role='alert' on an error message versus a separate aria-live='polite' region, and which is generally more appropriate for a form validation error?

question: What are the key differences between the App Router and the older Pages Router in Next.js?
concise: The App Router (directory-based, using page.tsx/layout.tsx/loading.tsx conventions inside app/) is built around React Server Components by default, supports nested layouts that persist across navigations without re-rendering, colocates loading and error UI per route segment, and uses the fetch API's own caching for data fetching; the Pages Router (pages/ directory) renders every component as a Client Component by default (no RSC), uses page-level functions like getServerSideProps/getStaticProps for data fetching, and has no built-in nested layout system, requiring a custom _app.tsx-based workaround for shared layouts.
strong: The App Router's biggest conceptual shift is that every component is a Server Component by default unless explicitly marked with a 'use client' directive at the top of the file, which means large parts of a typical app, static layout, page shells, data-driven content with no interactivity, can render with zero client-side JavaScript shipped for those components at all, whereas in the Pages Router every component, and every library it imports, always ships to and hydrates on the client regardless of whether it's actually interactive. Nested layouts are also a first-class concept in the App Router: a layout.tsx file wraps every route segment beneath it in the folder structure and persists across navigations between sibling routes without re-rendering or losing its own local state (like a scroll position or an open sidebar), which the Pages Router has no native equivalent for, historically requiring a shared _app.tsx wrapper that re-runs on every navigation instead. Data fetching also changed fundamentally: the Pages Router's getServerSideProps and getStaticProps run once per page at specific, predetermined times, while the App Router lets you just await fetch (or a database call) directly inside any Server Component, with Next.js's extended fetch API providing its own fine-grained caching and revalidation controls per request. In practice, a new Next.js project today defaults to the App Router, and I'd only reach for the Pages Router on an existing legacy codebase already built with it, or in the rare case a specific library or pattern genuinely isn't yet well supported under the App Router's model.
weak: A weak answer says 'App Router is just the new folder structure for Pages Router' without understanding that the actual, more consequential difference is the default shift to Server Components and the resulting change in what ships to the client at all.
followUp: What specifically happens if you try to use useState or an onClick handler directly inside a component that hasn't been marked with 'use client' in the App Router?

question: Explain the boundary between Server Components and Client Components in the App Router, and a common mistake teams make with the 'use client' directive.
concise: 'use client' at the top of a file marks that module, and everything it imports, as part of the client bundle, meaning it and its entire import tree hydrate and run in the browser; a common mistake is putting 'use client' too high up the tree, like on an entire page or layout file just because one small piece deep inside it needs interactivity, which unnecessarily converts a much larger subtree into client-rendered code than actually needs to be, inflating the client bundle and losing the server-rendering benefits for everything in that subtree.
strong: Once a file has 'use client' at its top, Next.js treats that file, and by extension everything it statically imports (unless that imported thing is itself passed in as a child/prop from a Server Component ancestor), as belonging to the client bundle, meaning all of it needs to be shipped to and hydrated in the browser; this boundary is directional, a Client Component can't 'go back' to being server-rendered simply by being imported from a server file, since once you're inside a client boundary, everything nested directly inside it via static imports is client too. The mistake I see most often is a team adding 'use client' at the very top of a whole page.tsx or layout.tsx file just because one small interactive piece, like a single 'Add to cart' button, lives somewhere within that page, which unintentionally pulls the entire rest of that page's component tree, including large chunks of otherwise static, server-renderable content, into the client bundle, along with all of its own imports, completely defeating the bundle-size benefit that Server Components were meant to provide in the first place. The better pattern is to keep 'use client' as narrowly scoped as possible, ideally on just the specific small leaf component that genuinely needs state or an event handler, like extracting just the AddToCartButton into its own small client component file, and letting the surrounding page and layout remain Server Components that import and render that one small client island directly, which keeps the client bundle proportional to how much of the page is actually interactive, rather than to how much of the page merely contains an interactive piece somewhere inside it.
weak: A weak answer doesn't realize 'use client' pulls its entire import tree into the client bundle, and defaults to marking whole pages or layouts as client components reflexively whenever any interactivity is needed anywhere within them.
followUp: If a Server Component needs to render a small interactive island in the middle of otherwise-static content, how does it pass data down into that Client Component correctly, given the serialization constraint on props crossing that boundary?

question: Compare SSR, SSG, ISR, and CSR as rendering strategies, and how you'd choose between them for different pages of a real app.
concise: SSR (server-side rendering) generates the HTML fresh on every request, best for pages with per-request, frequently-changing, or personalized data; SSG (static site generation) generates HTML once at build time, best for content that rarely changes, like marketing or documentation pages, since it's the fastest to serve (just a static file); ISR (incremental static regeneration) is SSG with a revalidation interval, serving a cached static page instantly while regenerating it in the background after a specified time or on-demand, a good middle ground for content that changes occasionally but doesn't need to be render-fresh on literally every single request; CSR (client-side rendering) fetches and renders data entirely in the browser after an initial mostly-empty HTML shell loads, appropriate for highly interactive, per-user, behind-auth views where SEO doesn't matter and content is genuinely dynamic per session.
strong: For a marketing homepage or a blog post that changes rarely, SSG gives the best possible performance since the HTML is already fully built and can be served instantly from a CDN edge node with zero server compute needed per request. For a product listing page where prices and stock levels change periodically throughout the day but don't need to be instantly, always up-to-the-second fresh on every single request, ISR is usually the sweet spot, serving the previously-generated static page instantly to users while Next.js regenerates a fresh version in the background after the configured revalidation window passes, or immediately on-demand via a webhook-triggered revalidation call when the underlying data actually changes. For something genuinely per-request and personalized, like a page showing a specific logged-in user's account balance or their real-time order status, SSR makes sense since the content is meaningfully different on every single request and can't be usefully cached and shared across users at all. For an authenticated internal dashboard with highly interactive widgets, frequent client-side filtering, and no SEO requirement whatsoever, CSR (or, more precisely, a Server Component shell around client-heavy interactive pieces) is often the simplest and most appropriate choice, since there's no benefit to server-rendering content nobody but one specific logged-in user will ever see and that's going to be immediately re-fetched and re-filtered client-side anyway.
weak: A weak answer treats SSG, SSR, and CSR as strictly ranked from 'best' to 'worst' rather than understanding they're different tools suited to genuinely different data-freshness and personalization requirements, and can't explain ISR's actual middle-ground trade-off at all.
followUp: How would you trigger an on-demand revalidation of a specific ISR page immediately after its underlying data changes, rather than waiting for the configured revalidation interval to pass?

question: How does data fetching and caching work with Next.js's extended fetch in the App Router, and what do the different cache/revalidate options actually control?
concise: Next.js extends the native fetch API so that, on the server, a fetch call's response can be automatically cached and reused across requests; passing { cache: 'force-cache' } (the historical default in some versions) caches the response indefinitely (like static generation), { cache: 'no-store' } opts that specific fetch call out of caching entirely (fully dynamic, fresh on every request), and { next: { revalidate: N } } caches the response but automatically treats it as stale and triggers a background refetch after N seconds have passed (time-based ISR-style revalidation scoped to that individual fetch call, not the whole page).
strong: Because caching is configured per individual fetch call rather than per whole page, a single page can mix and match strategies naturally: for example, a product page might fetch static product description data with a long revalidate window, alongside real-time inventory data fetched with no-store so it's always fresh, all within the same Server Component, with each fetch call independently controlling its own caching behavior rather than needing the entire page to commit to one single rendering strategy. { next: { tags: ['product-' + productId] } } lets you tag a specific cached fetch response so it can later be explicitly invalidated on-demand, via revalidateTag, from a server action or an API route, for example immediately after an admin updates a product's price, rather than waiting for a time-based revalidation window to naturally expire; this on-demand tag-based invalidation is generally the more precise and preferable mechanism for content that changes at unpredictable times triggered by a specific event, versus time-based revalidate for content that just naturally goes stale after some duration. It's worth knowing that Next.js's default caching behavior for fetch calls has actually changed across versions (moving toward being uncached, or opt-in, by default in more recent versions rather than cached by default), so I always explicitly specify the caching behavior I actually want for each fetch call rather than relying on assumed defaults, both for clarity and to avoid being surprised by a version upgrade silently changing behavior.
weak: A weak answer assumes every fetch call in Next.js behaves identically and caches (or doesn't cache) the same way by default across the whole app, without realizing caching is configured per fetch call and that the framework's own default behavior has changed meaningfully across versions.
followUp: What's the difference between time-based revalidation (next.revalidate) and tag-based on-demand revalidation (revalidateTag), and when would you use each for the same piece of data?

question: What are common use cases for Next.js middleware, and what are its execution constraints?
concise: Middleware runs before a request completes, at the edge, for every matching request, and is commonly used for auth redirects (checking a session cookie and redirecting unauthenticated users away from protected routes before the actual page even starts rendering), A/B testing (rewriting or redirecting based on a cookie-assigned variant), geolocation-based redirects/rewrites, and setting custom response headers like a security header or a locale cookie; it runs in the restricted Edge Runtime, not full Node.js, meaning it cannot use Node-specific APIs or most npm packages that depend on Node built-ins, and it should stay fast and lightweight since it runs on the hot path of every matching request.
strong: A very common real use case is protecting a set of authenticated routes: middleware reads the session cookie directly from the incoming request, and if it's missing or invalid, immediately redirects to the login page before any of the actual protected page's Server Component code runs at all, which is more efficient than letting the page start rendering and only then discovering the user isn't authenticated. Middleware is also commonly used for locale detection and redirection, reading an Accept-Language header or a geolocation signal and redirecting or rewriting the request to the appropriate localized route, and for lightweight A/B testing, assigning a user to a variant via a cookie on their first visit and then consistently rewriting their subsequent requests to the correct variant based on that cookie. The key constraint to know well is that middleware runs in the Edge Runtime, a deliberately restricted JavaScript environment (not full Node.js) designed to start up near-instantly across globally distributed edge locations, which means it can't use Node-specific built-in modules like fs, and most npm packages that internally depend on Node APIs (rather than being genuinely universal/isomorphic) won't work inside it either; this is a real practical limitation, for example a full-featured JWT verification library that depends on Node's crypto module in a Node-specific way may need an Edge-compatible alternative. It's important to remember that middleware-based auth checks are a UX optimization, redirecting unauthenticated users away quickly and cheaply, not a substitute for the actual backend/API also independently verifying authorization on every real data-fetching or mutating request, since middleware can, in principle, be bypassed by calling an underlying API route directly.
weak: A weak answer treats a middleware-based redirect as a complete, sufficient authorization mechanism on its own, without recognizing that the actual backend or API layer must still independently re-verify every request's authorization, since middleware can be bypassed by calling underlying endpoints directly.
followUp: Why can't a typical Node-specific npm package (one that relies on the fs or a Node-only crypto API internally) be used directly inside Next.js middleware, and how would you work around that limitation?

question: How would you implement authentication in a Next.js App Router app, covering session storage, protecting Server Components, and protecting API/server actions?
concise: Store the session as an HttpOnly, Secure cookie set by the server (via a library like NextAuth/Auth.js, or a custom implementation), read and validate that cookie in middleware for fast route-level redirects, and additionally re-check authentication and authorization directly inside every Server Component, route handler, and server action that touches protected data or performs a protected mutation, since middleware alone only controls page-level navigation and does not, by itself, secure the actual underlying data-fetching or mutation logic those pages or actions call.
strong: For session storage, an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie remains the right default even in the App Router, since it can't be read or stolen by client-side JavaScript, and Next.js Server Components and route handlers can read cookies directly on the server via the cookies() function without needing to expose the token to client-side code at all. Middleware is a good place for a fast, cheap first-pass check, redirecting an unauthenticated user away from an entire protected route segment before any of that segment's actual Server Component code even starts executing, which improves both security posture and performance by failing fast. However, that middleware-level check should never be the only line of defense: every individual Server Component that fetches sensitive data, every route handler, and every server action needs to independently re-verify the session and check the specific authorization rules relevant to that particular operation, since a server action in particular can, in principle, be invoked directly (its endpoint is a real, callable network request under the hood) bypassing whatever page-level middleware logic exists, so the action's own server-side code must itself re-validate the session and check that the specific authenticated user is actually allowed to perform that specific operation on that specific resource, not merely that they're logged in at all. For role-based access control specifically, I'd keep the actual permission-checking logic centralized in one shared, well-tested helper function called from every protected route handler and server action, rather than duplicating ad hoc authorization checks inline in many different places, which is much more error-prone to keep consistent as the app's permission model evolves over time.
weak: A weak answer relies entirely on a middleware-level redirect as the sole authentication and authorization mechanism, without independently re-verifying the session and specific permissions inside the actual server actions and route handlers that perform the real protected work.
followUp: Why can a server action potentially be invoked directly, bypassing a page's middleware-level auth check entirely, and what does that mean for where the real authorization logic must actually live?

question: What causes a hydration mismatch error in Next.js, and how would you fix one caused by reading browser-only state like window or localStorage?
concise: A hydration mismatch happens when the HTML the server actually rendered doesn't match what React's client-side render produces on the very first client render pass, most commonly because a component's output depends on something only available in the browser, like window, localStorage, or the current time/date, which the server either doesn't have access to at all or would compute differently at build/request time versus when the client actually hydrates; the fix is to ensure the server and the very first client render produce identical output, typically by rendering a safe, consistent placeholder value on the server and updating to the real browser-derived value only after mounting, inside a useEffect.
strong: Since the server has no window object, no access to the user's localStorage, and no way to know the client's precise local time at the exact moment of hydration, any component that reads one of these directly during its initial render and uses that value to affect its output will produce different HTML on the server than what React then tries to reconcile against on the client's very first render, and React detects that mismatch and either logs a warning (patching the DOM to match the client's version) or, in some cases, throws an outright hydration error depending on the severity and location of the mismatch. The standard, correct fix is to render something safe and deterministic (identical on both server and the client's very first render pass) initially, like a loading placeholder, a default value, or simply nothing for that piece of content, and then read the actual browser-only value inside a useEffect, which only runs after the component has mounted on the client, updating state and re-rendering with the real value at that point, after hydration has already successfully completed and matched; this necessarily means the user sees a brief flash from the placeholder to the real value on first load, and if there's a legitimate reason to avoid that flash for some reason, a blocking inline script executed before hydration (as covered in the dark-mode question) is the usual workaround, accepting a small amount of added complexity in exchange for avoiding that visible flash.
weak: A weak answer tries to 'fix' a hydration mismatch warning by just suppressing it (like passing suppressHydrationWarning) without addressing the actual underlying cause, which papers over the specific mismatch but doesn't fix the deeper problem of the component legitimately rendering different content depending on where it executes.
followUp: What does the suppressHydrationWarning prop actually do, and in what narrow, legitimate case would using it be the correct choice rather than a workaround for a real bug?

question: How does the Metadata API in the App Router work for SEO, and how would you generate dynamic metadata (like a per-product title and description) for a dynamic route?
concise: Static metadata is exported as a metadata object from a page or layout file (title, description, Open Graph tags, etc.), which Next.js automatically injects into the document head; for metadata that depends on the actual data of a dynamic route (like a specific product's name and description), you export an async generateMetadata function instead, which receives the route's params, can fetch the same data the page itself needs, and returns the appropriately populated metadata object, letting Next.js correctly deduplicate that fetch call if the page component fetches the identical data too.
strong: For a static page like an About page, exporting a plain metadata object with a fixed title and description is enough, and Next.js merges metadata from nested layouts and the specific page together, with more specific (deeper) values overriding broader ones, so a shared layout can define default Open Graph tags that most individual pages simply inherit unless they override them. For a dynamic route, like /products/[id], a fixed title obviously wouldn't be correct since it needs to reflect that specific product's actual name; exporting an async generateMetadata({ params }) function instead lets you fetch the specific product's data (using the exact same params the page component itself receives) and return a metadata object built from real data, like title: product.name + ' | Store'. A subtlety worth knowing is that if both generateMetadata and the page component itself need to fetch the same underlying data, Next.js's request deduplication (for identical fetch calls made during the same render pass) means that data is only actually fetched once from the network, not duplicated just because two separate functions both need it, as long as the fetch calls are genuinely identical. Getting dynamic metadata genuinely correct matters a lot for real-world SEO and for link previews on social platforms and messaging apps, since those platforms scrape the actual rendered head tags when generating a link preview card, and a generic or missing title/description/image there noticeably hurts click-through rates on shared links.
weak: A weak answer only knows how to set static metadata and doesn't know generateMetadata exists at all for dynamic routes, which means dynamic pages in their apps would all share the same generic title and description regardless of their actual specific content.
followUp: How does Next.js's automatic request deduplication actually determine that two separate fetch calls (one in generateMetadata, one in the page component) are 'the same' request and should only hit the network once?

question: How does next/image improve on a plain img tag, and what trade-offs come with using it?
concise: next/image automatically serves appropriately-sized, modern-format (WebP/AVIF where supported) images based on the actual rendered size and the requesting device, lazy-loads offscreen images by default, and requires explicit width/height (or fill with a sized parent) up front specifically to prevent layout shift, since it can reserve the correct aspect ratio before the image itself has finished loading; the trade-offs are that it requires either a compatible image optimization backend (built into Vercel's platform, or configurable for self-hosting) that adds some infrastructure complexity, and that width/height (or a sized parent container with fill) must be known or intentionally handled, which is a bit more upfront setup than just dropping in a plain img tag.
strong: Beyond just lazy loading, which a plain img tag can now also do natively with loading='lazy', next/image's bigger value is automatic, on-demand generation of appropriately-sized image variants: instead of shipping one large source image and letting the browser scale it down (wasting bandwidth) or manually maintaining your own srcset by hand, next/image generates and serves the right size for each specific device and viewport automatically, and serves a modern, smaller format like WebP or AVIF to browsers that support it, transparently falling back to the original format otherwise. Requiring width and height (or the fill prop combined with a properly sized, positioned parent container) up front is deliberate, not an unnecessary hurdle: it lets Next.js reserve exactly the right amount of layout space for the image before it has actually finished loading, directly preventing the cumulative layout shift that a plain img tag causes when its dimensions aren't otherwise specified in CSS or attributes. The real trade-off worth knowing is that this optimization pipeline needs an actual image-processing backend to generate those resized variants on demand, which is built in automatically on Vercel's hosting platform, but self-hosting Next.js elsewhere requires either configuring a compatible external image loader/CDN or accepting some additional server-side image-processing infrastructure, which is a genuine added operational consideration compared to just serving a static img tag directly from a CDN with no processing step involved at all.
weak: A weak answer treats next/image as purely 'a lazy-loading wrapper around img' without knowing about its automatic responsive-size generation, format conversion, and the deliberate layout-shift-prevention reasoning behind requiring width/height up front.
followUp: When would you use the priority prop on next/image, and what does it actually change about how that specific image is loaded compared to the default behavior?

question: What's the difference between a dynamic route segment ([id]) and a catch-all segment ([...slug]) in Next.js, and when would you use each?
concise: A dynamic segment like [id] matches exactly one path segment (so /products/[id] matches /products/123 but not /products/123/reviews), useful when a route always has a fixed, known number of path parts; a catch-all segment like [...slug] matches one or more path segments as an array (so /docs/[...slug] matches both /docs/intro and /docs/guide/setup), useful for routes with a variable, unknown-in-advance depth, like a documentation site's nested pages or a CMS-driven page tree where the URL structure mirrors an arbitrarily nested content hierarchy.
strong: [id] is the right choice whenever a route's shape is fixed and known, like a specific product detail page, a specific user's profile page, or a specific order's detail view, where there's always exactly one meaningful dynamic value at that specific position in the URL. [...slug] is for genuinely variable-depth routes, most commonly a documentation site or a CMS-backed page tree, where /docs/getting-started, /docs/api/authentication, and /docs/api/authentication/tokens might all need to resolve to the same dynamic route handler, receiving the full remaining path as an array (['api', 'authentication', 'tokens']) that the page then uses to look up the correct content, rather than needing a separate, explicitly defined route file for every possible depth of nesting. There's also an optional catch-all variant, [[...slug]] with double brackets, which additionally matches the exact parent route itself with zero extra segments (so /docs alone also matches, with slug being an empty array), which is useful specifically when the base route itself should render some default content (like a docs homepage) rather than resulting in a 404 for that exact base path.
weak: A weak answer doesn't know catch-all routes exist at all and would instead try to manually define a separate dynamic route file for every possible level of URL nesting, which doesn't scale for content whose depth isn't known or fixed in advance.
followUp: What's the difference between [...slug] and the optional catch-all [[...slug]] specifically in terms of whether the base parent route itself (with no additional segments at all) matches?

question: What is generateStaticParams for, and how does it interact with rendering strategy for dynamic routes?
concise: generateStaticParams, exported from a dynamic route's page file, tells Next.js which specific parameter values (like which product ids) should be pre-rendered at build time as static pages, rather than rendered on-demand per request; any dynamic route param values not included in that list are, by default, either rendered on-demand on first request and then cached (if dynamicParams isn't set to false), or result in a 404 if you explicitly opt out of on-demand generation for anything outside the pre-generated set.
strong: For a product catalog with, say, a few hundred products, exporting an async generateStaticParams function that returns an array of { id: '...' } objects for every known product id tells Next.js to actually build and pre-render each of those specific product pages as static HTML at build time, which serves those pages with the same instant, CDN-cacheable performance as a purely static page, while still technically being a 'dynamic route' in terms of its file structure. If a new product is added after the build already happened, and its id wasn't included in generateStaticParams's returned list, Next.js's default behavior (dynamicParams defaulting to true) is to render that specific page on-demand the first time it's actually requested, and then cache that rendered result going forward, effectively behaving like ISR for any params outside the pre-built set; setting dynamicParams to false instead makes Next.js return a genuine 404 for any param value not explicitly included in generateStaticParams's list, which is the right choice specifically when you want a hard guarantee that only a known, fixed, pre-approved set of pages can ever exist, and anything else should be treated as not found rather than silently generated on demand. For a catalog with a genuinely huge number of products, generating every single one at build time might make builds impractically slow, so a common real pattern is to pre-generate only the most popular or most recently added subset via generateStaticParams, and let the long tail render on-demand and get cached the first time each one is actually visited.
weak: A weak answer assumes generateStaticParams is required for every dynamic route to work at all, without understanding that dynamic routes work fine on-demand without it, and that its real purpose is specifically to pre-build a known, chosen subset of pages at build time for performance.
followUp: For a catalog with millions of products, why might pre-generating every single one via generateStaticParams at build time actually be the wrong choice, even if it were technically possible?

question: How does streaming with Suspense and loading.tsx work in the App Router, and what real user-experience problem does it solve?
concise: Without streaming, a server-rendered page waits for every piece of data across the entire page to be ready before sending any HTML at all, so one slow data source anywhere on the page delays the entire page's first paint; wrapping slower parts of a page in a Suspense boundary (or using the file-based loading.tsx convention for a whole route segment) lets Next.js send the fast, ready parts of the page's HTML immediately, streaming in the slower parts' actual content (and swapping out their fallback) progressively as each one's data becomes ready, all within the same initial server response.
strong: On a dashboard page with several independent widgets, say a fast-loading account summary and a slower-loading, heavier analytics chart pulling from a slow downstream data source, rendering the whole page as one atomic unit means the entire page, including the fast account summary, waits behind whichever single piece of data happens to be slowest, which is a genuinely bad and needless user experience, since the user could have seen most of the page's real, meaningful content far sooner. Wrapping the slow analytics widget specifically in its own Suspense boundary with a fallback (like a skeleton loader) lets Next.js send the rest of the page, including the fast account summary, as soon as it's ready, with the slow widget's fallback UI streamed in as a placeholder in its exact final position, and then the real content for that widget streamed in and swapped into place once its data actually resolves, all as part of the same ongoing HTTP response rather than a second separate client-side round trip. The file-based loading.tsx convention applies this same streaming mechanism at the level of an entire route segment automatically, showing that file's exported component as an instant fallback for the whole page while its data loads, without needing to manually wrap the page's own content in an explicit Suspense boundary yourself. This meaningfully improves perceived performance metrics like actual visible content appearing sooner, though it's worth being precise that it doesn't change the total time until every piece of data is fully ready, it changes the order and progressive manner in which the user actually gets to see meaningful content.
weak: A weak answer thinks streaming just makes the overall page load faster in some general sense, without understanding the actual mechanism: it changes the order and progressive manner of content delivery within one response, letting fast content appear sooner rather than making every individual data source itself resolve any faster.
followUp: What HTTP mechanism actually allows the server to keep sending additional HTML into the same, already-started response after the initial fast content has already been sent to the browser?

question: What's the difference between NEXT_PUBLIC_-prefixed environment variables and regular ones in Next.js, and why does this matter for secrets?
concise: An environment variable prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ is inlined directly into the client-side JavaScript bundle at build time, meaning its value is visible to anyone who opens the browser's dev tools or views the page source, while a regular, unprefixed environment variable is only ever available on the server side (in Server Components, route handlers, server actions, and middleware) and is never included in the client bundle at all; this makes it critical to never put a genuine secret (an API key, a payment provider's secret key, a database credential) behind the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, since doing so ships it directly to every visitor's browser.
strong: The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix exists specifically as an explicit, opt-in signal that a given environment variable's value is meant to be public and safe to expose to the browser, like a publishable (not secret) Stripe key, an analytics tracking id, or a public API base URL; Next.js's build process actually finds and inlines the literal value of any NEXT_PUBLIC_-prefixed variable directly into the client-side JavaScript bundle wherever it's referenced, which means, quite literally, its value can be read by anyone by just viewing the page's source or the network tab. A regular environment variable without that prefix is only ever accessible in code that genuinely runs exclusively on the server, like inside a Server Component's async function body, a route handler, or a server action, and Next.js's bundler specifically excludes it from ever being included in anything shipped to the client, which is exactly why real secrets, a payment provider's actual secret key, a database connection string, an internal service's API token, must always be stored as a regular, non-prefixed environment variable and only ever read from server-side code, never passed down as a prop into a Client Component or referenced anywhere inside a file marked 'use client'. A genuinely dangerous but surprisingly common mistake is accidentally prefixing a real secret with NEXT_PUBLIC_ out of habit or copy-paste, which silently and permanently ships that secret to every visitor's browser the moment the app is deployed, with no error or warning from the framework at all, since from the framework's own perspective that's exactly the behavior the prefix was explicitly asked for.
weak: A weak answer doesn't realize the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix has this literal, build-time bundling consequence, and might casually prefix a genuine secret with it, silently and permanently exposing that secret to every visitor's browser with no runtime error or warning at all.
followUp: If you accidentally shipped a real secret key prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ to production, what's the full remediation, beyond just removing the prefix and redeploying?

question: What are practical techniques for keeping a Next.js app's client bundle size small, and how would you actually measure where the bundle size is going?
concise: Use @next/bundle-analyzer to visualize exactly what's contributing to bundle size, prefer Server Components by default (so entire subtrees ship zero client JS unless they're genuinely interactive), use next/dynamic to lazy-load large client-only components (like a heavy chart library or a rich-text editor) that aren't needed for the initial render, check for accidentally-duplicated or unnecessarily-large third-party dependencies (importing an entire library instead of just the specific function you need from it), and use next/image and next/font to avoid unoptimized image and font payloads inflating what actually needs to load for a fast first paint.
strong: The first, concrete step is always to actually measure rather than guess: running the build with @next/bundle-analyzer enabled produces an interactive treemap visualization showing exactly which specific modules and dependencies are contributing how many kilobytes to each page's bundle, which very often surfaces a genuinely surprising culprit, like an entire date-formatting or icon library being pulled in wholesale because of how it was imported, rather than the specific handful of functions actually being used from it. Since the App Router defaults every component to a Server Component unless explicitly marked otherwise, deliberately keeping 'use client' boundaries as narrow and deep in the tree as possible (as covered in the Server/Client Components question) is itself one of the biggest bundle-size levers available, since anything that stays a Server Component contributes literally zero bytes to the client JavaScript bundle regardless of how large or dependency-heavy its own server-side logic is. For genuinely large, client-only pieces of functionality that aren't needed for the initial page view, like a rich-text editor that's only shown after a user clicks 'edit', or a heavy charting library only needed on an analytics tab a user might never visit, next/dynamic with a loading fallback lets you split that code into its own separate chunk that's only actually downloaded when (and if) it's genuinely needed, rather than bloating the initial page load for every visitor regardless of whether they ever use that feature. Fonts and images are also easy, often-overlooked contributors to overall page weight (even if not strictly 'JavaScript bundle size'), and next/font (which self-hosts and subsets fonts automatically) and next/image (covered earlier) both directly address that.
weak: A weak answer suggests generic advice like 'minify the code' or 'use fewer libraries' without knowing about @next/bundle-analyzer as the actual tool to identify where bundle size is genuinely going, or without knowing next/dynamic exists specifically for deferring large, non-critical client-only code.
followUp: Why would you set ssr: false on a next/dynamic import, and give a concrete example of a library that genuinely requires that option to avoid a server-side rendering error.

question: How would you set security headers (like a Content-Security-Policy) in a Next.js app, and what's a common mistake when doing so?
concise: Security headers can be set either in next.config.js's headers() function (applying to matched routes at build/deploy configuration time) or dynamically in middleware (useful when the header's value needs to vary per request, like a per-request CSP nonce); a common mistake is copying a strict CSP policy from documentation or another project without actually testing it against the app's real third-party scripts (analytics, payment SDKs, font/CDN origins), which silently breaks those integrations in production since the browser just refuses to load or execute anything not explicitly allow-listed, often with no obviously connected error message pointing back to the CSP as the actual cause.
strong: Setting headers via next.config.js's async headers() function is the simpler, more common approach for static, unchanging security headers, like X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, or a CSP policy that doesn't need to vary per request; for a CSP that requires a fresh, unpredictable nonce on every single request specifically to allow a small number of legitimately necessary inline scripts, middleware is the right place instead, since it runs per-request and can generate and inject a new nonce value into both the response header and the actual rendered page (so the nonce used in the header matches the one embedded in the script tags Next.js renders). The mistake I see constantly is deploying a CSP that hasn't actually been tested against the app's real, full set of third-party integrations, since a properly strict script-src directive will silently block anything not explicitly allow-listed, including a payment provider's SDK script, an analytics tag's script, or a font loaded from a CDN origin not included in the policy, and the resulting failure often doesn't look like an obvious CSP error to someone unfamiliar with it, it just looks like 'the payment button silently doesn't work' or 'the font isn't loading', with the actual CSP violation logged quietly in the browser console rather than surfacing as an obvious application error. The safe rollout pattern is to first deploy the intended policy in report-only mode (Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only), which logs what would have been blocked without actually blocking anything yet, monitor those reports for a reasonable period to catch every legitimate integration the policy would otherwise break, and only then switch it to the actual enforcing header once confident nothing legitimate is being caught by it.
weak: A weak answer copies a strict CSP policy directly from a blog post or another project without testing it against the app's actual real third-party scripts first, which silently breaks legitimate integrations like a payment SDK or analytics tag in production with no obviously connected error message.
followUp: Why is report-only mode (Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only) specifically useful for safely rolling out a new, stricter CSP policy on an existing production app?

question: What's the difference between the Node.js runtime and the Edge runtime for a Next.js route handler or middleware, and how would you decide between them?
concise: The Node.js runtime is the full, familiar Node environment, supporting the complete Node standard library and virtually all npm packages, but it runs in a traditional server instance (or serverless function) with comparatively slower cold starts and typically fewer, more centralized deployment regions; the Edge runtime is a deliberately minimal, V8-based JavaScript environment (not full Node) that starts up near-instantly and can run at many geographically distributed edge locations close to the user, but it only supports a restricted Web-standard API surface and can't use Node-specific built-ins or many npm packages that depend on them internally.
strong: For latency-sensitive logic that needs to run on essentially every request and benefits from executing physically close to the user, like an auth check redirecting unauthenticated users, a geolocation-based redirect, or straightforward request/response header manipulation, the Edge runtime's near-instant cold starts and distributed execution locations are a genuine, measurable performance win, and this is exactly why Next.js middleware runs on the Edge runtime by default. For anything that needs genuine Node.js capabilities, direct filesystem access, a database driver that depends on Node-specific TCP/socket APIs, certain image-processing or PDF-generation libraries, or just broader, more mature npm ecosystem compatibility in general, the Node.js runtime remains the right and often only viable choice, even though its cold starts are typically slower and it usually runs from fewer centralized deployment regions rather than being distributed globally the way Edge functions are. Route handlers can explicitly opt into either runtime via an exported runtime config, so the actual decision is genuinely per-route: a route handler that just proxies a lightweight request to another API and applies simple logic might reasonably run on Edge for speed, while a route handler that needs to talk to a traditional database driver, generate a PDF invoice, or use a Node-specific crypto library likely needs Node. A concrete real trade-off worth naming explicitly in an interview: many popular database client libraries (some traditional Postgres or MySQL drivers, for example) historically don't work on Edge at all because they depend on raw Node TCP sockets, which is exactly the kind of constraint that would force a specific route to run on Node instead of Edge, regardless of how much you might otherwise prefer Edge's performance characteristics for that route.
weak: A weak answer assumes Edge is simply 'the newer, strictly better, always-preferred option' without understanding its real API and library-compatibility restrictions, or doesn't realize the runtime is actually configurable on a genuinely per-route basis rather than being one single, fixed, app-wide choice.
followUp: Give a concrete, realistic example of an npm package commonly used in a Next.js API route that would fail to run under the Edge runtime specifically because of a Node-only dependency, and explain why.

question: What are Server Actions in Next.js, and what security considerations apply to them, especially around input validation?
