weak: A weak answer treats Lighthouse and the Performance panel as interchangeable tools for the same job, or only knows how to run a Lighthouse audit and read its score, without knowing how to actually dig into a specific slow interaction's real cause using the Performance panel's timeline and flame graph.
followUp: If Lighthouse reports a poor LCP score but you can't reproduce any visible slowness yourself when testing the page locally, what would you check next to understand the discrepancy?

question: Explain the difference between unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests, and roughly what proportion of each a healthy frontend test suite has.
concise: Unit tests verify a single function, hook, or component in isolation, mocking away its dependencies, and are fast and cheap to write and run; integration tests verify that several units work correctly together (like a form component actually submitting through a real, unmocked validation library, or several components interacting through shared state), catching bugs unit tests miss at the seams between pieces; end-to-end tests drive a real browser through an actual user flow against a real (or close-to-real) running app and backend, catching issues no lower-level test can, at the cost of being slower, more expensive to maintain, and more prone to flakiness; a healthy suite generally has many unit tests, a meaningful but smaller number of integration tests, and relatively few, carefully chosen end-to-end tests covering only the most critical user flows.
strong: This is often visualized as a pyramid: a large base of fast, cheap, focused unit tests that give quick feedback and pinpoint exactly what broke when they fail, a smaller middle layer of integration tests that verify real interactions between pieces (like a form's fields, its validation, and its submit handler genuinely working together, not just each individually mocked), and a small top layer of end-to-end tests that drive an actual browser through a handful of the most business-critical flows, like signup, checkout, and login, since these catch real, production-representative issues (a CSS class name collision breaking a click, an actual network request failing) that no amount of mocked-out unit testing would ever surface. The proportions matter because end-to-end tests are dramatically more expensive along every dimension that matters day to day: they're slow to run (each one might take many seconds or minutes), they're the most prone to intermittent flakiness (network timing, animation timing, environment differences), and a failure often requires real debugging effort to figure out which specific step actually broke, versus a failing unit test that tells you precisely which function's behavior changed. In practice, on a dashboard or forms-heavy app, I'd write extensive unit tests for individual utility functions, hooks, and isolated component logic, a solid layer of integration tests using Testing Library for components that involve real interaction between several pieces (a filterable table, a multi-field form), and a deliberately small, curated set of Playwright or Cypress end-to-end tests covering only the handful of flows where a real regression would be genuinely costly to the business, like the actual payment checkout flow working end to end.
weak: A weak answer either can't clearly distinguish the three test types at all, or advocates for a large number of end-to-end tests as the primary testing strategy, without acknowledging their real cost in speed, flakiness, and maintenance burden compared to unit and integration tests.
followUp: Why specifically is an end-to-end test more prone to being flaky (intermittently failing for reasons unrelated to an actual bug) than a well-written unit test?

question: What is the core philosophy behind React Testing Library (query by role/text, avoid testing implementation details), and why does it matter?
concise: Testing Library's guiding principle is 'test your software the way a real user actually uses it', which means finding elements the way a user would perceive them, by their visible text, their accessible role, or their label, rather than by an internal implementation detail like a component's internal state variable name or a specific CSS class; this makes tests resilient to internal refactors (like renaming a piece of internal state, or changing which HTML element renders a button, as long as it's still perceivably a button to the user) and, as a valuable side effect, actively encourages writing more accessible markup, since a query like getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }) simply doesn't work at all on an inaccessible div-based fake button with no proper role or accessible name.
strong: A test written against implementation details, like directly checking a component's internal state value, or selecting an element by a CSS class name that exists purely for styling purposes, breaks the moment you refactor the component's internals, even if the actual user-facing behavior hasn't changed at all, which produces exactly the kind of brittle, high-maintenance test suite that erodes a team's trust in tests and eventually leads people to just stop writing (or start ignoring failures from) them. Testing Library's query priority deliberately favors queries a real user (or an assistive technology user) would use to find and interact with something, getByRole, getByLabelText, getByText, in roughly that preferred order, over more implementation-coupled queries like getByTestId, which is intentionally positioned as a last-resort escape hatch rather than a default choice, since reaching for a test id first tends to lead to writing tests (and often markup) that don't reflect real accessibility or real user experience at all. A genuinely valuable side effect of this philosophy is that it makes accessibility gaps immediately visible during testing itself: if you can't easily query a button by its accessible role and name in a test, that's very often a sign the actual markup isn't properly accessible either, for example a clickable div with no role='button' and no accessible label, which a real screen reader user would have exactly the same trouble finding and understanding as your test does. In practice, this philosophy shifts what a passing test suite actually tells you: instead of 'the internal implementation still works exactly the way it did before', it tells you 'a real user can still find this button, and clicking it still produces the behavior they'd expect', which is a much more meaningful and durable guarantee.
weak: A weak answer defaults to querying elements by CSS class or by a data-testid attribute on nearly everything, without knowing that Testing Library's actual guiding philosophy specifically discourages that as anything other than a last resort, precisely because it couples tests to implementation details rather than user-perceivable behavior.
followUp: In what specific, legitimate case would reaching for getByTestId actually be the right choice, rather than a sign of testing implementation details?

question: How would you mock API calls in tests using Mock Service Worker (MSW), and why is it preferred over mocking fetch/axios directly?
concise: MSW intercepts actual outgoing network requests at the network layer (using a service worker in the browser, or request interception in Node for tests) and returns a mocked response, so the component or hook being tested calls the exact same real fetch or axios code it would in production, with no test-only conditional branches or manually swapped-out mock implementations required; this is more realistic and more resilient than directly mocking fetch or axios (like jest.mock('axios')), since it tests the component's actual real integration with its data-fetching layer rather than a stand-in that might drift out of sync with how the real network call is actually structured.
strong: Directly mocking axios or fetch with a manual test double means you're testing against a fake implementation of the entire HTTP layer that has to be manually kept in sync with how the real code actually calls it, headers, exact URL structure, request method, and if that mock's assumptions drift out of sync with reality (say, the real code adds a new required header later), a test using a hand-rolled mock might keep passing even though the real network call would now genuinely fail, because the mock was never actually validating the real request shape at all, just returning whatever canned response you told it to regardless of what was actually requested. MSW instead works by intercepting requests at the actual network boundary, meaning the component or hook under test runs its completely real, unmodified data-fetching code, a real fetch call with real headers and a real URL, and MSW's request handler inspects that real, fully-formed request and decides how to respond, which means your test is exercising the real integration between your component and its actual networking code, not a stand-in for it. This also means the exact same MSW request handlers can be reused across unit tests, integration tests, and even in local development (as an actual running mock server) to simulate specific backend states, like a slow response, an error response, or a specific edge-case payload, without needing to maintain separate mocking logic for each different testing context. Practically, this also lets you test genuinely realistic scenarios, like verifying your component correctly displays a specific error message when the API returns a 500, or correctly displays a loading state during the actual (mocked) network delay, in a way that closely mirrors how the real app would behave against the real backend.
weak: A weak answer defaults to jest.mock('axios') or manually mocking global.fetch with a hand-rolled implementation, without recognizing the real drawback: that approach doesn't validate the real request shape at all and can silently drift out of sync with what the actual production networking code does.
followUp: How would you use MSW to specifically test that your component correctly displays an error message when the API returns a 500 response, without needing to actually take down or misconfigure a real backend?

question: What are the pitfalls of snapshot testing, and when is it actually a good fit versus a bad fit?
concise: A snapshot test captures a component's entire rendered output and flags any difference from a previously-saved snapshot on subsequent runs; it's a poor fit as a primary testing strategy for frequently-changing UI, since developers quickly develop a habit of blindly running the 'update snapshot' command without actually reviewing what changed, turning the test into a rubber stamp rather than a meaningful check; it's a better fit for genuinely stable, rarely-changing output where any difference at all is inherently suspicious and worth a human's attention, like a pure data-transformation function's output shape, or a design system's low-level, intentionally-stable primitive components.
strong: The core problem with snapshot tests as a broad default testing strategy is behavioral, not technical: the moment a snapshot test starts failing frequently due to totally legitimate, intentional changes (a button's padding changed slightly, a prop was renamed), developers quickly learn to just run the update-snapshots command reflexively without actually reading the diff to confirm the change is correct and expected, which means the test has effectively stopped providing any real verification at all, it's just automatically re-approving whatever the code currently produces. This is especially bad for components that change often during active development, like a page still being actively iterated on, since the snapshot essentially becomes noise that gets rubber-stamped on every commit rather than a meaningful safety net that catches genuine, unintended regressions. Snapshot testing is a much better fit for output that's expected to be genuinely stable and where any difference at all is inherently suspicious and worth real scrutiny, for example a pure function that transforms raw API data into a specific shape for a chart, where the expected output structure shouldn't change unless you're deliberately changing that transformation logic, or a foundational, rarely-touched design-system primitive component, where an unexpected snapshot diff is a strong, meaningful signal that something changed that genuinely shouldn't have. Even when using snapshots, I'd keep them small and targeted, snapshotting a specific data structure or a small, focused piece of output rather than an entire large component's full rendered DOM tree, since a small, focused snapshot's diff is actually readable and reviewable by a human, while a snapshot of a huge, complex rendered tree produces a diff that's realistically too large and noisy for anyone to meaningfully review, encouraging exactly the blind-update habit that makes snapshot testing risky in the first place.
weak: A weak answer uses snapshot testing as the default, primary way to test every component's rendered output, without recognizing the well-known 'developers blindly update snapshots without reviewing them' failure mode that makes this an unreliable primary testing strategy for frequently-changing UI.
followUp: How would you specifically structure a snapshot test to keep its diff small and genuinely reviewable, rather than snapshotting an entire large component's full rendered output?

question: How would you correctly test an async operation in a component, like a button that triggers a fetch call and then displays the result?
concise: Use Testing Library's async utilities, findBy* queries (which wait for an element to eventually appear, retrying internally for a short period) or waitFor (which retries an arbitrary assertion until it passes or times out), rather than a getBy* query immediately followed by an assertion, since the fetched data won't have arrived yet at the exact moment right after triggering the action; avoid using an arbitrary fixed setTimeout/sleep in the test itself as a workaround, since that makes the test either flaky (too short a wait on a slow CI machine) or needlessly slow (too long a wait as a defensive habit).
strong: Immediately after simulating a user clicking a button that triggers an async fetch, the component almost certainly hasn't received and rendered the fetched data yet, since even a mocked network request usually still resolves on a subsequent microtask or macrotask rather than perfectly synchronously in the same tick as the click; a test that immediately calls getByText('Ana') right after firing the click, expecting to find already-loaded data, will fail even though the code is completely correct, since the assertion is simply running too early, before the async work has had a chance to resolve. findByText('Ana') (or any findBy* query) solves this correctly by internally polling and retrying for a short period, resolving as soon as the element actually appears, or failing with a clear timeout error if it genuinely never does, which is both correct and about as fast as the actual test needs to be, since it doesn't wait any longer than necessary once the element does show up. waitFor is the more general-purpose version of the same underlying mechanism, useful when you need to wait for an arbitrary assertion to become true, not specifically for an element to appear, like waiting for a mocked function to have been called a specific number of times. I specifically avoid a hardcoded setTimeout or sleep-based wait in a test as an anti-pattern, since it's fundamentally guessing at how long the async operation should take: too short a fixed delay makes the test genuinely flaky on a slower CI runner, and too long a delay just wastes real time on every single test run, whereas the retry-based findBy/waitFor approach adapts automatically to how long the actual operation genuinely takes, up to its own timeout.
weak: A weak answer writes a test with a fixed setTimeout/sleep delay before asserting on the async result, or uses a getBy* query immediately after triggering the action and is confused why the test intermittently fails, without understanding that findBy*/waitFor exist specifically to correctly and efficiently wait for async UI updates.
followUp: What specific error message does Testing Library give you when a findBy* query times out without ever finding the element, and how would that help you debug whether the actual bug is in the component or in the test's assumptions?

question: Compare Cypress and Playwright as end-to-end testing tools, and how you'd decide between them for a new project.
concise: Both let you drive a real browser through actual user flows and assert on real rendered output and network behavior; Playwright supports genuinely multiple browser engines (Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit/Safari) from one API and runs tests in true separate browser contexts in parallel efficiently, with built-in auto-waiting and strong TypeScript support out of the box; Cypress has a longer track record, an especially polished interactive time-travel debugging experience in its own dedicated test runner UI, and a mature ecosystem of plugins, though its cross-browser support (particularly for genuine Safari/WebKit testing) has historically been more limited than Playwright's.
strong: Both tools solve the same fundamental problem, driving a real browser to verify a real user flow actually works end to end, and both have moved well past the old Selenium-era pain points of manually managing explicit waits, since both provide solid auto-waiting behavior built in (retrying an assertion or an action until the element is actually ready, rather than requiring a hardcoded sleep). The genuinely significant differentiator for a lot of real-world QA needs is cross-browser coverage: Playwright runs the exact same test suite against Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit (which is the actual engine Safari uses) from one single, consistent API, which matters a lot if your actual user base includes a meaningful number of Safari or iOS users, since Safari-specific rendering or JavaScript engine quirks are a real, recurring source of bugs that Chromium-only testing simply never catches; Cypress's WebKit support has historically been more limited or experimental by comparison. Cypress's own dedicated interactive test runner, with its time-travel debugging (letting you click back through each step of a failed test and see exactly what the DOM and application state looked like at that precise moment) is genuinely excellent for a team's local day-to-day debugging experience while actively writing and troubleshooting tests. For a brand-new project starting today with no existing investment in either tool, I'd lean toward Playwright specifically because of its stronger multi-browser support and generally excellent, actively-improving developer experience, but a team with substantial existing Cypress test coverage and institutional familiarity with it has a perfectly legitimate reason to keep building on it rather than rewriting everything just to chase a marginal, incremental advantage.
weak: A weak answer treats the two tools as functionally identical, or picks one purely based on which is more popular or fashionable, without being able to name the actual, concrete differentiator (Playwright's genuine multi-engine including WebKit support) that would drive a real, informed decision for a project with real Safari/iOS user traffic.
followUp: Why does genuine WebKit (Safari engine) test coverage matter specifically, beyond just 'more browsers is generally better', for a real production frontend app?

question: Why is a high test coverage percentage not the same thing as a well-tested codebase, and what would you look at instead?
concise: Coverage percentage only measures which lines of code were executed at least once while running the test suite, it says nothing about whether the test suite actually asserted anything meaningful about the correctness of that code's behavior, so a codebase can have very high coverage with tests that execute every line but assert nothing useful (or trivially assert something that's always true), while genuinely important edge cases and failure paths go completely unverified; a more meaningful signal is whether the test suite actually catches real regressions when a real bug is deliberately introduced, whether critical business logic and edge cases are specifically covered (not just the easy, happy-path lines), and whether the tests give the team genuine confidence to refactor and deploy without manually re-checking everything by hand.
strong: A test that renders a component and asserts only that it doesn't crash technically executes every line of that component's code, contributing to a high coverage number, without verifying a single meaningful thing about whether the component's actual behavior is correct, whether the right data is displayed, whether an error state renders the right message, whether a callback is actually called with the right arguments, none of that is captured by the coverage percentage at all, which purely measures execution, not assertion quality or completeness. I've seen codebases with impressively high coverage numbers that still ship real regressions constantly, precisely because the tests were largely coverage-driven, written specifically to hit lines of code for the metric, rather than genuinely designed around what could realistically break and specifically verifying that it doesn't; conversely, a smaller, more deliberately targeted set of tests that specifically covers the trickiest edge cases, error paths, and business-critical logic (even at a lower overall coverage percentage) often provides genuinely more real confidence and catches genuinely more real bugs. A better practical exercise than staring at a coverage report is mutation testing in spirit, if not literally running a mutation-testing tool: deliberately introduce a specific, realistic bug into the code (flip a comparison operator, off-by-one an index, skip a null check) and see whether the existing test suite actually catches it; if a meaningful number of deliberately-introduced bugs sail through completely undetected despite a high coverage number, that's a much more honest, meaningful signal that the test suite's real bug-catching quality doesn't match what the coverage percentage would suggest. I do still use coverage reports, but mainly as a rough tool for spotting completely untested files or obviously-missed error branches, not as a target number to chase or a measure of genuine test quality on its own.
weak: A weak answer treats a coverage percentage target (like '100% coverage') as an end goal in itself, without recognizing that coverage measures only code execution, not assertion quality, and that a codebase can have high coverage with genuinely weak, low-value tests.
followUp: How would you specifically identify which parts of a codebase have technically-high coverage but genuinely weak, low-value tests, without manually reading every single test file by hand?

question: How would you approach visual regression testing, and what problem does it solve that functional tests (unit/integration/e2e) don't catch?
concise: Visual regression testing captures a screenshot of a component or page in a known state and compares it, pixel by pixel (or via a perceptual diffing algorithm), against a previously-approved baseline screenshot, flagging any meaningful visual difference for human review; this catches a category of real bugs that functional tests are largely blind to, purely visual regressions like a CSS change that breaks an unrelated component's spacing, a color contrast issue, an overlapping element, or a broken responsive layout at a specific viewport width, none of which typically cause any functional test's assertions (which usually check text content, element presence, or behavior, not actual visual appearance) to fail at all.
strong: A functional test can pass with complete confidence, correctly verifying that a button exists, has the right accessible name, and calls the right function when clicked, while the button is simultaneously rendering visually broken, overlapping another element, or using illegible white-on-white text, because none of those specific visual details are things a typical functional assertion actually checks at all; visual regression testing exists specifically to catch that entire category of bug, which is a real, common one, especially in a codebase using a shared, widely-reused CSS utility or design-system component, where a seemingly-small, well-intentioned style change can have unexpected visual side effects on other, seemingly-unrelated parts of the app that happen to share the same underlying styles. In practice, tools like Chromatic (commonly paired with Storybook) or Percy capture screenshots of individual components or full pages across a defined set of viewport sizes and states, and on every subsequent run, a perceptual diffing algorithm (which tolerates trivial anti-aliasing or sub-pixel rendering noise between runs, rather than requiring byte-for-byte pixel identity) flags anything that changed meaningfully, presenting a clear visual diff for a human reviewer to either approve as an intentional design change or reject as an unintended regression. The main practical trade-off is that visual regression tests need genuine human review to correctly triage each flagged diff (was this change intentional or not), and they can be sensitive to environment differences (font rendering, GPU differences) if not run in a consistent, controlled environment, which is why these tools typically run comparisons in a consistent, standardized cloud rendering environment rather than trusting screenshots taken locally on different developers' machines.
weak: A weak answer assumes a passing functional test suite (unit, integration, and e2e) is sufficient to catch any real regression, without recognizing that purely visual bugs (broken layouts, overlapping elements, illegible color contrast) typically don't fail any functional assertion at all and require a fundamentally different testing approach to catch.
followUp: Why do visual regression tools use a perceptual diffing algorithm rather than requiring an exact, byte-for-byte identical screenshot match on every run?

question: What makes a test suite 'flaky', and what are common root causes specifically in a frontend testing context?
concise: A flaky test is one that intermittently passes or fails against the exact same, unchanged code, with no actual bug being introduced or fixed between runs; common frontend-specific causes include a race condition between an async operation (a fetch, an animation, a debounce timer) and an assertion that runs before it resolves, tests that depend on shared, un-reset state (like leftover data in a test database, or a browser's localStorage not being cleared between test runs), reliance on real timing (like a fixed sleep instead of properly waiting for a specific condition), and tests run in parallel that unintentionally interfere with each other by sharing some resource, like the same test user account or the same server-side data.
strong: The single most common cause I've personally debugged is a race condition between the test's assertions and something asynchronous the app itself is doing, an animation that hasn't finished, a debounced input that hasn't yet fired its underlying callback, or a network request that resolves slightly later on a loaded CI runner than it did on a fast local machine, which is exactly why properly using findBy*/waitFor-style retrying assertions (as covered in the async-testing question), rather than a fixed-delay sleep or an immediate getBy* assertion, is so important for genuinely eliminating this entire category of flakiness rather than just reducing its frequency. Shared, un-reset state between test runs is another very common culprit, especially for integration or end-to-end tests that hit a real (even if test-only) backend or database: if one test creates a user record and a later, supposedly-independent test assumes a clean slate but actually depends on (or is broken by) that leftover data, the test suite's overall pass/fail outcome can depend on the specific order tests happen to run in, or on whether a previous test run's cleanup step actually completed successfully, which is exactly the kind of hidden inter-test dependency that produces intermittent, hard-to-reproduce failures. Tests run in parallel (which most CI setups do deliberately, for speed) can also flake if they unintentionally share some resource, like two parallel test workers both mutating the same shared test database row, or both trying to use the same fixed test user account simultaneously; the fix there is usually ensuring proper test isolation, each test (or at least each parallel worker) getting its own genuinely independent data and environment, rather than sharing a single fixed fixture across everything. Whenever I see a flaky test, my first instinct is specifically to look for one of these three patterns, an async race condition, shared un-reset state, or unintended parallel interference, rather than just re-running the test suite repeatedly and hoping it eventually passes.
weak: A weak answer's response to a flaky test is to just re-run it (or add an artificial retry-until-it-passes wrapper) rather than actually investigating and fixing the specific root cause, which leaves the underlying race condition or shared-state problem in place indefinitely.
followUp: Why is simply adding an automatic retry-on-failure wrapper around a known-flaky test a risky long-term habit for a team, even though it makes CI green more often in the short term?

question: How would you structure a CI test strategy to give fast feedback on every pull request while still running the full, slower test suite (including end-to-end tests) somewhere?
concise: Run the fast, cheap layer (linting, type-checking, and the full unit/integration test suite, ideally parallelized across several CI workers) on every single pull request, gating the merge on it, since it typically completes in a few minutes and directly tells the author whether their specific change broke something; run the slower, more expensive end-to-end test suite either on a reduced, smoke-test subset per pull request (covering just the most critical flows) plus the full end-to-end suite on merges to the main branch or on a scheduled interval, since running every single end-to-end test on every single pull request would make the feedback loop for every contributor uncomfortably slow, discouraging frequent, small commits.
strong: The guiding principle is that the cost of a test (in CI minutes, and more importantly in a human's waiting time before they get feedback on their specific change) should roughly match how quickly and how often it needs to run: unit and integration tests are fast enough, usually a few minutes even for a fairly large suite, especially when parallelized across multiple CI workers or sharded by test file, that running the full suite on every single pull request is both affordable and genuinely valuable, since it gives the contributor fast, specific, actionable feedback on exactly what their change broke, ideally within the same review cycle they're actively working in. Linting and type-checking should run even faster and even earlier, often as a pre-commit hook locally in addition to CI, since those catch the cheapest, most mechanical class of errors before a human reviewer's time is even spent looking at the change. The full end-to-end suite is a different story: since it's inherently slower (individual tests take real seconds each, and a comprehensive suite covering many flows can take a genuinely long time even parallelized) and more prone to occasional environmental flakiness, requiring every contributor to wait for the complete end-to-end suite on every single pull request creates real friction that discourages frequent small commits and quick iteration; a smarter split is to run a small, deliberately curated smoke-test subset of the most business-critical end-to-end flows (login, checkout, the core primary feature) on every pull request for a reasonably fast sanity check, and reserve running the full, comprehensive end-to-end suite for merges into the main branch, a nightly scheduled run, or right before an actual production deployment, where a slightly longer wait is a genuinely acceptable trade-off in exchange for much more thorough coverage. Whichever split is chosen, I'd also make sure flaky end-to-end tests are actively tracked and fixed rather than tolerated, since a flaky test in a gating CI check that people learn to just re-run until it passes quietly erodes the entire team's trust in what a passing CI check actually means.
weak: A weak answer either runs every single test, including the entire end-to-end suite, on every single pull request regardless of how slow that makes the feedback loop, or conversely skips end-to-end tests almost entirely from CI, missing the actual balanced middle-ground strategy that gives fast feedback while still ensuring thorough coverage happens somewhere in the pipeline.
followUp: How would you decide which specific handful of end-to-end tests belong in the fast, per-pull-request smoke-test subset, versus which ones can wait for the full suite run on merge to main?

question: How would you structure the folder/module organization of a large frontend codebase as it scales past a small team?
concise: A small app can reasonably organize by file type (a components folder, a hooks folder, a utils folder), but as the codebase and team grow, a feature-based (or 'colocation') structure, grouping each feature's components, hooks, types, and tests together in their own folder, scales much better, since it keeps everything related to one feature physically close together, makes it obvious what's safe to change or delete when a feature is removed, and reduces the number of unrelated files a given change has to touch; a small, deliberately shared layer (design-system components, generic hooks, cross-cutting utilities) still lives centrally, but application feature code should default to being organized by feature, not by technical file type.
strong: Organizing purely by file type works fine for a small app with a handful of features and a small team, since everyone can hold the whole codebase's structure in their head, but it breaks down as the app grows: a components folder with two hundred files gives you no signal at all about which ones are actually related to each other or safe to change together, and a single feature's logic ends up scattered across several distant folders (its component in components/, its data-fetching hook in hooks/, its types in types/), so understanding or safely modifying one feature requires jumping between many unrelated parts of the codebase. A feature-based structure instead groups everything related to one cohesive piece of functionality, its components, its specific hooks, its types, its tests, physically together in one folder, which means a new engineer working on the billing feature only really needs to understand the billing folder to make most changes confidently, and if a feature is ever deprecated or removed entirely, deleting its folder cleanly removes almost everything related to it, rather than requiring an error-prone hunt across several separate, file-type-organized folders to find every related piece. The genuinely shared layer, reusable design-system components, generic cross-cutting hooks (like useDebounce), and truly generic utilities used by many unrelated features, still deserves its own clearly-separated, centralized location, since promoting something into that shared layer should be a deliberate decision (recognizing it's genuinely reusable, not feature-specific) rather than the default, and a clear boundary between 'shared, stable, cross-cutting code' and 'feature-specific code that's expected to evolve independently' helps prevent features from becoming tightly, awkwardly coupled to each other through supposedly-shared code that was really only ever meant for one specific feature in the first place.
code:
src/
  features/
    billing/ (components, hooks, types, tests, all colocated)
    dashboard/
  shared/
    components/ (design system)
    hooks/ (generic, reusable across features)
    utils/
weak: A weak answer defaults to organizing purely by technical file type (a components folder, a hooks folder, a utils folder) regardless of the app's actual size or team size, without recognizing that this structure specifically breaks down as a codebase grows past a small handful of features and contributors.
followUp: How would you decide whether a piece of code (a hook, a utility function) belongs in the shared layer versus staying local to one specific feature's own folder?

question: How would you design a component library / design system so it's genuinely reusable across teams, rather than becoming a source of friction?
concise: Build components around a small set of composable, low-level primitives (following patterns like compound components and headless/unstyled behavior separated from visual styling) rather than large, rigid, highly-configured monolithic components with dozens of props trying to anticipate every use case; version and document the library deliberately (with clear, enforced semantic versioning and a changelog, since consuming teams need to trust that a minor version bump won't silently break their app), and treat accessibility, theming, and consistent design tokens as first-class, built-in requirements of every component rather than something individual consuming teams are expected to bolt on themselves.
strong: A design system that ships large, highly-configured monolithic components, each with dozens of boolean and enum props trying to anticipate every possible layout and behavior variation up front, tends to become a source of real friction over time, since some genuinely reasonable customization a consuming team needs inevitably doesn't fit any existing prop, and the design system team either has to keep adding new props reactively (which the compound components question covered in more depth) or the consuming team works around the library entirely with ad hoc custom CSS, defeating the actual point of having a shared system at all. Building around smaller, composable primitives, following the compound components and headless-UI patterns, lets consuming teams assemble the exact structure and behavior they need directly in their own markup, while still getting the design system's built-in accessibility, keyboard behavior, and consistent visual language for free, without requiring the design system team to have anticipated that exact specific combination ahead of time. Versioning discipline matters more for a shared library than for typical application code, since many different consuming teams, potentially on different release cadences, depend on it simultaneously; a genuinely reliable semantic versioning practice (patch releases never break anything, minor releases only add new, backward-compatible capability, major releases are the only place breaking changes are allowed, clearly documented with a migration guide) is what lets consuming teams actually trust upgrading without needing to carefully re-test their entire app after every single release. Accessibility specifically needs to be built into the design system's own components once, correctly, by a team with the expertise and incentive to genuinely get it right (keyboard navigation, focus management, proper ARIA roles), rather than left as something each individual consuming team is expected to separately implement correctly on every project, which in practice means it gets implemented inconsistently, or not at all, across different teams and features.
weak: A weak answer designs the shared component library around large, rigid, prop-heavy monolithic components, without recognizing that this specific structure is what causes design systems to become a source of team friction and inconsistent workarounds over time, rather than a source of genuine leverage.
followUp: How would you handle a specific, reasonable customization request from one consuming team that the current design system genuinely doesn't support, without either bloating the shared component with a one-off prop or forcing that team to abandon the design system entirely for that use case?

question: How do you decide where a specific piece of state should live: local component state, lifted/shared client state, or server state?
concise: Server state (anything that ultimately originates from an API and can go stale) belongs in a dedicated server-state layer like React Query, not in a general client-state store, since it has fundamentally different needs (caching, revalidation, background refetching) that client-state tools don't address; genuinely global, cross-cutting client-only state (like a shopping cart, the current theme, or feature flags) belongs in a shared client-state store; everything else, meaning state that's only ever read or modified by one component or one small, closely-related subtree, should default to local component state (useState/useReducer) and only get lifted or shared once there's an actual, concrete need for more than one unrelated part of the tree to read or modify it.
strong: My default instinct is to keep state as local as possible, in the specific component that owns it, and only lift it or move it into a shared store once there's a real, demonstrated need, not preemptively 'just in case' a distant future feature might need it; over-lifting state that's genuinely local (like whether one specific dropdown is currently open, or the current draft value of one specific form field) into a global store adds real, ongoing coupling and complexity with no corresponding benefit, and makes that piece of state harder, not easier, to reason about, since now understanding its behavior requires understanding the entire global store rather than just the one component. Once a genuine need for sharing does arise, the next question is what kind of state it actually is: if it originated from a server (fetched data of any kind), it belongs in a server-state layer specifically designed for that, since server-state has fundamentally different concerns, staleness, background revalidation, deduplication across simultaneous requests for the same data, cache invalidation after a mutation, that a generic client-state store like plain Redux or Zustand was never designed to handle well on its own; treating server-fetched data as if it were just another piece of client state, manually managing its loading/error/staleness yourself, is a very common and avoidable source of both bugs and unnecessary boilerplate. Genuinely global, purely client-side state, meaning state with no server origin that many unrelated parts of the app legitimately need to read or modify, like a shopping cart's contents or the app's current theme, is the correct, narrow case for a dedicated client-state store, and even there, I'd keep the actual global store's surface area deliberately small and focused, resisting the temptation to dump increasingly more state into it just because the store already exists and is convenient to reach for.
weak: A weak answer treats all state as one undifferentiated category and defaults to putting everything, including server-fetched data and state that's genuinely local to one component, into one single global store, missing the meaningful distinctions between local, global client, and server state that actually drive good architectural decisions here.
followUp: Give a concrete, realistic example of state that seems like it should be global at first glance, but that you'd actually argue should stay local to one component or one small subtree instead.

question: What are the real trade-offs of adopting a monorepo (with a tool like Nx or Turborepo) versus separate repositories for multiple related frontend projects?
concise: A monorepo makes it much easier to share code (a design system, shared types, shared utilities) across multiple apps with atomic, single-commit changes and consistent tooling/versioning, and modern build tools like Nx and Turborepo add smart caching and dependency-graph-aware task running so only the actually-affected projects rebuild or retest on a given change; the trade-offs are a real increase in tooling and CI complexity to set up and maintain correctly, a larger single repository that can feel unwieldy without good tooling in place, and a real risk of teams becoming more tightly, sometimes unintentionally, coupled to each other's release timing and shared code's stability if boundaries between projects aren't deliberately enforced.
strong: The single biggest, most concrete win of a monorepo is atomic cross-project changes: if a shared design-system component or a shared TypeScript type needs to change in a way that affects three different consuming apps, a monorepo lets you make that change and update all three consumers in one single, coherent commit and one single pull request, whereas across separate repositories, that same change requires publishing a new version of the shared package, then separately updating and testing each consuming repository's dependency on it, which is slower and creates a real window where different apps are running against different, potentially incompatible versions of the same shared code. Modern monorepo tooling like Nx or Turborepo specifically addresses the historical performance complaint about monorepos, that running every single project's full build and test suite on every single change doesn't scale, by building an actual dependency graph of which projects depend on which, and then only rebuilding, retesting, and relinting the projects genuinely affected by a given change, combined with aggressive build-output caching (both locally and shared across a team via a remote cache) so an unchanged project's build can be served instantly from a cache hit rather than genuinely rebuilt from scratch. The real, legitimate trade-offs are worth being honest about: the initial tooling and CI setup for a well-functioning monorepo is genuinely more complex than a handful of independent repositories each with their own simple CI pipeline, and without deliberate architectural boundaries and ownership conventions enforced within the monorepo (like clear module boundaries and lint rules preventing improper cross-project imports), teams can end up more tightly and unintentionally coupled to each other's code and release cadence than they would be with the harder, more deliberate boundary that a separate repository and a versioned package naturally enforces.
weak: A weak answer treats a monorepo as an unconditional upgrade with no real downsides, or conversely dismisses it entirely as 'too complex to ever be worth it', without being able to articulate the specific, concrete trade-off (atomic cross-project changes and shared tooling, versus increased setup complexity and coupling risk) that should actually drive this decision for a specific team.
followUp: How would Nx or Turborepo's dependency-graph-aware task running actually determine which specific projects are 'affected' by a given code change, and only rebuild/retest those?

question: How would you implement feature flags in a frontend app, and what are the trade-offs of different flag evaluation strategies?
concise: Feature flags let you ship code to production while controlling its actual visibility/behavior separately, decoupling deployment from release, and typically support targeting rules (roll out to a percentage of users, a specific user segment, or a specific list of accounts); evaluating flags server-side (or during SSR) avoids a visible flash of the wrong UI state and keeps the actual flag-check logic (and any related sensitive targeting rules) off the client entirely, while evaluating them purely client-side is simpler to set up but risks a flash of incorrect content before the flag's actual value is fetched, and exposes the flag names and targeting logic to anyone inspecting the client bundle or network requests.
strong: Feature flags are valuable specifically because they decouple the act of deploying code (getting it running in production) from the act of releasing a feature (actually making it visible/active for real users), which lets a team merge and deploy a large, in-progress feature safely behind a flag well before it's finished, test it in production with real infrastructure and real data using a small internal or beta user segment, and then gradually roll it out to a wider percentage of users, all without needing a separate, risky, all-at-once deployment specifically timed to when the feature happens to be fully finished. For a server-rendered app (or one using Next.js's App Router), evaluating flags server-side, deciding what to render before the HTML is ever sent to the browser, avoids the classic 'flash of unflagged content' problem, where a purely client-side flag check briefly shows the wrong version of the UI for a moment before a fetched flag value arrives and the correct version swaps in, which is both visually jarring and, for something like a pricing or feature-gating flag, can very briefly reveal something to a user that shouldn't have been visible to them at all. Server-side evaluation also keeps the actual flag names, targeting rules, and rollout percentages entirely on the server, invisible to anyone inspecting the client-side bundle or network requests, which matters for anything sensitive, like an unreleased feature's actual existence, or a targeting rule based on a user's specific account tier that you'd rather not casually reveal to every visitor's browser. The trade-off is that server-side flag evaluation requires the server to have access to whatever context is needed to evaluate the flag correctly (the user's id, their segment, sometimes needing a request out to a flag-evaluation service), which adds real latency and infrastructure complexity that a simpler client-side-only flag check, just reading a value from a config endpoint after the page has already loaded, doesn't need to deal with at all.
weak: A weak answer implements feature flags purely as a client-side conditional (like reading a hardcoded boolean from an environment variable) without considering the flash-of-wrong-content problem, or without recognizing that a purely client-side flag check exposes the flag's existence and logic to anyone inspecting the browser.
followUp: How would you implement a gradual percentage-based rollout (like 'enable this feature for 10% of users') consistently, so the same specific user always gets the same flag value across multiple requests, rather than getting a randomly different value each time?

question: What's a good app-wide error handling strategy, covering both unexpected runtime errors and expected/handled errors like a failed API validation?
concise: Distinguish expected errors (a failed form validation, a 404 for a resource that legitimately doesn't exist, a permission denial) from unexpected errors (a genuine bug, an unhandled exception, a truly unexpected server failure), and handle each differently: expected errors should be caught and displayed as clear, specific, actionable UI feedback exactly where they occur; unexpected errors should be caught by a small number of strategically-placed error boundaries (to prevent one broken feature from crashing the entire app) and automatically reported to an error-tracking service (like Sentry) with enough context to actually debug them, rather than being silently swallowed or shown as a generic, unhelpful message with no logging at all.
strong: Treating every single error the same way, either by swallowing all of them silently or by showing the exact same generic 'something went wrong' message regardless of what actually happened, is a common but real mistake, since expected and unexpected errors genuinely call for different handling: a form validation failure or a legitimate 'this resource doesn't exist' 404 is a completely normal, anticipated outcome of user interaction that deserves specific, clear, in-context UI feedback (a message next to the exact field that failed, or a proper 'not found' page), while a genuinely unexpected error, an unhandled exception from a bug, an API returning a malformed response the code didn't anticipate, represents something that shouldn't have happened at all and needs to be both contained (so it doesn't take down the entire application) and actually reported somewhere a developer will see it and can debug it, with enough context (the user's action, relevant state, a stack trace) to actually understand what went wrong. For unexpected errors specifically, I'd place error boundaries at deliberate, strategic points in the component tree, typically around independent features or widgets rather than one single boundary wrapping the entire app, so a bug in one specific dashboard widget shows a small, contained 'something went wrong with this widget' fallback while the rest of the dashboard continues working normally, and every error caught by a boundary (or by a global window.onerror/unhandledrejection handler, for the async errors boundaries don't catch) gets automatically reported to an error-tracking service with real context, not just a generic message, so the team has actual visibility into production errors happening to real users rather than only finding out about them when a user happens to complain. I'd also make sure custom error types (as covered in the JavaScript custom error hierarchy question) are used consistently so this distinction between 'expected, handle-in-place' and 'unexpected, boundary-catch-and-report' can actually be made systematically in code, rather than every error handler needing to guess based on an error's message text.
weak: A weak answer either wraps every possible error in a generic try/catch that silently swallows it with no user feedback and no reporting at all, or shows the exact same unhelpful generic error message for every kind of failure regardless of whether it was an expected, normal outcome or a genuine unanticipated bug.
followUp: Where specifically would you place error boundaries in a dashboard app with several independent widgets, and why would one single top-level boundary wrapping the entire app be a worse choice than several smaller, more targeted ones?

question: What are the trade-offs of adopting a micro-frontend architecture, and when would it actually be the right call versus a single, well-organized monolithic frontend?
concise: Micro-frontends let independent teams build, test, and deploy their own part of a larger application on their own schedule, using their own tech stack if genuinely needed, which can be valuable for a very large organization with many autonomous teams that would otherwise be bottlenecked sharing one single frontend codebase's release cycle; the real costs are significant added complexity around integration (routing between micro-frontends, shared authentication/session state, consistent styling and design-system usage across independently-built pieces), a real risk of shipping duplicate dependencies (multiple copies of React, for example) inflating bundle size unless carefully managed, and a genuinely harder end-to-end debugging and testing story compared to one single, unified codebase; for most teams and most apps, a well-organized, feature-based monolithic frontend (as covered in the codebase-scaling question) gets most of the same organizational benefits with dramatically less integration complexity.
strong: The genuine, legitimate case for micro-frontends is organizational, not technical: at a large enough company with many largely-independent teams, each owning a distinct part of a large product, forcing all of them to share one single frontend codebase and one single release cycle can become a real bottleneck, where one team's in-progress, half-broken change blocks or slows down every other team's ability to ship, and micro-frontends let each team genuinely own their own deployment pipeline and release cadence independently. But this organizational benefit comes with substantial, very real technical costs that are easy to underestimate: getting independently-built and independently-deployed pieces to actually feel like one single, coherent application to the end user requires solving genuinely hard problems, consistent client-side routing across pieces built and deployed independently, sharing authentication and session state seamlessly across them, ensuring visual and interaction consistency when different teams might drift on which version of the shared design system they're using, and avoiding each micro-frontend shipping its own separate, duplicate copy of large shared dependencies like React, which can meaningfully bloat the total amount of JavaScript a user ends up downloading unless genuinely carefully managed (like properly sharing a single instance of common dependencies across the micro-frontends at runtime). For the large majority of teams and apps, a single, well-organized, feature-based monolithic frontend codebase (with clear internal module boundaries and ownership conventions, even without literally being split into separate deployable applications) captures most of the same 'clear ownership and reduced cross-team stepping-on-toes' benefit with a small fraction of the integration complexity and technical overhead, which is exactly why I'd only genuinely reach for a true micro-frontend architecture once a team has concretely experienced the specific organizational pain (a real, ongoing deployment bottleneck across many independent teams) that it's specifically designed to solve, rather than adopting it preemptively because it sounds like a more 'scalable' architecture in the abstract.
weak: A weak answer treats micro-frontends as a straightforward, generally 'more scalable' architecture to adopt by default for any sufficiently large app, without weighing the very real integration complexity, potential bundle-size duplication, and harder debugging story against the actual specific organizational problem (many independent teams bottlenecked on one shared release cycle) that alone justifies the trade-off.
followUp: How would you prevent multiple independently-deployed micro-frontends from each shipping their own separate, duplicated copy of a large shared dependency like React, which would otherwise significantly bloat the total amount of JavaScript a user has to download?

question: How would you design the API/data-fetching abstraction layer of a frontend app so that components aren't tightly coupled to a specific backend's exact response shape?
concise: Introduce a thin data-access layer (a set of typed functions per resource, like getUser, updateOrder) that's the only part of the codebase allowed to call fetch/axios directly, responsible for translating the backend's actual raw response shape into a clean, stable, frontend-friendly shape (and validating it, as covered in the runtime-validation TypeScript question) before anything else in the app ever sees it, so components and hooks depend only on that stable, app-owned shape, not on the backend's specific field names, casing conventions, or nesting structure directly.
strong: Without this layer, if components call fetch directly and destructure fields straight off the raw API response throughout the codebase, the backend's specific response shape effectively becomes part of the contract that dozens of unrelated components across the app are all directly, individually coupled to, so a backend change, renaming a field, changing a naming convention from snake_case to camelCase, restructuring a nested object, requires hunting down and updating every single place in the frontend that happens to reference that specific field, which is fragile, error-prone, and gets worse as the codebase grows. Introducing a dedicated data-access layer, a set of functions specifically responsible for calling the actual API and mapping its raw response into a clean, stable, frontend-owned shape, means that mapping/translation logic lives in exactly one place; if the backend changes its response shape, you update the mapping function in that one place, and every consuming component, which only ever depended on the clean, stable, frontend-owned shape, continues working completely unaffected, without ever needing to know the backend's shape changed at all. This same layer is also the natural place to apply runtime validation (parsing the raw response through a schema, as covered in the TypeScript runtime-validation question), so any actual mismatch between what the backend returns and what the frontend expects is caught immediately, at the boundary, with a clear error, rather than silently propagating malformed or unexpectedly-shaped data deep into the app where it eventually causes a confusing, hard-to-trace bug several components away from the actual root cause. In a React app I'd typically pair this data-access layer directly with the server-state layer (React Query's useQuery/useMutation), so each resource's typed fetch/mutate functions and their query-key-based caching live together, cleanly separating 'how do we talk to this specific backend and what shape does it actually return' from 'how does this specific component want to display or interact with that data'.
weak: A weak answer lets components call fetch/axios directly and destructure fields straight off the raw API response throughout the codebase, tightly coupling many unrelated components directly to the backend's exact field names and shape, which makes any backend response change require hunting down and updating every individual consuming component.
followUp: Where specifically should input validation (checking the raw response actually matches the expected shape) live in this layered architecture, and why does that boundary make sense as the one place to catch a mismatch?

question: How would you approach versioning and evolving a shared internal component library without breaking the many applications that depend on it?
concise: Follow strict semantic versioning (patch for pure bug fixes with no behavior change consumers could be relying on, minor for genuinely backward-compatible new capability, major only for actual breaking changes), deprecate a prop or component with a clear, visible warning (and a documented migration path) for at least one full release cycle before actually removing it, and provide codemods (automated code-transformation scripts) for any non-trivial breaking change in a major version, so consuming teams can mechanically migrate most of their usage automatically rather than manually rewriting every single call site by hand.
strong: Consuming teams need to be able to trust the version number itself as an honest, reliable signal of risk, a patch release should be safe to accept with essentially zero review, a minor release should be safe to accept with only a light scan of the changelog, and only a major release should require an actual, deliberate migration effort, and violating that trust even once, shipping an actual breaking change inside what was labeled as a minor or patch release, teaches every consuming team to stop trusting version numbers at all and start manually re-testing everything on every single update regardless of its labeled version, which defeats much of the actual point of having a versioned shared library in the first place. For an intentional, necessary breaking change, like renaming a confusing prop or fundamentally changing a component's underlying behavior, the respectful path for consuming teams is to first ship the new API alongside the old one in a minor release, with the old one marked as deprecated (ideally with a runtime console warning, and a clear note in the documentation and changelog pointing to the new API and explaining why), giving consuming teams real time to migrate at their own pace before the old API is actually removed in a subsequent major version. For any breaking change that's mechanical and repetitive across many call sites, a codemod, an automated script that parses and rewrites the actual consuming code, is worth the real investment to write, since it turns what would otherwise be a tedious, error-prone, manual find-and-replace effort repeated independently by every single consuming team into a single command each team can run to have most (sometimes all) of their affected usage automatically migrated, dramatically lowering the real-world cost and friction of adopting a new major version, which in turn makes consuming teams meaningfully more willing to actually upgrade in a timely way rather than getting stuck on an old, increasingly unsupported version indefinitely.
weak: A weak answer ships breaking changes inside a minor or patch version 'because it seemed like a small change', without understanding that this specific practice, more than almost anything else, destroys consuming teams' trust in the shared library's versioning and discourages them from ever upgrading promptly again.
followUp: How would a consuming team's own CI pipeline help catch an accidental breaking change in what was supposed to be a non-breaking minor or patch release of the shared component library, before it actually reaches their production app?

question: How would you choose between Redux, Zustand, and plain React Context plus useReducer for a new app's global client state needs?
concise: Redux is the right choice when a team specifically wants its mature, opinionated structure (actions, reducers, middleware), strong time-travel debugging via Redux DevTools, and a large, well-established ecosystem, and is willing to accept its comparatively higher boilerplate, though modern Redux Toolkit has significantly reduced that boilerplate versus classic Redux; Zustand is a good default for most new apps needing genuine global client state, since it gives selector-based subscriptions (avoiding Context's broad re-render problem) with a small, minimal API and very little boilerplate; plain Context plus useReducer is reasonable only for state that's global in scope but changes infrequently, since Context's lack of selective subscription becomes a real, measurable performance problem the moment the shared state updates often and many components consume it.
strong: For most new applications today, especially ones without a large existing team already deeply invested in Redux's specific patterns and tooling, I'd default to Zustand for genuine global client-only state, since it gives you selector-based subscriptions, meaning a component only re-renders when the specific slice of state it actually subscribes to changes, with a dramatically smaller API surface and far less boilerplate than even modern Redux Toolkit requires, while still supporting middleware-like patterns (persistence, devtools integration) when genuinely needed. Redux (via Redux Toolkit, not classic hand-rolled Redux, which has become genuinely unnecessary boilerplate today) remains a solid, defensible choice specifically for larger teams that want its more rigid, opinionated structure enforced consistently across many contributors, its mature time-travel debugging experience via Redux DevTools, and its large, battle-tested middleware ecosystem for things like complex async flow orchestration, particularly on teams that already have deep institutional Redux experience and tooling investment. Plain Context plus useReducer is genuinely fine, and adds zero new dependencies, specifically for state that's global in the sense that several unrelated parts of the tree need to read it, but that changes relatively infrequently, like the current authenticated user, a theme setting, or a locale preference, since Context's fundamental lack of selective subscription (every consumer re-renders on any change to the context's value, as covered in the Context performance question) only actually becomes a real, measurable problem once the shared state updates frequently and many components are subscribed to it; using Context for something that updates on every keystroke or every few hundred milliseconds is where I'd specifically steer away from it toward a proper selector-based store instead.
weak: A weak answer picks whichever single tool they personally know best and applies it uniformly to every project regardless of its actual specific needs (update frequency, team size, existing tooling investment), rather than being able to articulate the real, concrete trade-offs that should genuinely drive the choice for a specific app and team.
followUp: At what rough threshold, in terms of how often the shared state updates and how many components consume it, would you actually recommend migrating from Context to a proper selector-based store like Zustand?

question: How would you architect authentication and authorization consistently across a frontend app that has both server-rendered pages and client-side interactive features, ensuring the frontend and backend never drift out of sync on permission rules?
concise: Keep the actual source of truth for permission logic (which roles can perform which actions) defined once, ideally on the backend (or in a shared package both frontend and backend import, if the stack allows genuinely sharing code), and have the frontend's own UI-level checks (hiding a button, disabling a form) simply query or reflect that same source of truth rather than reimplementing the rules independently in a second, separate place; regardless of how elegantly the frontend mirrors the rules for a good UX, every actual protected operation must still be independently, redundantly re-verified against the real source of truth on the backend for every single request, since frontend checks alone are a UX layer, never a security boundary, as covered in the RBAC and Next.js auth questions.
strong: The single most important structural decision here is making sure permission logic is defined in exactly one authoritative place, not independently duplicated in both the frontend and the backend, since two independently-maintained copies of 'which roles can do what' will inevitably drift out of sync over time as the app evolves, some new permission gets added to the backend's enforcement logic but the frontend's UI-hiding logic never gets updated to match (or vice versa), leading to a confusing, inconsistent experience where a button is shown but the action fails, or a button is hidden even though the user actually has permission to perform that action. Where the tech stack genuinely allows it (a TypeScript monorepo sharing types and even some logic between a Next.js frontend and its backend, for example), defining the actual permission rules and role/permission type definitions in one shared package that both sides import is the cleanest solution, guaranteeing the frontend's UI decisions and the backend's actual enforcement are always looking at the exact same authoritative definition. Where genuinely sharing code isn't practical (a fully separate backend in a different language, for instance), the frontend should still treat the backend as the single source of truth by fetching the current user's actual resolved permissions (not just their role name) once after authentication, and driving all of its UI-level show/hide decisions from that fetched, backend-provided permission set, rather than independently reimplementing the role-to-permission mapping logic itself in frontend code, which is exactly the kind of duplicated logic that drifts out of sync over time. And regardless of how well-synchronized the frontend's UI-level checks are, they remain purely a UX convenience, every single protected server action, API route, and data mutation must still independently and redundantly re-verify the actual authenticated user's real permissions against the real source of truth on every single request, since a determined user can always bypass the frontend's UI entirely and call the underlying protected operation directly.
weak: A weak answer implements the actual permission-checking logic independently, separately, in both the frontend (for UI decisions) and the backend (for real enforcement), without recognizing that these two independently-maintained copies will inevitably drift out of sync as the app's permission model evolves over time.
followUp: If the frontend fetches a user's resolved permission set once right after login and caches it, what real problem could arise if an admin changes that specific user's role or permissions while they're still actively using the app in an existing session?

question: How would you plan and execute a large-scale frontend migration (for example, migrating a large legacy app from a class-component/Redux-heavy codebase to modern hooks-based React with React Query), while the app keeps shipping new features throughout?
concise: Avoid a big-bang rewrite (stopping all new feature work to rewrite everything at once), since that's high-risk, takes a long time before delivering any value, and competes directly with the business's ongoing need to keep shipping; instead migrate incrementally, feature by feature or module by module, keeping old and new patterns coexisting side by side in the same codebase for an extended transition period, prioritizing the migration of whichever specific areas are both actively being touched for other reasons anyway (so the migration cost is naturally amortized into work that's already happening) and/or causing the most real, ongoing pain in their current legacy form.
strong: A full big-bang rewrite, freezing all other feature work to migrate the entire codebase to a new pattern all at once, is tempting because it feels clean and conceptually simple, but it's genuinely high-risk in practice: it takes a long time before delivering any actual user-facing value, it competes directly and continuously with the business's real, ongoing need to keep shipping features and fixing bugs, and it risks introducing an enormous number of new regressions all at once across the entire app, discovered only once the full rewrite is finally complete and tested, rather than being caught and contained incrementally along the way. A much safer, more sustainable approach is incremental migration: old and new patterns are explicitly allowed to coexist in the same codebase for an extended transition period (a legacy class component and a new hooks-based component can absolutely render side by side within the same app, and Redux and React Query can coexist, with server-state responsibilities gradually migrating over to React Query while Redux continues handling whatever genuinely global client state remains, until it's eventually reduced enough to potentially be replaced too), which lets the team ship the migration in small, individually low-risk, individually reviewable and testable increments rather than one enormous, high-risk change. I'd specifically prioritize migrating whichever areas of the codebase are already being actively touched for unrelated feature work or bug fixes anyway, so the migration's actual cost gets naturally amortized into work the team is already doing rather than requiring dedicated, separate migration-only time that's harder to justify and schedule, and I'd also prioritize whichever legacy areas are causing the most real, measurable ongoing pain, frequent bugs, slow development velocity, difficulty onboarding new engineers, since migrating those specific areas first delivers real, tangible value early and helps build momentum and buy-in for continuing the migration, rather than starting with whichever area happens to be architecturally simplest or most convenient to migrate first but delivers comparatively little real benefit.
weak: A weak answer proposes a full big-bang rewrite, pausing all other feature work to migrate the entire codebase to the new pattern all at once, without recognizing the real business risk (a long period with no shipped value, competing directly with ongoing feature work, and a large batch of untested changes landing all at once) that this approach carries compared to a safer, incremental migration strategy.
followUp: How would you specifically decide, at the very start of an incremental migration like this, which particular module or feature to migrate first, given limited team time and an ongoing need to keep shipping other work?

question: Walk me through a complex feature you built, from initial requirements to shipping it in production.
concise: A strong answer covers the actual problem being solved (not just the tech used), the key technical decisions and trade-offs made along the way, at least one genuine complication that came up and how it was resolved, how correctness was verified before and after shipping, and the real, observable outcome, using the situation-task-action-result structure without turning it into a pure feature-list recitation.
strong: I'd start by briefly framing the actual problem, what user or business need the feature addressed, not just diving straight into implementation details, since an interviewer wants to understand judgment and reasoning, not just a list of libraries used. Then I'd walk through the key technical decisions specifically as decisions, meaning naming at least one real alternative that was considered and explaining why the chosen approach won, for example choosing cursor-based pagination over offset-based for a real-time feed once we identified the trade-off around consistency and performance on deep pages. I'd include at least one genuine complication or thing that didn't go as expected, since every real, non-trivial feature has one, and describing how it was diagnosed and resolved (not just that it eventually worked out) is what actually demonstrates real engineering judgment under uncertainty, rather than a rehearsed, frictionless success story. I'd also mention how correctness was verified, what tests were written, whether it was rolled out gradually behind a feature flag, how a specific edge case was caught before or after shipping, and finish with the real, concrete outcome, ideally something at least loosely measurable (adoption, performance improvement, reduced support tickets), while being honest and specific rather than inflating vague, unverifiable claims.
weak: A weak answer lists technologies and features built without ever explaining the actual reasoning behind any specific decision, omits any real complication or setback (making the story feel rehearsed and implausible), and has no concrete, specific outcome to point to.
followUp: What would you do differently if you were building that same feature again today, knowing what you know now?

question: Describe how you handle a production bug that users are actively reporting right now.
