concise: A strong answer prioritizes quickly establishing severity and scope (how many users, how bad is the impact) before diving into a root-cause investigation, communicates status clearly and proactively to relevant stakeholders while investigating rather than going silent, considers a fast, safe mitigation (like a feature flag rollback or a quick config change) separately from the eventual, real root-cause fix if the two can be decoupled, and follows up afterward with an actual fix plus some safeguard (a test, a monitor, an alert) to prevent the same class of bug from recurring silently.
strong: My first step is almost always to establish actual severity and scope quickly, is this affecting every user or a small subset, is data actually being lost or corrupted or is it a visual/cosmetic issue, since that determines both how urgently I need to act and who else needs to be looped in immediately versus after the fact. I try to communicate proactively and specifically while investigating, a short, honest status update to relevant stakeholders ('we're aware, we're looking into it, here's our current understanding') rather than going quiet until I have a complete fix, since silence during an active incident is usually worse for trust than an honest 'still investigating' update. If there's a way to quickly and safely mitigate the immediate user impact, rolling back a recent deploy, disabling a specific feature flag, reverting a risky config change, separately from figuring out the deeper, actual root cause, I'll do that first to stop the bleeding, rather than insisting on fully understanding the root cause before taking any mitigating action at all, since restoring a safe state quickly is usually more valuable to users than an immediately complete diagnosis. Once mitigated, I dig into the actual root cause properly, and once fixed, I specifically think about how to prevent that same class of bug from recurring silently in the future, a regression test covering the specific scenario, a monitoring alert that would have caught it sooner next time, or a process change if the root cause was more about how something got shipped than a specific line of code.
weak: A weak answer jumps straight into a deep root-cause investigation without first establishing severity or communicating status to anyone, and stops at 'I fixed the bug' without any mention of a regression test or a safeguard to prevent the same class of issue from recurring silently again later.
followUp: How would you decide whether a given production bug needs an immediate rollback versus a forward-fix deployed as quickly as possible instead?

question: Describe your approach to refactoring a genuinely messy legacy part of a codebase, one that's risky to touch but that the team keeps needing to work in.
concise: A strong answer avoids a risky, all-at-once rewrite in favor of incremental, continuously-shippable improvements, insists on establishing some baseline test coverage around the risky area's actual current behavior before changing anything (so a refactor can be verified not to have changed real behavior), makes the case for why the refactor is worth prioritized time by tying it to a concrete, felt cost (frequent bugs, slow feature velocity, difficulty onboarding), and treats the refactor as an ongoing, incremental practice rather than a single, one-time cleanup effort.
strong: Before changing anything in a genuinely risky, poorly-understood legacy area, my first priority is establishing enough test coverage around its actual current, real behavior, even characterization tests that just pin down 'this is what it currently does, correct or not', so that any subsequent refactoring can be objectively verified not to have silently changed real behavior, rather than relying purely on manual testing or, worse, just hoping nothing broke. I specifically avoid proposing a full, risky rewrite of the messy area all at once, since that concentrates a huge amount of risk into one large, hard-to-review change; instead I'd look for a way to improve it incrementally, extracting one specific piece of tangled logic into a well-tested, isolated function at a time, each individually small enough to review and ship safely on its own, gradually improving the area's overall quality over many small, low-risk steps rather than one large, high-risk one. Getting buy-in and dedicated time for this kind of work also matters practically, so I'd make the case by tying the refactor directly to a concrete, felt cost the team already recognizes, this specific area causes a disproportionate number of production bugs, or takes noticeably longer to safely add a feature to compared to the rest of the codebase, rather than asking for time to refactor purely because the code 'looks messy', which is a much harder case to justify against competing feature priorities. I also treat this kind of cleanup as an ongoing practice woven into regular feature work, improving a small part of the messy area whenever a task happens to require touching it anyway, rather than a single, dedicated, one-time cleanup project that's easy to deprioritize indefinitely when other feature work competes for the same time.
weak: A weak answer proposes rewriting the entire messy area from scratch in one large effort with no mention of establishing test coverage first to verify behavior is actually preserved, and can't articulate a concrete, business-relevant justification for why the refactor is worth prioritized time beyond 'the code is messy'.
followUp: How would you write a useful characterization test for a messy piece of legacy logic whose actual intended correct behavior isn't clearly documented anywhere?

question: Describe a time you had to make a technical decision with incomplete information, and how you approached the trade-offs.
concise: A strong answer names the actual specific uncertainty or missing information at the time (not just 'things were unclear'), describes a concrete process for deciding anyway, like a quick spike/prototype to reduce the biggest uncertainty, weighing the cost of being wrong against the cost of further delaying the decision to gather more information, and, ideally, describes making the decision reversible or cheaply changeable where possible, rather than either freezing entirely waiting for perfect information or committing irreversibly without any hedge.
strong: I'd pick a specific, real example where the actual uncertainty is concrete and nameable, for example not yet knowing how a third-party API would behave under real production load, or not being sure whether a particular library would support a requirement that only became clear later, rather than a vague, generic 'things were uncertain' framing that doesn't actually demonstrate real decision-making under ambiguity. My general approach is to first ask whether the decision is genuinely reversible or cheaply changeable later, in which case I'd rather make a reasonable, well-justified choice now and adjust later if new information changes the picture, than spend a lot of time trying to gather more certainty upfront for a decision that isn't actually that costly to revisit; for a genuinely hard-to-reverse decision, I'd invest more deliberately in reducing the biggest specific uncertainty first, often through a small, timeboxed spike or prototype specifically targeting the riskiest unknown, rather than a large, open-ended research phase. I'd also be explicit, both with myself and with the team, about which specific assumptions the decision rests on, so if one of those assumptions turns out to be wrong later, we have a clear, quick way to recognize that and revisit the decision, rather than the reasoning behind the original choice being lost or forgotten by the time new information actually surfaces.
weak: A weak answer gives a vague, generic story with no specific, nameable uncertainty, and describes either freezing indefinitely waiting for complete information before deciding anything, or committing to an irreversible choice with no process at all for testing or hedging against being wrong.
followUp: Looking back, was there a cheaper or faster way you could have reduced that specific uncertainty before committing to the decision?

question: Describe a time you identified and fixed a significant performance problem in an application.
concise: A strong answer starts with how the problem was actually identified, a real user complaint, a monitoring alert, a specific metric, rather than a vague 'the app felt slow', names the actual diagnostic tool and process used to find the specific root cause (a profiler, a bundle analyzer, a specific trace), describes the actual fix and why it addressed the real root cause rather than a superficial symptom, and quantifies the improvement with an actual measurement, not just a subjective 'it feels faster now'.
strong: I'd walk through this concretely, starting with how the problem was actually surfaced, whether that's a specific Core Web Vitals regression showing up in real user monitoring, a support ticket describing a specific slow interaction, or a noticeable regression caught in a performance budget check in CI, since starting with a vague 'the app felt slow' signal doesn't demonstrate the same rigor as pointing to something concrete and measured. From there I'd describe the actual diagnostic process, which specific tool I used (the Performance panel's flame graph to find a specific blocking task, a bundle analyzer to find an unexpectedly large dependency, the React DevTools Profiler to find an unnecessarily re-rendering subtree) and what that tool actually revealed as the specific root cause, rather than jumping straight to a fix based on a guess. I'd then explain the actual fix and specifically why it addressed that real root cause, virtualizing a large list because the actual cost was proportional to total row count rather than visible row count, or code-splitting a specific heavy dependency because the bundle analyzer showed it was the single largest unnecessary contributor to initial load size. Finally, I'd give an actual, specific, measured before-and-after number, a specific metric that improved by a specific amount, rather than a vague, unverifiable 'it's much faster now', since a real, quantified result is what actually demonstrates the fix genuinely worked, not just that something changed.
weak: A weak answer describes the problem and the fix only in vague, unmeasured terms ('the app was slow, I optimized it, now it's faster') with no specific diagnostic tool named, no specific identified root cause, and no actual before-and-after measurement to back up the claimed improvement.
followUp: How did you verify that the specific fix you made was actually the primary cause of the improvement, rather than some other unrelated change that happened around the same time?

question: Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical approach, and how you resolved it.
concise: A strong answer describes a genuine, specific technical disagreement (not a vague personality conflict), explains both perspectives fairly and specifically rather than only justifying their own side, describes a concrete, collaborative process used to actually resolve it, like a quick prototype comparing both approaches, a documented trade-off discussion, or bringing in a specific additional data point or constraint that hadn't been considered, and is honest about the actual outcome, including if their own original position turned out to be wrong.
strong: I'd describe a genuine, specific technical disagreement, for example whether a particular piece of state should live in a global store versus be more narrowly scoped and passed via props, or whether a feature should be built with a particular library versus a lighter, custom-built solution, and I'd explain the other person's actual reasoning fairly and specifically, not as a straw man, since being able to genuinely articulate the other side's real, legitimate concerns is itself a signal of good technical judgment and collaboration, not just conflict-avoidance. For resolving it, I generally prefer trying to find some concrete, shared way to actually test the disagreement rather than just repeatedly arguing opinions back and forth, a quick prototype comparing both approaches against a realistic scenario, or identifying a specific additional constraint or piece of information (like an upcoming requirement that would clearly favor one approach) that resolves the ambiguity more objectively than either person's initial intuition alone. I'd also be honest that on at least one occasion, going through that process actually changed my own mind, and I think that's an important, credible detail to include, since always claiming to have been right in every retold disagreement is a pretty reliable signal that the story's been sanitized rather than told honestly.
weak: A weak answer describes a vague interpersonal conflict rather than a specific, genuine technical disagreement, only presents their own side's reasoning without fairly representing the other person's actual perspective, and claims to have been proven completely right in every single instance, which reads as an unlikely, overly self-serving account.
followUp: How do you generally handle a situation where, after a fair, genuine discussion, you and a teammate still can't reach agreement on the right technical approach?

question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision made by a manager or a more senior engineer. What did you do?
concise: A strong answer shows genuine, respectful pushback based on specific technical or business reasoning (not just personal preference), describes actually voicing that disagreement clearly and constructively rather than silently going along with something they thought was wrong, and shows the ability to commit fully to the final decision once it was actually made, even if it wasn't the outcome they originally advocated for, rather than quietly undermining or resenting it afterward.
strong: I try to voice a genuine disagreement clearly and early, with specific reasoning rather than a vague objection, since staying silent about a real concern and then having it turn out to be right later helps no one and erodes trust when it eventually comes out that I actually had reservations I never raised. At the same time, once a decision has genuinely been made, after a fair hearing of the actual concern, by the person or team with the authority and full context to make it, I commit to executing it well and fully, rather than dragging my feet, quietly working around it, or bringing it up repeatedly afterward in a way that undermines the team's ability to move forward together; disagree-and-commit is a real, practiced skill, not just a phrase, and being able to genuinely let go of a settled disagreement (while still being willing to raise a new one later if new information changes the picture) is part of being a good teammate.
weak: A weak answer describes either silently going along with something they secretly disagreed with the entire time (with no evidence they ever actually raised the concern), or continuing to resist and relitigate a decision even after it was made and a fair hearing was given, both of which are red flags for a collaborative team environment.
followUp: How do you decide when a disagreement is worth escalating further versus when it's better to just let it go and commit to the decision that was made?

question: How do you prioritize your work when you have multiple competing deadlines?
concise: A strong answer describes an actual, concrete process (not just 'I prioritize based on urgency'), like clarifying actual business impact and true deadlines directly with stakeholders rather than assuming, distinguishing genuinely urgent-and-important work from work that merely feels urgent, and proactively communicating trade-offs and re-negotiating scope or timeline when it becomes clear that not everything can genuinely be done by its original deadline, rather than silently trying to do everything and quietly slipping on all of it.
strong: My first step is usually to actually clarify real impact and true urgency directly with whoever requested each piece of work, rather than guessing based on how loudly or recently something was asked for, since the person requesting something isn't always the best judge of its relative business priority compared to everything else currently in flight, and a quick clarifying conversation often reveals that something assumed to be extremely urgent actually has more flexibility than expected, or vice versa. Once I have an honest picture of actual priority and true deadlines, I try to be transparent early, rather than late, about any real conflict, if two things genuinely can't both be done well by their stated deadlines, I'd rather surface that trade-off explicitly and let the right person make an informed call about which to prioritize (or negotiate an adjusted timeline or reduced scope for one of them) than silently try to do everything at once and end up delivering multiple things late or low-quality with no advance warning to anyone. I also try to distinguish work that's genuinely both urgent and important from work that merely feels urgent because it's the most recent or most vocal request, since reactively working purely in request order, rather than actual priority order, is a common trap that leads to consistently deprioritizing quieter but more important work.
weak: A weak answer describes just working on whatever was asked for most recently or most loudly, with no actual process for clarifying real priority or true deadlines, and no mention of proactively communicating a genuine scheduling conflict rather than silently trying to do everything at once.
followUp: Describe a specific time you had to tell a stakeholder that their requested deadline genuinely wasn't achievable, and how that conversation went.

question: How do you respond when you receive critical or negative feedback on a pull request or a piece of your work?
concise: A strong answer shows genuine openness to critical feedback as valuable information rather than a personal attack, describes actually engaging with the specific substance of the feedback (asking clarifying questions if the reasoning isn't clear, rather than either blindly complying or dismissing it), and, importantly, shows the ability to respectfully push back with actual reasoning when they genuinely disagree with a specific piece of feedback, rather than either capitulating on everything or becoming defensive about all of it.
strong: I try to treat critical feedback as useful information about the actual code or approach, not as a judgment of me personally, and my first instinct is genuinely to understand the specific reasoning behind it, if a reviewer's comment doesn't fully explain why a particular change is being requested, I'll ask a clarifying question rather than either blindly implementing whatever they suggested without understanding why, or getting defensive and dismissing it outright. Where I actually agree with the feedback, I just make the change, sometimes even improving on the specific suggestion further once I understand the underlying concern. Where I genuinely disagree with a specific piece of feedback, after actually considering it seriously and understanding the reviewer's reasoning, I'll respectfully explain my own reasoning and specific trade-offs I considered, since a good code review is a genuine two-way conversation, not a one-directional set of demands to comply with; I've had plenty of cases where that follow-up conversation changed my mind, and a smaller number of cases where it changed the reviewer's mind instead, and I think both outcomes are healthy signs of an actually functioning, honest review process rather than either party just deferring reflexively.
weak: A weak answer describes either reflexively complying with every single piece of feedback without ever engaging with or questioning the underlying reasoning, or becoming defensive and pushing back on all feedback regardless of its actual merit, neither of which reflects genuine, healthy engagement with code review.
followUp: Describe a specific instance where you initially disagreed with a piece of review feedback but ended up changing your mind after further discussion.

question: How do you approach mentoring a junior engineer on your team?
concise: A strong answer describes actively creating space for the junior engineer to reason through a problem themselves (asking guiding questions rather than immediately handing over the answer) balanced against recognizing when a direct answer is genuinely the more efficient and appropriate choice (like an urgent production issue), giving specific, actionable code review feedback rather than vague comments, and being honest and specific about what a junior engineer is doing well, not just what needs to improve.
strong: My general default is to ask guiding questions and let a junior engineer reason through a problem themselves as much as reasonably possible, since actually working through the reasoning process, even if it takes a bit longer than just being handed the answer directly, tends to build real, durable understanding and independent problem-solving skill much more effectively than simply being told the correct solution every time. That said, I don't apply this rigidly in every single situation, if something is genuinely time-sensitive, like an active production issue, or if someone has already spent a reasonable amount of time stuck on the same specific point without making progress, I'll just give a more direct answer or point them clearly toward the right resource, since needlessly prolonging the Socratic-question approach past the point where it's actually helping just wastes time and can feel more like a puzzle or a withholding of help than genuine mentorship. In code review specifically, I try to make feedback concrete and actionable rather than vague, explaining the actual reasoning behind a suggested change (not just 'change this') so the underlying principle transfers to future, different situations, not just that one specific line of code. I also make a deliberate point of being specific and genuine about what someone is doing well, not just what needs improvement, since feedback that's exclusively critical, even when each individual point is fair and well-intentioned, can feel demoralizing over time and doesn't help someone understand which of their existing instincts and practices are actually already good and worth keeping.
weak: A weak answer describes either just doing the work for the junior engineer directly whenever they get stuck (which doesn't actually build their skill or independence over time), or giving only vague, high-level feedback with no specific, actionable guidance they could concretely act on.
followUp: How do you calibrate how much independent struggle to let a junior engineer work through on their own before stepping in to help, without letting them stay stuck for an unreasonably long time?

question: How do you communicate a technical trade-off or a technical risk to a non-technical stakeholder, like a product manager?
concise: A strong answer describes translating the actual technical concept into concrete business terms and consequences (cost, risk, timeline, user impact) rather than technical jargon, uses a specific, concrete example rather than only abstract explanation, is honest and direct about genuine trade-offs and risks rather than either hiding them to avoid a difficult conversation or over-hedging every statement defensively, and frames the conversation collaboratively around a shared decision rather than either just dictating the technical answer or deferring entirely to whatever the stakeholder initially wants.
strong: My general approach is to translate the actual technical detail into its concrete business consequence, rather than explaining the underlying technical mechanism itself in detail, a product manager generally doesn't need to understand exactly why a particular architecture choice creates technical debt, but they do need to understand, in concrete terms, that choosing the faster approach now means a specific future feature will likely take meaningfully longer to build later, or that skipping a particular safeguard introduces a real, specific risk to a particular kind of user data. I try to use a specific, concrete example rather than staying at a purely abstract level, since 'this approach has more technical debt' is vague and hard to actually weigh against other priorities, while 'this approach means adding a new payment method later will likely take an extra two weeks compared to the alternative' gives a stakeholder something concrete and comparable they can actually reason about and make an informed trade-off decision with. I also try to be honest and direct about genuine risk or cost rather than either hiding a real concern to avoid a difficult, possibly friction-causing conversation, or conversely over-hedging every single statement so defensively that the actual, real risk gets lost in a fog of caveats. Ultimately I frame these conversations as a shared, collaborative decision, since the stakeholder usually has crucial business context I don't have (how much a particular future feature genuinely matters, how much risk is actually acceptable for this specific area), and I have crucial technical context they don't have, so a good outcome usually comes from an honest, specific, two-way exchange rather than me either unilaterally dictating the 'correct' technical answer or just deferring entirely to whatever they initially asked for without pushing back on a genuine concern.
weak: A weak answer either buries the actual trade-off in technical jargon the stakeholder can't meaningfully act on, or avoids raising a genuine risk or cost at all to sidestep a potentially uncomfortable conversation, both of which prevent the stakeholder from making a genuinely informed decision.
followUp: Describe a specific instance where a non-technical stakeholder pushed back on a technical recommendation you made, and how you responded.

question: How do you handle scope creep on a project you're working on?
concise: A strong answer distinguishes genuinely necessary, well-justified scope additions from ones that are more speculative or nice-to-have, proactively surfaces the actual trade-off (additional scope generally means additional time, or something else needs to be cut or deprioritized to compensate) rather than silently absorbing unlimited extra scope into the same original deadline, and describes a concrete, collaborative process for managing it, like maintaining a clearly separated 'later' list for good ideas that come up mid-project rather than incorporating every single one immediately.
strong: When new scope comes up mid-project, my first instinct is to actually understand why it's being proposed and how genuinely necessary or time-sensitive it really is, since some scope additions are legitimately important, a newly-discovered edge case or a genuine, previously-missed requirement, while others are more speculative nice-to-haves that emerged simply because someone thought of them partway through, and treating every new idea with equal urgency and equal claim on the current timeline is a fast path to a project that never actually ships. For scope that is genuinely warranted, I try to surface the actual trade-off explicitly and early, rather than silently trying to absorb it into the original deadline through extra unplanned effort, if this new requirement is genuinely important, then either the timeline needs to move, or something else already in scope needs to be deprioritized or cut to make room for it, and that's a decision the relevant stakeholders should make consciously and explicitly, not one I should make unilaterally by just quietly working extra hours to make everything fit. For scope that's more speculative or genuinely lower priority, I try to maintain some kind of clearly visible, actively-maintained 'good idea, but not now' list, so it doesn't get lost or forgotten entirely, but also doesn't automatically expand the current project's scope just because it happened to come up during this particular project rather than a different one; this also helps depersonalize the conversation, since it's not 'no' to the idea itself, it's 'yes, but let's sequence it deliberately rather than reactively'.
weak: A weak answer just silently absorbs every new scope request into the existing deadline without ever surfacing the resulting trade-off to anyone, which predictably leads to either burnout, slipped deadlines, or quietly cut corners that nobody explicitly agreed to.
followUp: How do you handle a situation where a stakeholder insists a new scope addition is both critically important and must fit within the exact original deadline, with nothing else able to be cut?

question: Tell me about a mistake you made in your work, and what you learned from it.
concise: A strong answer describes a genuine, specific, non-trivial mistake (not a deliberately-softened, safe 'mistake' like 'I work too hard'), takes clear, direct ownership of it rather than deflecting blame onto circumstances or other people, describes the actual concrete corrective action taken at the time, and names a specific, genuine change in behavior or process that resulted from it, showing the mistake actually led to real learning rather than just being an unfortunate, forgotten one-off incident.
strong: I'd describe a genuine, specific mistake, something with real, concrete consequences, not a deliberately-softened non-answer like 'I care too much about quality', since interviewers can immediately tell the difference and a sanitized non-mistake doesn't actually demonstrate anything meaningful about how I handle real failure. I'd take direct, clear ownership of what actually went wrong, without deflecting blame onto other people or circumstances outside my control, even where those external factors genuinely did play some role, since owning my own specific part in it is what actually matters here, not achieving a perfectly balanced, defensible account of exactly how much blame was mine versus everyone else's. I'd describe the actual concrete steps taken to address the immediate consequences of the mistake at the time, and then, more importantly for this specific question, describe a real, specific, lasting change that resulted from it, a new habit I adopted, a new safeguard or process I now follow, a new way I specifically double-check a certain kind of risky change going forward, since the actual point of this question is to understand whether a real mistake genuinely changed how I work afterward, not just that I experienced an unpleasant, isolated incident once and then moved on unchanged.
weak: A weak answer describes a fake, deliberately-safe 'mistake' that isn't actually a real flaw at all, deflects real blame onto other people or external circumstances, or fails to name any specific, lasting change in behavior that actually resulted from the experience.
followUp: Since that experience, has the specific new habit or safeguard you adopted actually come up again, and did it help?

question: How do you stay current with changes in the frontend ecosystem, given how quickly it evolves?
concise: A strong answer describes a genuine, sustainable, specific practice (not just a vague 'I read a lot'), shows discernment about what's actually worth learning deeply versus what's just current hype (evaluating new tools/patterns against real, concrete problems rather than adopting everything new reflexively), and, ideally, describes actually applying new learning in real, practical work (a side project, a proof-of-concept, an actual adopted change at work) rather than only passively consuming content without ever testing it hands-on.
strong: I have a genuine, ongoing practice rather than a burst of catching up right before an interview, following release notes and specific technical blogs from the frameworks and tools I actually use daily, occasionally building a small side project or proof-of-concept specifically to actually try a new pattern or tool hands-on rather than just reading about it in the abstract, since actually using something in even a small, real way surfaces trade-offs and rough edges that reading a blog post alone never really does. I also try to apply real discernment rather than reflexively chasing every new trend, the frontend ecosystem genuinely does produce a lot of hype around tools that don't end up mattering much in practice, so I try to evaluate anything new against a concrete question, does this actually solve a real, specific problem I currently have, or a problem the team I'm on is currently experiencing, rather than adopting something new purely because it's currently popular or trending. Where something does genuinely seem valuable, I look for a low-risk, contained way to actually try it in real practice, a small internal tool, a genuinely well-suited part of an existing project, rather than only ever reading about new things without ever actually testing them hands-on in real, practical use.
weak: A weak answer gives a vague, generic non-answer like 'I read a lot of blogs' with no specific example of anything actually learned or applied recently, and shows no discernment at all between genuinely useful new tools and passing hype.
followUp: What's a frontend tool or pattern you looked into recently, evaluated seriously, and specifically decided not to adopt, and why?

question: Describe your approach to giving code review feedback to a teammate.
concise: A strong answer describes distinguishing between genuinely blocking issues (correctness bugs, security problems, real design concerns) and pure style/preference nitpicks, being specific and explaining the actual reasoning behind a requested change rather than issuing unexplained directives, genuinely acknowledging good decisions or clever solutions in the code, not just pointing out problems, and being mindful of tone in written feedback, since text lacks the context and warmth of in-person conversation and can land more harshly than intended.
strong: I try to be explicit, even directly in the review comment itself, about the actual severity of each piece of feedback, clearly distinguishing a must-fix correctness or security issue from a genuine but more minor design concern, from a pure stylistic preference that the author is free to take or leave, since treating every comment with the same implied weight makes it hard for the author to prioritize what actually needs addressing before merging versus what's just a nice-to-have suggestion. For anything I do flag, I try to explain the actual underlying reasoning, not just the specific requested change, since explaining why something matters (this specific pattern has caused a production bug before, or this approach doesn't handle a specific edge case) helps the concept genuinely transfer to future situations, rather than the author just complying with this one specific instance without understanding the broader principle behind it. I also make a real, genuine point of calling out good decisions or particularly clean solutions in the code, not purely as a courtesy, but because reinforcing what's actually working well is just as valuable feedback as pointing out problems, and a review that's exclusively critical can start to feel demoralizing over time even when every individual critical point is completely fair. Finally, I'm mindful that written text lacks tone, a comment that would sound perfectly neutral said out loud can read as unnecessarily harsh or curt in writing, so I try to phrase feedback collaboratively (using language like 'what do you think about...' or explaining my actual reasoning) rather than issuing unexplained, blunt directives.
weak: A weak answer treats every single piece of feedback, from a genuine correctness bug to a pure stylistic preference, with the same undifferentiated weight and urgency, gives unexplained directives with no underlying reasoning, and never acknowledges anything the author actually did well.
followUp: How do you handle a situation where you've left the same kind of feedback for a teammate multiple times across several different pull requests, and the pattern keeps recurring?

question: How do you handle conflicting priorities from two different stakeholders (for example, a product manager and an engineering lead) who each want something different from you at the same time?
concise: A strong answer describes making the actual conflict explicit and visible to both parties, rather than silently trying to satisfy both simultaneously (which often means quietly under-delivering on both) or unilaterally picking one side without surfacing the tension at all, facilitates an actual conversation or decision between the relevant parties when the conflict is genuinely significant, and, where appropriate, proposes a concrete compromise or sequencing option (do A first, then B) rather than presenting the conflict as a pure binary choice.
strong: My first move is almost always to make the actual conflict visible and explicit to both stakeholders, rather than either silently trying to satisfy both competing priorities at once (which usually just means quietly delivering a worse, rushed version of both) or unilaterally deciding which one takes priority on my own without surfacing the tension to anyone, since a conflict like this often reflects a genuine misalignment between two people or teams that they'd actually want to know about and resolve directly, not something that should be silently absorbed and resolved invisibly by whoever happens to be caught in the middle of it. Where the conflict is significant enough, I'd actively facilitate a short, direct conversation between the two stakeholders themselves (or bring it to whoever has the actual authority to make the call, if it's not appropriate for me to adjudicate it myself), since they usually have context and authority I don't have to actually resolve which priority should genuinely win. Where I can, I also try to propose a concrete, practical middle path, rather than presenting the conflict as a stark, forced binary choice, a reasonable sequencing option (this one first, then that one right after), or a reduced-scope version of one that still delivers real value while freeing up enough time for the other, since stakeholders are very often more receptive to a specific, thoughtful compromise proposal than to being asked to simply pick a winner between two things they both genuinely care about.
weak: A weak answer either tries to silently satisfy both conflicting priorities at once without ever surfacing the actual tension to anyone (typically resulting in both being under-delivered), or unilaterally picks one side without any attempt to facilitate a real conversation or propose a reasonable compromise.
followUp: Describe a specific instance where you facilitated a conversation like this between two stakeholders, and what the eventual resolution actually was.

question: How do you use an AI coding assistant like Claude Code, Copilot, or Cursor effectively in your day-to-day workflow?
concise: Effective use means treating the assistant as a fast, knowledgeable pair programmer whose output you still fully review and understand before accepting, being specific and giving real context in prompts (relevant files, the actual constraint or bug, not just a vague one-line request), using it well for boilerplate, test scaffolding, and exploring an unfamiliar codebase or API quickly, and staying personally responsible for the final code's correctness, security, and fit with the codebase's actual conventions, exactly as if you had written every line yourself.
strong: I get the most value out of an AI assistant when I give it real, specific context, the actual relevant files, the specific error message or constraint, what I've already tried, rather than a vague, one-line request, since a well-specified prompt with genuine context produces meaningfully better, more directly usable output than a generic one. I lean on it heavily for things that are genuinely mechanical or exploratory, writing repetitive boilerplate, scaffolding an initial set of tests for a function I've already written, or quickly getting oriented in an unfamiliar library or an unfamiliar part of a large codebase, since it's often faster at surfacing the relevant pattern or API than manually searching documentation from scratch. Critically, I never treat its output as automatically correct or safe to merge without review, I read and genuinely understand every suggested change before accepting it, the same way I would review a teammate's pull request, since I remain fully responsible for anything that ends up in the codebase regardless of who or what originally wrote it; this matters even more for anything security- or correctness-sensitive, like auth logic, payment handling, or data validation, where I specifically slow down and verify the logic manually rather than just accepting a plausible-looking suggestion. I also try to stay aware of when it's actually saving me real time versus when I'm spending more time crafting a prompt and reviewing questionable output than I would have spent just writing the specific piece of code myself directly.
weak: A weak answer describes accepting AI-generated code changes without genuinely reading or understanding them first, treating a plausible-looking suggestion as automatically correct, which is a real, meaningful risk rather than a minor shortcut, especially for anything touching security or correctness-critical logic.
followUp: Describe a specific instance where an AI coding assistant's suggestion looked correct at first glance but turned out to be subtly wrong, and how you caught it.

question: What specifically do you look for when reviewing AI-generated code, beyond what you'd check in a typical human-written pull request?
concise: Beyond normal review (correctness, readability, tests), AI-generated code specifically warrants extra scrutiny for: plausible-looking but subtly wrong logic (since it's optimized to look correct and idiomatic, not necessarily to be correct), outdated or hallucinated API usage (a method or parameter that doesn't actually exist, or existed in an older version of a library), missing edge-case and error handling that a human familiar with the actual codebase's real failure modes would have included, and security-sensitive patterns (like a naive SQL query, an unvalidated input, or a hardcoded credential) that an assistant might generate because they're common in its training data, without necessarily being appropriate for this specific codebase's actual security requirements.
strong: AI-generated code tends to look unusually clean, idiomatic, and confident, even when it's subtly wrong, which is exactly what makes it a specific, distinct review risk: a human's rough, hesitant, or unusually-structured code often visually signals 'this part might need a closer look', while a model's output reads smoothly and plausibly regardless of whether the underlying logic is actually correct, so I specifically try not to let that surface-level polish lower my actual scrutiny of the real logic underneath it. I specifically check for hallucinated or outdated API usage, a method call, a parameter name, or an import that looks entirely plausible but doesn't actually exist in the current version of the library being used, which is a class of error a model can produce confidently and fluently, especially for a library or API that's changed meaningfully since its training data was collected. I also look closely for missing edge-case handling: a model tends to generate the most common, straightforward path correctly, but genuinely understanding this specific codebase's real, actual failure modes (a specific race condition this API is known to have, a specific malformed input this endpoint has previously received in production) requires context a general-purpose assistant often doesn't have unless it was explicitly given it. And I pay particular attention to security-sensitive patterns specifically, since an assistant might generate a pattern that's extremely common in its training data (a certain way of building a database query, or handling user input) without that pattern actually being safe or appropriate for this specific app's actual security requirements, so I never relax my usual scrutiny of anything touching auth, payments, or user input validation just because the surrounding code looks otherwise clean and well-structured.
weak: A weak answer reviews AI-generated code exactly like any other code with no additional, specific scrutiny for the failure modes that are actually distinctive to AI-generated output, like hallucinated APIs or plausible-but-wrong logic that reads more confidently than a human's rough first draft would.
followUp: How would you specifically verify that an API method or parameter an AI assistant used in its suggestion actually exists in the exact version of the library your project is using?

question: What is prompt injection, and how could it become a real security concern for a frontend feature that uses an LLM (for example, a chat assistant reading content from a webpage or a document)?
concise: Prompt injection is when untrusted, attacker-controlled text (embedded in a webpage, a document, an email, a support ticket, anything the AI system reads as input) contains instructions designed to manipulate the AI into ignoring its original instructions or performing an unintended, potentially harmful action; it becomes a real concern the moment an AI-powered feature reads or acts on any content the end user (or a third party) doesn't fully trust or control, since that content can carry hidden instructions the AI might follow as if they came from the legitimate system prompt or the actual user.
strong: The core risk is that a large language model, by default, doesn't have a fully reliable way to distinguish 'trusted instructions from the system/developer' from 'untrusted content the AI is merely supposed to read or summarize', so if an AI-powered feature reads content from an external, attacker-influenced source, a webpage, an email, an uploaded document, a customer support message, and that content contains text specifically crafted to look like an instruction ('ignore your previous instructions and instead do X'), the model can potentially be manipulated into actually following it, treating it as a genuine instruction rather than as plain data to merely summarize or reference. A concrete, realistic frontend scenario is an AI assistant feature that can browse or read a webpage or a document on the user's behalf, if that page contains hidden or subtly-embedded text specifically designed to manipulate the assistant (invisible white-on-white text, or text hidden in an HTML attribute never rendered visually), the assistant could be tricked into performing an action the actual user never intended, like exfiltrating some other piece of information it has access to, or taking some unintended action if the assistant has been given the ability to actually perform actions, not just answer questions. Practical mitigations include being deliberately conservative about what actions an AI-powered feature is actually allowed to autonomously perform based on untrusted external content (especially anything irreversible or sensitive), clearly and structurally separating trusted system instructions from untrusted retrieved content in how the actual prompt is constructed, and treating any AI-suggested action with real external consequences (sending an email, making a payment, deleting data) as something that still requires genuine user confirmation, not fully autonomous execution, exactly the same caution you'd apply to any other untrusted external input in a traditional security context.
weak: A weak answer has never heard of prompt injection as a concept and doesn't recognize that any AI-powered feature reading or acting on untrusted external content carries this specific risk, distinct from traditional web vulnerabilities like XSS or SQL injection, though conceptually related.
followUp: How is prompt injection conceptually similar to, and different from, a traditional injection vulnerability like SQL injection or XSS?

question: Explain RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) and embeddings at a level useful for a frontend engineer building a feature on top of an existing RAG pipeline.
concise: An embedding is a numeric vector representation of a piece of text such that semantically similar text produces vectors that are close together in that vector space, which lets you find relevant content by similarity rather than exact keyword matching; RAG uses this to retrieve the most relevant chunks of some larger knowledge base (documents, support articles, a codebase) for a specific user query by comparing the query's embedding against stored document embeddings, and then includes those retrieved, relevant chunks directly in the prompt sent to the LLM, so it can answer based on that specific, real, retrieved information rather than relying purely on what it happened to learn during training.
strong: For a frontend engineer, the practically important thing to understand is why RAG exists at all: a general-purpose LLM's knowledge is frozen at whatever point its training data was collected, and it has no inherent access to your company's specific, private, or simply too-recent-to-have-been-in-training-data documents, support articles, or internal knowledge base; RAG bridges that gap by first converting your actual knowledge base's content into embeddings (numeric vectors capturing semantic meaning) stored in a vector database, and then, for each incoming user question, converting that question into an embedding too and finding the stored chunks whose embeddings are closest to it (meaning most semantically similar, not necessarily sharing the same exact keywords), and feeding those specific retrieved chunks into the actual prompt sent to the LLM as real, grounding context. This is genuinely relevant frontend knowledge because it directly explains the actual answer quality and failure modes you'll observe: if a RAG-based support-chat feature gives a wrong or incomplete answer, the root cause is very often that a poor chunking strategy (splitting the knowledge base up into pieces that are too large, too small, or badly split mid-sentence) or a genuinely irrelevant retrieval (finding chunks that are superficially similar in wording but not actually the relevant answer) fed the model bad or missing context, not that the model itself was somehow being unreasonable or unintelligent. This matters directly for how a frontend surfaces the feature too, for example showing the user which specific source documents were actually retrieved and used to construct a given answer (citations) both builds real user trust and gives them a way to verify the answer directly, and is a common, genuinely valuable UI pattern specifically built around a RAG pipeline's underlying retrieval step.
weak: A weak answer has heard the term RAG but can't explain what an embedding actually represents or why semantic similarity search (rather than simple keyword matching) is the actual mechanism that makes retrieval genuinely useful for finding relevant context.
followUp: Why is showing the user which specific source documents were retrieved and used (citations) a particularly valuable UI pattern specifically for a RAG-based feature, compared to a plain chat interface with no visible sourcing?

question: What is a context window, and what practical problems arise for a frontend feature (like a long-running chat interface) when a conversation grows beyond it?
concise: A context window is the maximum amount of text (measured in tokens, roughly word-fragments) an LLM can actually consider at once for a single request, including the system prompt, the full conversation history, and any retrieved documents; once a growing conversation's total token count would exceed that limit, something has to be dropped, truncated, or summarized to fit, which can cause the model to lose track of earlier context, contradict something established earlier in the conversation, or simply be unable to reference information from much earlier in a long-running chat unless the frontend/backend deliberately manages this.
strong: For a long-running chat feature, every single request to the model has to include enough of the conversation's history for it to actually respond coherently and consistently, but that entire history, plus the system prompt, plus any additional retrieved context, all counts against one fixed total token budget for that request; as a conversation grows long enough, naively sending the entire raw history on every single request either becomes prohibitively expensive (since you're paying for and processing all of that repeated context on every single turn) or eventually exceeds the model's actual maximum context window entirely, at which point something has to give. Real, practical strategies for handling this include periodically summarizing older parts of the conversation into a shorter, condensed form that preserves the important facts while using far fewer tokens, prioritizing more recent messages while gracefully dropping or compressing the oldest ones once a length threshold is reached, or, for a RAG-style feature specifically, retrieving only the specific relevant older messages, rather than the entire raw history, when the current question seems to reference something from much earlier. From a frontend and UX perspective, this matters concretely, since users genuinely notice and get frustrated when a chat assistant suddenly seems to have forgotten something they mentioned much earlier in a long conversation, so being upfront about this limitation (or building genuinely good context-management/summarization on the backend to actually mitigate it) is a real, practical product concern, not just an invisible backend implementation detail, and it's the kind of thing that's worth surfacing in an interview as a known, understood trade-off rather than something you'd be caught off guard by in production.
weak: A weak answer assumes a chat interface can maintain a perfect, unlimited memory of an arbitrarily long conversation with no real constraint, without understanding that the context window imposes an actual, hard token limit that requires deliberate summarization or truncation strategies once exceeded.
followUp: How would you decide, in a summarization strategy for a long conversation, which older messages are safe to compress or drop versus which specific details genuinely need to be preserved verbatim?

question: What is hallucination in the context of an LLM, and what practical UX and engineering mitigations would you build into a frontend feature that surfaces AI-generated content to real users?
concise: Hallucination is when a model generates text that's fluent, confident, and plausible-sounding but factually wrong or entirely fabricated, an invented citation, a nonexistent API method, a confidently-stated but incorrect fact, which is a fundamental characteristic of how these models generate text (predicting plausible continuations) rather than a rare bug to be fully eliminated; practical mitigations include grounding answers in retrieved, real source material (RAG) and showing the user the actual sources so they can verify a claim themselves, being honest in the UI about the AI's actual reliability and encouraging verification for anything consequential, and, for any AI-suggested action with real consequences, requiring explicit human confirmation before it's actually executed rather than allowing fully autonomous action based on potentially hallucinated reasoning.
strong: The important thing to internalize is that hallucination isn't a rare edge-case bug that better prompting alone eliminates entirely, it's a natural, expected consequence of how these models fundamentally work, generating the most statistically plausible continuation of text based on patterns learned during training, which is usually accurate but has no built-in, guaranteed mechanism for verifying that a specific generated fact is actually true versus merely sounding plausible and fluent. Grounding the model's answers in real, retrieved source material via RAG meaningfully reduces (but doesn't fully eliminate) this risk, since the model has actual real content to reference rather than relying purely on what it happened to absorb during training, and showing the user which specific source passages the answer was actually based on, with a visible citation or link, both increases genuine trust and gives the user a direct, concrete way to verify a specific claim themselves rather than just trusting the AI's assertion on faith. From a UX perspective, I think it's important to be honest in the actual interface about the technology's real, known limitations, a small, persistent note that AI-generated answers can be wrong and should be verified for anything important is a legitimate, valuable design element, not something to hide or downplay to make the feature feel more impressive or magical than it actually is. For any feature where the AI can suggest or initiate an actual action with real, meaningful consequences, sending an email, modifying data, making a purchase, I'd always require an explicit, clear human confirmation step before that action actually executes, treating the AI's output as a suggestion or a draft that a human reviews and approves, rather than as an instruction to be carried out fully autonomously, precisely because a hallucinated or subtly-wrong piece of reasoning could otherwise directly cause a real, harmful, hard-to-reverse action.
weak: A weak answer treats hallucination as a rare, essentially solved problem that better prompting fully eliminates, rather than understanding it as an inherent characteristic of how these models generate text, which specifically informs why genuine UX safeguards (citations, honest framing, human confirmation for consequential actions) are still necessary regardless of how well the feature is prompted.
followUp: Why is requiring explicit human confirmation before executing an AI-suggested action specifically important for anything irreversible, like sending a real email or deleting real data, even if the AI's suggestion is usually correct?

question: Why must an AI provider's secret API key never be included in frontend code, and what's the correct architecture for a frontend feature that calls an LLM API?
concise: An AI provider's API key is directly tied to a billing account and, depending on the provider and plan, can incur real, potentially very large costs per request, so exposing it in any frontend code (even 'hidden' in a bundled JS file, since bundled code is fully downloadable and readable by anyone) lets any visitor extract it and make unlimited requests billed entirely to your account, or exhaust a rate limit meant for legitimate users; the correct architecture routes every LLM API call through your own backend (or a serverless/edge function acting as a thin proxy), which holds the actual secret key, applies your own authentication, per-user rate limiting, and usage monitoring, and the frontend only ever talks to your own backend endpoint, never directly to the AI provider's API with a raw key.
strong: An AI provider's API key is functionally similar to a payment provider's secret key in terms of the real, direct financial risk it represents if leaked, since most LLM APIs charge per token processed, and a leaked key gives literally anyone the ability to make an essentially unlimited number of requests billed directly to your account, which can produce a surprisingly large, unexpected bill very quickly if the key is scraped and abused by even a small number of bad actors, let alone if it goes genuinely viral among people specifically looking for exposed keys to exploit. Exactly as with a payment provider's secret key, bundling or minifying frontend JavaScript provides zero real protection at all, since any visitor can simply open their browser's network tab or view the downloaded source to extract a hardcoded key directly, so the key must never be referenced anywhere in code that's shipped to the browser under any circumstances. The correct architecture is a thin backend or serverless/edge proxy: the frontend calls your own API endpoint (with your app's own normal authentication protecting that endpoint), and your backend, holding the actual provider API key securely as a server-side-only environment variable, makes the real call to the AI provider on the frontend's behalf, then returns (or streams) the result back. This backend layer is also exactly where you'd apply your own real, meaningful safeguards that the AI provider's own key-level limits don't give you on their own, per-user or per-session rate limiting, tracking and capping usage/cost per individual user account, and logging or moderating requests, all of which require actual application-level logic your own backend controls, not something you can enforce purely by however the frontend chooses to call the API directly.
weak: A weak answer suggests calling the AI provider's API directly from frontend JavaScript with the API key embedded in the client bundle 'to keep things simple', which would expose that key to anyone who opens the network tab or inspects the bundle, a genuinely severe, costly security vulnerability in a real production app.
followUp: Beyond just keeping the key server-side, what per-user safeguard would you add on your own backend to prevent one single user from running up a very large AI usage bill through excessive or abusive requests?

question: How would you implement a streaming response from an LLM API in the frontend, and why is streaming preferable to waiting for the full response?
concise: Rather than waiting for the entire response to be generated before showing anything, streaming sends and renders the response incrementally, token by token (or chunk by chunk) as it's generated, typically over Server-Sent Events or a chunked HTTP response the frontend reads with a ReadableStream reader, updating the UI progressively as each new piece arrives; this dramatically improves perceived responsiveness, since the user sees the answer actually beginning to appear almost immediately, rather than staring at a blank loading state for however long the full response takes to fully generate, which can be many seconds for a longer answer.
strong: For anything longer than a very short response, generating the complete answer server-side before sending anything back to the client means the user perceives the entire generation time as pure, unproductive waiting, a blank spinner with zero feedback, even though the model may have already generated a perfectly readable first sentence or two within the first second; streaming instead sends each piece of the response to the frontend as soon as it's actually generated, so the user sees text appearing progressively, almost immediately, which both feels dramatically faster (even though the total time to the very last token might be similar) and lets the user start reading and processing the answer well before it's even fully finished generating. On the frontend, this typically means making a request that returns a streamed response (often using the Server-Sent Events format, or a plain chunked response) and reading it incrementally using the Fetch API's ReadableStream reader, appending each new chunk of text to the displayed message as it arrives, rather than making one single request-response call and waiting for the entire body before rendering anything at all. A few practical details matter for building this well: handling the stream being interrupted or erroring partway through gracefully (showing what was received so far, plus a clear error rather than silently cutting off), and, for accessibility, making sure the incrementally-updating text is announced sensibly to screen reader users (typically via a properly-configured aria-live region, tuned carefully so it doesn't announce every single incremental token change individually in an overwhelming, unusable way, but rather in reasonably-sized, sensible chunks).
weak: A weak answer implements a plain, single request-response call and shows a generic loading spinner until the entire response is fully generated, missing the significant perceived-performance benefit that incremental streaming provides for anything beyond a very short response.
followUp: How would you handle a screen reader user's experience with a streaming, progressively-updating chat response, given that naively announcing every single incremental text update would be overwhelming and unusable?

question: How would you handle rate limits and cost control for a frontend feature that calls an LLM API on behalf of many users?
concise: Enforce per-user (and possibly per-organization) rate limits and usage caps on your own backend, independent of and in addition to whatever rate limit the AI provider itself enforces at the account level, since the provider's limit protects your account as a whole but doesn't by itself prevent one individual user from monopolizing a disproportionate share of that shared capacity or cost; surface rate-limit and cost-related errors to the user with clear, specific, actionable UI feedback (like 'you've reached your usage limit for today, try again at X' or a graceful queued/degraded response) rather than a generic, confusing failure, and design the feature to degrade gracefully (falling back to a simpler, non-AI experience, or clearly communicating a temporary limitation) rather than breaking entirely when a limit is hit.
strong: The AI provider's own rate limit is typically set at the level of your whole account or API key, so it protects you from your application as a whole exceeding some ceiling, but it says nothing at all about how that shared capacity and cost gets divided fairly among your many individual end users; without your own separate, application-level enforcement, a single user (or a bot, or an abusive script) making a very large number of requests could consume a disproportionate share of your account's total capacity or cost, effectively degrading or completely blocking the experience for every other legitimate user, or simply running up an unexpectedly large bill on its own. I'd implement genuine per-user (and, if relevant, per-organization or per-plan-tier) usage tracking and enforcement on my own backend, a specific number of requests or tokens allowed per user per day or per billing period, tracked in a database or a fast counter store, checked before making the actual upstream call to the AI provider, and rejecting (or gracefully degrading) requests that would exceed that specific user's own limit, independent of whether the provider's own account-wide limit has been reached yet. When a limit is actually hit, the frontend should show a clear, specific, actionable message, telling the user exactly what happened and, ideally, exactly when they'll be able to try again, rather than a confusing generic error that looks like the feature is simply broken. I'd also think about graceful degradation as a real design goal, if the AI-powered part of a feature is temporarily unavailable due to a rate limit or a cost cap being hit, does the rest of the feature (or a simpler, non-AI fallback) still work reasonably well, rather than the entire feature becoming completely unusable the moment that specific limit is reached.
weak: A weak answer relies purely on the AI provider's own account-level rate limit as the only safeguard, without implementing any separate, application-level per-user usage tracking, which leaves the feature exposed to one abusive or heavy user degrading or exhausting shared capacity for every other legitimate user.
followUp: How would you design the specific per-user limit itself, for example a fixed number of requests per day versus a token-based budget, and what are the trade-offs between those two approaches?

question: When reviewing a pull request that was substantially written by an AI coding assistant, what specific questions would you ask the author, and how does this change your review process, if at all?
concise: The actual code should be reviewed with the same rigor as any other pull request, correctness, tests, security, fit with existing conventions, regardless of who or what wrote the initial draft, since once it's submitted for review it's the author's own responsibility, not the AI's; what's worth specifically asking about is whether the author actually understands the logic well enough to explain and maintain it themselves (not just that it happened to pass tests or look plausible), whether they specifically verified any external API calls or library usage the AI generated against real, current documentation (given the risk of hallucinated or outdated APIs), and whether security- and correctness-sensitive parts received genuinely careful manual scrutiny rather than being accepted purely because the AI's suggestion looked clean and plausible.
strong: I review the pull request itself exactly as rigorously as I would any other, correctness, test coverage, adherence to the codebase's actual existing conventions, and security implications, since the code's origin doesn't change what actually matters once it's proposed as a change to the shared codebase, and the person submitting it is fully responsible for it regardless of how it was originally drafted. Where I do specifically probe further is by asking the author direct questions to confirm genuine understanding, not just that the code happens to work, but why this specific approach was chosen, what happens in a particular edge case, or what a particular piece of logic is actually doing, since a real risk with AI-assisted code is an author submitting something that passed tests and looks plausible without having genuinely internalized or verified the reasoning behind it themselves, which becomes a real liability later when that same code needs to be debugged, modified, or extended and the original author can't actually explain how it works. I'd also specifically ask whether any external API or library usage in the diff was verified against current, real documentation, given the known risk of a plausible-looking but subtly outdated or entirely hallucinated method or parameter, and I'd apply extra manual scrutiny myself to anything security- or correctness-critical in the diff (auth, payments, input validation) regardless of how confident or clean the surrounding code looks, treating AI-assisted origin as a specific reason for a bit more diligence in exactly those areas, not less.
weak: A weak answer either applies noticeably less scrutiny to a pull request because 'the AI already checked it', or conversely rejects AI-assisted code out of hand regardless of its actual quality, rather than reviewing the actual code on its genuine merits while specifically probing for genuine understanding and verified correctness.
followUp: How would you respond if an author couldn't actually explain why a specific, non-trivial piece of AI-generated logic in their own pull request works the way it does?
